To this well, then, that is, to faith in Christ, the Law calls us together. For he himself says: "Moses wrote of me." For what does it call us together? That we may drink the waters and sing to it a song, that is, that we may believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Initiate the well for it," it says. This is the sense: set, it says, the well as the beginning of all things, just as the Apostle also says that "he is the beginning, and the firstborn of every creature, and in him all things were created." Initiate the well for it, therefore — that is, confess the well to be the beginning of all things. But it can also be understood in this way, that the words seem to be directed from the person of Moses, exhorting the people and saying: Give a beginning to your heart, that it may begin to understand what the well is, from which the spiritual waters are to be drawn and by which the people of believers is to be refreshed. Initiate this well, therefore, for it, that is, for Israel, so that whoever sees God with the heart may be able to draw the mystical sense from the depths. That Moses, that is the Law, should gather us to this well does not seem to be said in vain. For it can happen that someone may seem to come to this well, but unless he is gathered through Moses, he is not accepted by God. Marcion seems to himself to have come to this well, and Basilides and Valentinus, but because they did not come through Moses nor receive the Law and the prophets, they cannot praise the Lord God from the fountains of Israel. Therefore those who are of this kind do not come to the well which the princes dug and the kings hewed out. But do you wish me to show you from the Scriptures to what wells these men come? There is a certain salt valley, in which valley are wells of bitumen; every heresy therefore and every sin is in a valley, and in a salt valley. For sin and iniquity does not ascend upward, but always descends to the lowest and infernal places. Every heretical understanding, therefore, and every act of sin is both set in a valley and salt and bitter. For what sweet, what pleasant thing can sin have? But it has something even more. For if you come to a heretical opinion, if you come to the bitterness of sin, you have come to the wells of bitumen. Bitumen is food and nourishment for fire. If therefore you too taste water from these wells, if you take up a heretical understanding, if you receive the bitterness of sin, you will prepare within yourself the kindling of fire and the burnings of Gehenna. And therefore to those who are unwilling to drink water from that well which the princes dig and the kings, but from these which are in the valley of sin and feed the fuel of fire, it is said: "Walk in the light of your fire and of the flame which you have kindled for yourselves." What, then, is sung at this well? "Initiate the well for it," it says; "the princes dug it, the kings hewed it out." The princes and the kings can indeed seem to be the same; but if it is necessary to distinguish them, let us understand the princes as the prophets. For they placed the meaning and prophecy concerning Christ dug down and submerged in the depth of the letter, and therefore one of them said: "Unless you hear in secret, your soul will weep." And likewise another prophet says to the Lord: "How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!" These, then, are the princes who dug this well, but the kings are those who hewed it out. That it said "hewed out" (excuderunt) is said from "hammering out" (excudere), not from "cutting away" (excidere); for that is said to be "hammered out" which is either cut or shaped in stone. The princes therefore, as being somewhat inferior, are said to dig the well, that is, as it were to sink a certain depth in the softness of the earth. But these, whom it calls kings, as being stronger and more eminent, penetrate not only the depth of the earth but also the hardness of the rock, that they may be able to reach the deeper waters and, if it may be said, search out in it the very veins of the abyss, knowing that the judgments of God are a great abyss. These kings, then, who can search out things so deep and so hidden of the well, we may rightly call the Apostles, one of whom said: "But to us God has revealed it through the Holy Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God." Because, therefore, through the Spirit they too can search out the deep things of God and penetrate the high and deep mysteries of the well, they are for that reason said to be kings, who hewed out this well even in the rock and penetrated the hard and difficult secrets of knowledge. That the Apostles too can be called kings, I think can easily be proved from this, which is said of all believers: "But you are a royal race, a great priesthood, a holy nation." If, then, they call kings those who believed through their word, how much more are they themselves to be held as kings, who make kings? But from this too it is easily gathered: for if kings are named from ruling, then certainly all who rule the churches of God will rightly be called kings, but much more rightly those who by their words and writings rule even those very men by whom the churches are ruled. And on account of this the Lord is rightly called King of kings; for unless these and the rest who imitate them are kings, he will not appear as King of kings. But the Apostle Paul himself too, writing to the Corinthians and rebuking them as it were with a certain irony, says: "Without us you reign; and would that you did reign, that we too might reign with you." In which he certainly declares that the Corinthians ought to be kings and that he himself wishes to reign with them, but he reproaches their elation over an honor not yet assumed according to merit. All these princes, then, dig this well, and the kings of the nations hew it out; for the Apostles are especially the kings of the nations, who gathered the nations to the obedience of faith and laid open the knowledge of Christ to all — in whom are the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God hidden — going around the circle of the earth according to the command of the Lord and fulfilling what was commanded, that they should teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; and by these things they hewed out, that is, laid open the knowledge of the well and brought it into the knowledge of all the nations. But these things too which we now have in hand, which have been recited to us, are a well, and all the scripture of the Law and the prophets together; the Evangelical and Apostolic scripture also, all together, is one well, which they cannot dig or hew out unless they are found to be kings and princes. For truly they are to be held kings, truly princes, who can remove the earth from this well and take away the surface of the letter and from the inner rock, where Christ is, bring forth the spiritual senses like living water. This, therefore, it is fitting that those alone do who are either kings or princes; called kings from this, that they have driven out the reign of sin from their body and have prepared the reign of righteousness in their members. For it is fitting that he teach others who has first done the very things which he teaches. For thus it is written: "Whoever shall do and shall so teach men, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven." But to be great in the kingdom, this is to be a king. "The kings of the nations hewed it out," it says — in their kingdom, while they ruled over them. For in very truth they cannot dig this well nor open the hidden veins of living water, unless they have first held dominion over the barbarous nations. For everything whatsoever that was wild in them in their acts, whatever was barbarous in their conduct — if they have tamed it and subjected it to the royal understanding and held dominion over it, so that henceforth they act not like the heathen but lawfully — these are truly kings, probing the depths of the well and searching out the hidden and mystical things of the Word of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After these things "they set out," he says, "from the well to Mattanah, and from Mattanah to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamoth, and from Bamoth to the grove which is in the field of Moab, from the top of the hewn mountain that looks toward the face of the desert." These names, which appear to be the designations of places, seem — from their significations, which they denote in their own tongue — to display the sequence of things rather mystical rather than merely a naming of places. "For having set out," he says, "from the well they come to Mattanah." For Mattanah is interpreted "their gifts." You see, then, that if anyone has drunk from this well which the kings and princes dug, he straightway advances to this, that he has gifts to offer to God. But what is it that a person offers to God? This very thing which is written in the law: "my gifts, my offerings." From those things, therefore, which God has given, human beings nonetheless make offerings to God. What did God give to man? Knowledge of himself. What does man offer to God? His faith and his affection. This is what God seeks from man. And indeed it is thus written: "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, except that you fear the Lord your God, and walk in his ways, and love him, and keep all his commandments, and serve the Lord your God with your whole heart and with your whole soul?" These are the gifts, these the offerings which ought to be given to the Lord. And we give to the Lord these gifts of our heart after we have come to know him and have drunk from the depth of his well the knowledge of his goodness. Observe, however, how the prophet said: "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you?" Let these words put to shame those who deny that it lies within man's choice that he be saved. For how would God ask of man, unless man had within his own power that which he ought to offer to God who asks? There are, then, things which are given by God, and there are things which are furnished by man. For example, it lay within the man to make one mina into ten minas, or one mina into five minas; but it was from God that the man had a mina from which he could make ten minas. But when he offered from himself the ten minas, he received in turn from God no longer money, but power and rule over ten cities. Again God asks of Abraham that he offer to him his son Isaac upon a mountain, whichever one he should show him. Abraham offered his only-begotten undaunted, laid him upon the altar, drew the knife to slay him — he is at once restrained, and a ram is given to him for a victim in place of his son. You see, then, that the things which we offer to God remain ours, but we are asked for them to this end, that in them our affection toward God and our faith may be tested. So much for what we said, that the children of Israel set out from the well and came to Mattanah, which is interpreted "their gifts." And from Mattanah we come to Nahaliel, which is interpreted "from God." What is "from God"? After we have offered the things that are from ourselves, we come to this, that we may attain the things that are from God. For when we have offered to him our faith and our affection, then he too bestows upon us the various gifts of the Holy Spirit, of which the Apostle says: "But all things are from God." And from Nahaliel we come to Bamoth, which is interpreted "the coming of death." What coming of death do we understand here, except that by which we die together with Christ, so that we may also live together with him, and by which we ought to mortify our members which are upon the earth, and again: "for we are buried together with him through baptism into death"? If anyone, then, holds to the order of this saving way, he ought to journey through each of these things which we have recalled, and to come after many stages to this place, which we said signifies the coming of death. But, as we are taught from the Scriptures, there is a certain death that is an enemy of Christ, and a certain death that is his friend. He does not, therefore, speak of that death that is the enemy of Christ, of which it is said: "the last enemy, death, shall be destroyed," which is the devil, but of this death, by which we die together with him, so that we may also live together with him — according to which death God says: "I will kill and I will make alive." For he kills, that we may die together with Christ, and he makes alive, that we may live together with him. It is therefore to be wished by us that we come to Bamoth and most readily receive the coming of this blessed death, so that we may deserve also to be made alive with Christ. "And from Bamoth," he says, "to the grove which is in the field of Moab, from the top of the hewn mountain that looks toward the desert." If we walk by this journey, which the reasoning of our explanation has asserted consists not so much of the names of places as of the advances of the soul, after all these things we come to the grove, or, as it stands in other copies, to Janah, which is interpreted "the ascent" or "the top of the mountain." Through these things, therefore, one arrives either at that most renowned grove of the divine paradise and the pleasant delights of the ancient habitation, or certainly at the summit of perfection and the height of blessedness, so that you too may be able to say that "he raised us up together with him, and made us sit in the heavenly places in Christ." Do you see how far one arrives from the well? Do you see by what stations, or rather by what advances, the soul's journey to heaven is prepared? If you examine these things diligently, you yourself, discerning within your own self your daily advances, will perceive in what places you are and how near you are held to be to the kingdom of heaven; just as also that man of whom the Lord said that "you are not far from the kingdom of God."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After this there follows yet another narrative. For it says: "And Moses sent" — or, as it stands in some copies, "And Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites with words of peace, saying: We will pass through your land; by the road we will pass; we will not turn aside either into a field or into a vineyard. We will not drink water from your well; we will go by the royal road, until we pass your borders. And Sihon did not grant that Israel should pass through his borders; and Sihon gathered all his people, and went out to make war against Israel in the desert; and he came to Jahaz, and joined battle with Israel. And Israel struck him down with the slaughter of the sword, and they took possession of his land." The narrative indeed is plain, but let us beseech the Lord that we may be able to discern something worthy in its inner meanings. Sihon has a double interpretation, either "unfruitful tree" or "lifted up." Israel therefore sends messengers to Sihon: it sends to the unfruitful tree, it sends to the one lifted up and proud. Now this Sihon is king of the Amorites, who themselves are interpreted as "those bringing into bitterness" or "speaking." Moses therefore sends to Sihon king of the Amorites with words of peace, saying: "We will pass through your land." If, according to the spiritual understanding, we say that Sihon the king holds the figure of the devil, because he himself is lifted up and unfruitful, I think you ought not to wonder that I have called him a king, since you hear even our very Lord and Savior in the Gospels saying concerning him: "Behold, now comes the prince of this world, and in me he will find nothing," and again: "Behold, now the prince of this world shall be cast out." If therefore he is called in the Gospels the prince of the whole world, it ought not to seem absurd if he is compared to Sihon king of the Amorites, or even to any other kings of the nations whatsoever. But he is called prince of the world not because he created the world, but because there are many sinners in this world. And because he himself is the prince of sin, therefore he has also been called the prince of the world — namely, among those who, not yet abandoning the world, are converted to the Father. For it is according to this that that also is said: "the whole world is set in wickedness." For what does it profit us to say that our prince is Christ, if by our deeds and works we are convicted that the devil holds the princedom in us? Or is it not plain under which prince the unchaste, the incestuous, the unjust man acts? Can a man of this sort say that, set under Christ, he does these things, even if he seems to be reckoned under the name of Christ? In whom Christ bears the princedom, there no uncleanness, no iniquity is admitted, nor can unjust desire have any place. According to this manner, then, rightly will Christ be called the prince of the virtues, and the devil of malice and of all iniquity. Israel therefore sends messengers to the king of the Amorites, the king of those who provoke into bitterness, the unfruitful king, the proud king. In what way will the devil be shown to be proud, in what way lifted up? He it is who said: "By my strength I will act, and by the wisdom of my understanding I will remove the borders of the nations, and I will plunder their might; and I will shake the cities which are inhabited, and the whole circle of the earth I will take in my hand like a nest." And again this lifted-up and proud one says: "I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of heaven I will set my throne, I will sit upon a lofty mountain above the high mountains which are toward the north, I will ascend above the clouds, and I will be like the Most High." Do you still ask whether he himself is lifted up and proud? Nay rather, both he himself is proud and lifted up, and that one who is, as it were, his only-begotten, of whom it is written that "he shall be exalted above everything that is called God or that is worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself off as though he were God." Everyone therefore who is lifted up and proud is either a son of this lifted-up one, or a disciple and imitator. And for this reason the Apostle says concerning a certain one: "lest perhaps, being lifted up, he fall into the judgment of the devil," showing by this that everyone who is lifted up will be condemned by a like judgment, as the devil is. We therefore are those who wish to pass through this world, that we may be able to arrive at the holy land, which has been promised to the saints; and we send with words of peace to Sihon, promising that we will not dwell in his land nor tarry with him, but only pass through and walk by the royal road, nor turn aside anywhere, neither into a field nor into a vineyard, but that we will not even drink water from his well. Let us see, then, when we promised these things, when we announced these words to the devil. Let each of the faithful call to mind, when he first came to the waters of baptism, when he received the first seals of the faith and approached the fountain of salvation, what words he then used there and what he announced to the devil: that he would not make use of his pomps, nor of his works, nor at all yield to any of his services and pleasures. And this is what is foreshadowed in these words of the law, that Israel would not turn aside either into his field or into his vineyard, but that it promises it will not drink water even from his well. For no longer will the faithful one take the cup of diabolical instruction, not of astrology, not of magic, not at all of any teaching which teaches anything against the piety of God. For he has his own fountains, and Israel drinks from the fountains, drinks from the fountains of salvation; he does not drink water from the well of Sihon, nor, forsaking the fountain of living water, does he gather for himself broken cisterns. But he also professes that he will walk by the royal road. What is the royal road? That one, without doubt, which says: "I am the way and the truth and the life." And rightly royal; for it is he of whom the prophet says: "God, give your judgment to the king." By the royal road, therefore, one must walk, nor turn aside anywhere, neither into his field nor into his vineyard — that is, the mind of the faithful ought no longer to turn aside either to diabolical works or to diabolical senses. In what way, then, do we wish to pass through the borders of the Amorites with peace? The Amorites can be taken as the portion of the unbelievers who are in this world; but these are interpreted, as we said above, either as "those bringing into bitterness" or "speaking." And in what way indeed the unbelievers and the incredulous bring God into bitterness needs no exposition; but what he says, "speaking," can be drawn to that part, that all who are unbelieving and act under the devil as prince know only how to speak, but they speak empty things. For example, as their poets, as the astrologers, as some even of the philosophers, who speak things empty and vain. But the kingdom of the faithful, which is from God, is not in speech, but in power. We therefore wish to pass through the world peacefully, but this very thing rather incites the prince of the world, that we say we are unwilling to remain with him nor to tarry nor to wish to touch anything of his; from that he is the more exasperated, from that he is provoked and grows angry and stirs up persecutions against us, rouses dangers, threatens torments. And therefore it says: "Sihon," it says, "gathered all his people, and went out to fight against Israel." Who is all the people of Sihon, whom he stirs up against Israel? The princes and judges of the world and all the ministers of wickedness, who always assail and persecute the people of God. But what does Israel do? "It came," it says, "to Jahaz." Jahaz is interpreted "the fulfilling of the commandment." If therefore we too come to this place, that is, to the fulfilling of the commandments, even if that lifted-up and proud Sihon, the devil, come against us with his whole army and fight against us, if he stir up all his demons against us, we overcome him, if we fulfill the commandments of God. For to fulfill the commandments is to overcome the devil and his whole army. And then there will be fulfilled in us the prayer of the Apostle, in which he says: "But God will crush Satan under your feet speedily," and that which the Lord says: "Behold, I give you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you." For all these things will be able to do us no harm, if we come to Jahaz, that is, if we keep the commandments and precepts of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Yesterday we spoke of how Sihon, king of the Amorites, who is the lofty one and the barren tree, having engaged with Israel was defeated; concerning whom Scripture also says pointedly that he fell "by the slaughter of the sword" or, as we read elsewhere, "by the mouth of the sword." But if you wish to know more carefully by what sword this barren and lofty one, "like the cedar of Lebanon," fell, let us learn from the Apostle Paul, who says: "For the word of God is living and effective and more piercing than any sword," and again in another place: "and the sword," he says, "of the spirit, which is the word of God." By the slaughter of this sword, then, fell the spiritual Sihon, who is the devil. After these things it is added: "and the sons of Israel," he says, "had dominion over all his land." All this earthly region indeed is called the land of Sihon, but Christ and his Church have dominion over all the land of Sihon. "And they had dominion from Arnon as far as Jabbok." Arnon and Jabbok were cities of the kingdom of Sihon, but the beginning of his kingdom was Arnon and the end was Jabbok, and therefore it is said that "they had dominion from Arnon as far as Jabbok." Now Arnon is interpreted "their curses"; the beginning, therefore, of the kingdom of this lofty and barren Sihon is curses. But the end is Jabbok, which is interpreted "wrestling"; for it is necessary that everyone who wishes to go out from the kingdom of the devil and to escape his borders should find wrestling, and that contests be stirred up against him by his ministers and satellites. But if he has wrestled and conquered, then Jabbok will no longer be a city of Sihon, but will be a city of Israel. This is doubtless what we read also concerning the patriarch Jacob, since, when he had come to a certain place, a wrestling was prepared for him, and there, when he had wrestled the whole night and had prevailed and grown strong before God, his name was called Israel. "And Israel took," he says, "all these cities; and Israel dwelt in all the cities of the Amorites." This Israel, who is Israel in Christ, who is Israel not in the flesh, nor a Jew in what is manifest, he himself dwells in all the cities of the Amorites when in all the world the churches of Christ are being propagated. But each one of us also was formerly a city of King Sihon, the lofty king; for there reigned in us folly, pride, impiety, and all the things that are on the devil's side; but when the strong one was overcome and vanquished and his vessels plundered, we were made cities of Israel and the inheritance of the saints—if indeed that power which formerly ruled over us has been utterly cut off in us, and the barren tree has been cut down, and the lofty king has been cast down, and we are under that king who says: "learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart." After these things he now enumerates one by one the cities of the proud and barren king, and says: "in Heshbon and in all its neighboring places." What is this, that he named Heshbon as the chief city of the kingdom of Sihon? Heshbon is interpreted "thoughts." Rightly, then, does the greatest part of the diabolical kingdom and the greater part of its power reign in thoughts; for so the Lord also said: "out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies; and these are the things that defile a man." And therefore this city is necessarily set ablaze and consumed by fire. By what fire? Surely by that of which the Savior says: "I came to send fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it be kindled!"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But after a few words it is reported concerning that very city: "For this reason," he says, "the riddlers shall say: come into Heshbon, that the city of Sihon may be built and constructed; for fire went forth from Heshbon and a flame from the city of Sihon, and it devoured as far as Moab." Sihon, as we said, was the king, whose city was Heshbon. Thus, then, the order of the words is to be understood, that these riddlers say: come, that Heshbon, which was the city of Sihon, may be built and constructed. But let us now inquire who these riddlers are. A riddle is a figured saying; riddlers therefore are those who speak figuratively. And who else is there who has spoken in figures except the law and the prophets? For hear how David says: "I will open my mouth in parables, I will utter propositions from the beginning." But Isaiah too, that the things he wrote are riddles, declares in this manner: "and the words of this book shall be," he says, "like the words of a sealed book; which if they give into the hands of a man who does not know letters and say to him: read, he will say: I do not know letters. But if they give it to one who knows letters, he will say: I cannot read, for it is sealed." Now the book is called sealed for the reason that it is entangled with figures and wrapped up in riddles. These riddlers, then, say: come into Heshbon, that it may be built. That first Heshbon fell, or rather was overturned and burned; another is to be rebuilt. But how this is done, let us show by taking up an example. If you see a Gentile placed in the disgrace of life and in the error of religion, do not hesitate to say of him that here is the city of Heshbon in the kingdom of King Sihon; for the barren and lofty king reigns in his thoughts. If Israel—that is, a son of the Church—approaches this man and applies the darts of the word of God and unsheathes against him the sword of the spirit, and destroys in him all the fortifications of Gentile teachings and burns up the loftinesses of his arguments with the fire of truth, say of this man that the city of Heshbon of Sihon is overthrown. But this man, in whom the teachings of the Gentiles are overthrown, is not straightway left deserted and abandoned. For it is not the discipline of the sons of Israel to leave in ruins the cities that they have destroyed; but when they have undermined and overturned in a man his evil thoughts and impious sentiments, they build again in the heart of him whom they have destroyed good thoughts, pious sentiments; they will implant the doctrine of truth, they will hand on the rite of religion, they will teach the order of living, honesty of morals, they will show the statutes of observance. And then these riddlers will truly say to one another in turn: come and let us build Heshbon, which was the city of Sihon. For they themselves too—that is, the sons of the Church—because they understand the figures of the law and the riddles spiritually, are called riddlers. This is what Jeremiah also designates by a no less figurative saying, where it is said to him by the Lord: "behold, I have put my words in your mouth; behold, I have appointed you this day over the nations and kingdoms, to root up and to overturn and to rebuild and to replant." What does he root up and what does he overturn? The city of Heshbon, which was Sihon's. What does he root up in it and what does he overturn? Impious and impure thoughts. What does he rebuild in it and what does he replant? Pious and chaste thoughts, so that Heshbon may be made a city not of the Amorites, but of the sons of Israel.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But if we wish to pursue each point, we shall be shut out from the discussion of those things which were read to us concerning Balaam; the reading of which is of such difficulty that we can scarcely arrive at explaining the account and sequence of the history itself. How great, then, will now be our difficulty in explaining the spiritual senses, if the very surface of the letter is wrapped in such great difficulties? But although desire snatches us toward discussing the things which are more obscure, nevertheless these things also, which are reported in between, are not to be entirely passed over. For after the sons of Israel had obtained the cities of the Amorites, they went up also by the way which leads into Bashan, where Og, king of Bashan, was; but to this one they neither deign to send envoys nor to ask of him that they may pass through his land, but immediately they clash with him and overcome both him and his people. Let us see, then, what Bashan is. Bashan is interpreted "baseness"; rightly, then, are neither envoys sent to that nation nor is passage through its land requested. For there ought to be for us no passage, no approach to baseness, but from the very beginning at once it must be assaulted and in every way guarded against. Now Og, who is said to be king of Bashan, is interpreted "enclosure." This can hold the figure of all carnal and material things, by love and desire of which the soul, being held fast, is shut out and separated from God. Against these, therefore, war is commanded to be waged in such a way that "you shall not leave," he says, "of him one living"; for none must be left by the sons of Israel living in the kingdom of baseness and disgrace. But it befits Israelite virtue to cut down and cut away base things and to rebuild in the soul whatever is pious and to plant honorable and religious things. Concerning the kingdom of Sihon it is not written that no living one be left, nor concerning the kingdom of Moab; for perhaps we have need of some of them, and we require certain of them for the contests and exercises of this life; otherwise we should have had to go out of this world. Of Bashan, however—that is, of baseness—we have need of none whatsoever; let us leave nothing of it; all things must be cut down, all the works of baseness must be overturned; for in nothing can that which is base be honorable.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And the sons of Israel, having set out from there, pitched their camp to the west of Moab beside the Jordan opposite Jericho. And when Balak, son of Zippor, saw," and the rest. Now all the things which are written concerning Balaam and his donkey are a history full of business; but the inner meaning is much more laborious, and I do not know whether it is even easy to explain merely the historical statements themselves. Yet, with God granting, we shall touch briefly on what we can. War is threatening you, O king Balak, son of Zippor; six hundred thousand armed men are rushing upon your borders. It behooved you also to prepare arms, to muster an army, to think about the drawing up of battle, so that you might meet the enemy, while still placed at a distance, equipped with arms. But you send to Balaam the diviner and send many gifts and promise greater ones and say: "come, curse for me the people that has gone out from Egypt." But Balaam, as Scripture teaches, referred these things to God, by whom also he is forbidden to come. But again the king sends envoys and, arms neglected, places all his hope in Balaam, that he may come and deliver words and hurl curses against the people in place of weapons, if perhaps the people, whom the king's army could not overcome, might be conquered by the words of Balaam. What consistency does this history have, what counsel does it show? Where or when was it heard that any of kings, with battle threatening him, having set aside his arms and neglected his army, took refuge in the words of some diviner or soothsayer? Whence again and again the grace of God must be implored by us, that we may be able to explain these things not by fabulous and Jewish narrations, but by rational senses worthy of the divine law. First of all, then, it must be confessed that in certain matters words can do more and avail more than bodies, since what the army of many nations could not accomplish, what could not be obtained by iron and arms, this is accomplished by words; and I do not say by holy words or words of God, but by certain words which are held among men, which how I should name I do not know; yet they are composed by a useless art, of which art let that be the name which each pleases to call it. There is, then, as I said, among men some work that is accomplished by words; which work, however, is such that it cannot be fulfilled by however great the strength of body. For example, there were in Egypt enchanters and magicians. Who among men can by strength of body change a rod into a serpent, which is reported to have been done by them, or who can by the powers of body turn water into blood? Yet the enchanters and magicians of the Egyptians did this. For Moses had first done these things; but because the king of Egypt knew that these things could be done by a certain art of words which is held among men, he thought that Moses too had done these things not by the power of God, but by magical art, and that what he had done by human art, this he was pretending to be done by the power of God. He immediately summons the enchanters and magicians of the Egyptians. Between him who was working by the power of God and those who were invoking demons he makes there be a contest. Yet the contrary power likewise makes the rod a serpent, as the power of God had done; but the serpent which had been made by the power of God swallowed up and devoured all those serpents which by magical art had been turned from rods into serpents: for the demonic power could not restore to good the evil which it had made out of good. It could make a serpent out of a rod, but it could not give back a rod out of the serpent; and therefore all are consumed by that rod which by the power of God had been turned into a serpent. But afterward, by the divine power, it is restored to its own nature, so that it might confess the Lord of nature. The enchanters of the Egyptians made water too be turned into blood, but they could not again turn blood into water; but the power of God turned not water, but the whole river into blood, and again, at the prayer of Moses, gave it back with clear and natural streams. And again the magicians of the Egyptians produced gnats, but they could not drive them away; but Moses both produced gnats and took them away; for our God both causes grief and again restores; but the contrary power can indeed do something evil, but it cannot restore to wholeness. Now we have sent all these things ahead, so that we may be able to observe the works of Balaam or his words; for there are also certain differences among magicians; for some avail more, others less. This Balaam was most famous in the magical art and most powerful in noxious incantations. For he did not have the power or art of words for blessing, but he had it for cursing; for demons are invited to cursing, not to blessing. And therefore, as one experienced in such things, he was held in repute by all who were in the East. For unless very many experiments of his had gone before—that he had frequently by curses routed an armed enemy—the king would surely not have presumed that this could be done by words which could scarcely be fulfilled by iron and the battle-line. Balak, then, being certain of this and having frequently made trial of it, setting aside all the instruments and aids of war, sends envoys to him, saying: "behold, a people has gone out from Egypt, and has covered the face of the earth; and this one has settled beside me." But I think also something more that moved the king; for he seems to have heard that the sons of Israel are accustomed to conquer their enemies by prayer, not by arms, and not so much by iron as by prayers. For Israel moved no arms against Pharaoh, but it was said to him: "the Lord will fight for you, and you shall be silent." But neither against the Amalekites did the force of arms avail so much as the prayer of Moses. For when Moses lifted up his hands to God, Amalek was conquered; but when they were let down and lowered, they made Israel to be conquered. These things surely Balak, king of Moab, had heard. For it is written: "the nations heard and were angry; pangs seized those who dwell in Philistia. Then the leaders of Edom hastened and the princes of the Moabites; trembling laid hold of them." You see that there had come to them what Moses foretold in the Canticle, when they crossed the Red Sea. The king of Moab, then, had heard that this people conquers by prayers and fights against its enemies with the mouth, not with the sword; and on account of this, without doubt, he thought within himself, saying: since indeed no arms can be matched against the prayers and supplications of this people, therefore for me too such prayers and such arms of words and such prayers must be sought as can overcome the prayers of these people.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But that you may know that the king thought something of this sort, understand it from the words of Scripture, which I learned expounded by a certain teacher who had come to believe from among the Hebrews. It is written thus: "And Moab said to the elders of Midian: now this assembly will lick up all who are round about us, as the calf licks up the grass of the field." That teacher, then, who had come to believe from among the Hebrews, would say: why, he says, did he use such an example, saying: as the calf licks up the grass of the field? For this reason, without doubt, because the calf breaks off the grass from the field with its mouth and with its tongue, as with a sickle, cuts whatever it finds; so also this people, like a calf, fights with mouth and lips and has its arms in words and prayers. Knowing this, therefore, the king sends to Balaam, that he too may deliver words contrary to words and prayers against prayers. And do not wonder if there is something of this sort in the magical art; for Scripture too indicates that this art exists, but forbids the use of it. For Scripture indicates also that demons exist, but forbids that they be worshipped and entreated. Rightly, then, it also forbids the use of magic, because the ministers of magicians are apostate angels and malign spirits and unclean demons; for none of the holy spirits obeys a magician. A magician cannot invoke Michael, he cannot invoke Raphael nor Gabriel; much more can a magician not invoke Almighty God nor his Son Jesus Christ our Lord nor his Holy Spirit. We alone have received the power of invoking God the Father; we alone have the power of invoking his only-begotten Jesus Christ. But this is what I say: he who has now received the power of invoking Christ cannot again invoke demons, and he who has been made a partaker of the Holy Spirit ought not further to summon unclean spirits; for if he invokes unclean spirits, the Holy Spirit flees from him. They are magicians who invoke Beelzebul. In fact, that people knew this, and therefore, lying against my Lord Jesus and saying false things, they said: "this man casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons." But the Savior, knowing that it is indeed true that a certain Beelzebul is prince of demons, did not in this convict them of falsehood, but answered them: "if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out?" Whence it is established that there are certain evil demons who, when invoked by magicians, are present to them for evil, not for good; for they are ready to do harm, but they do not know how to do good. These demons, then, by a certain art and composition of words, had passed, so to speak, into friendship with Balaam, and, relying on their friendships, he seemed great among men. On account of this, therefore, the king sends to him and says: "come now, and curse for me this people, for it is stronger than we, if perhaps we may be able to strike some of them and drive them out from the land." It seems to me that this king does not entirely trust in Balaam the diviner, being, I believe, greatly terrified by the report of the mighty deeds that had been done among the people of God; and therefore he says, if perhaps the curses of Balaam may prevail even to this extent, that he may be able to strike some of them, and to put the rest to flight, terrified, and drive them from their own land.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We meanwhile say that by a certain dispensation and wisdom of God all things in this world are so arranged that absolutely nothing is idle with God, whether it be evil, whether it be good. But let us explain more plainly what is said. God did not make wickedness; yet, though he could prohibit it when it has been invented by others, he does not prohibit it, but uses it, together with those very ones by whom it is held, for necessary purposes. For through those very persons in whom wickedness is, he makes those illustrious and approved who strive toward the glory of the virtues. For if wickedness were destroyed, there would surely be no one to oppose the virtues. But virtue, having nothing contrary to it, would not shine forth, nor become more splendid and more tested. And a virtue not proved nor tested is not even a virtue. But if these things be said without the testimonies of the divine words, they will seem contrived rather and composed by human art than true and beyond doubt. Let us therefore inquire whether the divine volumes also contain a meaning of this kind. Let us come to Joseph. Take away the wickedness of his brothers, take away envy, take away all that parricidal scheme by which they raged against their brother, to the point of selling him: if you take these away, see how great a dispensation of God you will at the same time have destroyed; for you will at the same time cut off all those things that were done in Egypt through Joseph for the salvation of all. There would have been no interpretation of Pharaoh's dream, if through the envy of his brothers Joseph had not been sold away and come into Egypt; no one would have understood what God had revealed to the king, no one would have gathered grain in Egypt, no one would have provided for the necessity of the famine by wise foresight; Egypt would have perished, the neighboring regions too would have perished by famine, Israel itself and its seed would have perished, and seeking bread it would not have entered Egypt, nor would the sons of Israel have gone out from it with the wonders of the Lord; nowhere would there have been the plagues upon the Egyptians nor those mighty works which God did through Moses and Aaron; no one would have walked through the Red Sea with dry footsteps; mortal life would not have known the food of manna; no streams of waters would have burst forth from the following rock; the law would not have been given by God to men; the things that are recounted in Exodus, in Leviticus, in Numbers too and Deuteronomy would not have come to the knowledge of the human race; certainly no one would have entered the paternal inheritance and the land of promise. And, to come to these things which are in hand, take away the wickedness of Balak, this most evil king, by which he desires to curse Israel, remove his cunning, by which he invites Balaam to curse the people: you will likewise have taken away God's dispensation toward the sons of Israel and the favor of his providence, and nowhere will those prophecies exist which through the mouth of Balaam are prophesied both to the sons of Israel and to the nations. But if you desire this to be confirmed also by testimonies of the New Testament, if you take away the wickedness of Judas and destroy his betrayal, you will likewise have taken away the cross of Christ and his passion; and if there be no cross, the principalities and powers are not stripped, nor are they triumphed over on the wood of the cross. If there had been no death of Christ, surely there would have been no resurrection either, nor would anyone have existed as the firstborn from the dead. But if there had been no firstborn from the dead, neither would there have been for us any hope of resurrection. In a like manner, then, let us suppose concerning the devil himself, for instance, that he had been constrained by some necessity, so as not to sin, or that after his sin the will to wickedness had been taken away from him: there would at the same time surely have been taken away from us the contest against the wiles of the devil, nor would a crown of victory be looked for by him who had lawfully striven. If we did not have those who resist us, there would be no contests, nor would prizes be set up for the victors, nor would the kingdom of heaven be prepared for those who conquer, nor would this momentary and light burden of our tribulation work for us beyond measure a weight of glory in the future, nor would any of us hope, for the endurance of tribulations, for the immense glory of things to come. From all which it is gathered that God uses not only good things for a good work, but also evil things; and this is truly marvelous, that God uses evil vessels for a good work. For in this great house of the world there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and of clay; and some indeed unto honor, but others unto dishonor, yet both necessary. But since these vessels of which we speak are to be understood as rational and of free choice, not by chance nor by accident is each one made either a vessel of honor or a vessel of dishonor, but he who has shown himself such as to deserve to be chosen is made a chosen vessel and a vessel of honor. But he who lives by unworthy and most base thoughts, this one is formed a vessel of dishonor, not by his maker, but by himself, the causes of his own dishonor having been given. The maker, then, did not make them to be such, but he dispenses minds of this kind according to their purpose by the justice of his providence and by a certain ineffable reason. Just as, for instance, in great cities, if there are men more unworthy and of hidden and most base life, they are condemned to work at all the meanest and most laborious tasks, and yet such tasks are necessary to the city (for example, they serve the furnaces of the bath for kindling the fires, that you may enjoy either the convenience or the delights, or they clean out the drains or perform other things of this kind, that for you the dwelling in the city may be made agreeable; and they indeed either act from their own purpose or suffer according to their deserving, yet their work is of use to those for whom the things that are good and useful are provided), so also with these things which we have set forth: God indeed did not make wickedness, yet, once it was invented by the intent of the purpose of those who turned aside from the right way, he was unwilling to take it away entirely, foreseeing this, that, even if it were useless to those who used it, he would nevertheless make it useful to those against whom it was exercised. And therefore we ought by all means to flee, lest wickedness ever be found in us; but in others we must be zealous to conquer it, not to destroy it, because even those in whom wickedness is confer some necessary work upon the universe. For nothing is idle, nothing empty with God, since either he uses the good purpose of a man for good things or he uses the evil purpose for necessary things. But you will be blessed, if rather from the virtues that are in you the universe of this life may be found to obtain some good thing from you, like those of whom the Apostle Peter says: that you may be as lights in this world, holding the word of life. Unto glory, therefore, are lights necessary to this world. And what is so delightful, what so magnificent as the work of the sun and moon, by which the world is illumined? Yet the world itself has need also of angels who are set over the beasts, and of angels who preside over earthly exercises. There is need also of angels who preside over the birth of animals, over the plantation of shrubs and plants and the rest of the increases of the fields. And again there is need of angels who preside over holy works, who teach the understanding of the eternal light and the acknowledgment of the hidden things of God and the knowledge of divine things. See, therefore, that you do not make yourself to be found among those angels who are set over the beasts, if you lead a beastly life, or among those who are set over earthly works, if you have loved bodily and earthly things. But be diligent, that you may rather be taken up into the fellowship of the angel Michael, who ever offers the prayers of the saints to God. And you will be taken up into this number or into that office, if you persist always in prayer and watch in it and fulfill what the Apostle says: "praying without ceasing." Or certainly that you may be taken up into the fellowship and office of Raphael, who presides over healing; if, when you see someone wounded by sins and pierced by the arrows of the devil, you apply the cure of words and confer the medicine of the word of God, that you may heal the wounds of sin through repentance and show the medicine of confession. He, therefore, who does works of this kind in this world, offers himself to be formed by the maker in the age to come as a vessel of election and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work; but if he does the contrary, he will offer himself as a vessel unto dishonor to the divine dispensation. And for this reason I think it is that in the divine volumes both the deeds of the good and of the evil are written, and that the divine Scriptures are woven together out of acts both on the left hand and on the right, that we may understand that with God neither the works of the evil nor of the good are idle. But now, after a very long digression, yet one necessary to the matter, let us return to our subject.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He adds moreover: "for I know," he says, "that those whom you have blessed will be blessed, and those whom you have cursed will be cursed." I do not believe that the king knew that whomever Balaam had blessed would be blessed; but it seems to me that he says these things for the sake of flattery, so that, exalting and extolling his art, he may render him more ready for the crime. For the magical art does not know how to bless, because neither do demons know how to do good. Isaac and Jacob know how to bless, and all the saints; none of the impious knows how to bless. But at length the envoys come to Balaam. For "there came," he says, "the elders of Moab and the elders of Midian, and the divinations in their hands." Among those arts of divination which human curiosity has devised, there are certain things which Scripture indeed has named "divinations," but which Gentile custom calls either tripods or cauldrons or by other terms of this kind; which, as if consecrated to this very purpose, are wont to be moved and handled by these people. Divine Scripture indeed names a certain ephod in the vernacular tongue in the prophets, which they hand down to be the garment of those who prophesy. Yet in the divine Scriptures one thing is held to be prophecy, another divination; for it says: "there shall be no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel. In due time it shall be told to Jacob and Israel what God is about to do." Divination, then, is utterly renounced; for it is fulfilled by the work and ministry of demons, as we have already said above. Balaam, therefore, having received the divinations, when the demons were wont to come to him, sees indeed that the demons are put to flight, but that God is present; and therefore he says that he is consulting God, because he nowhere sees the demons accustomed to obey him. God himself, then, comes to Balaam, not because he was worthy that God should come to him, but so that those might be put to flight who were accustomed to be present to him for cursing and doing harm; for from this point God was already providing for his people. He is present, then, and God says to him: "why have these men come to you?" And Balaam said to God: "Balak, son of Zippor, king of Moab, sent them to me, saying: behold, a people has gone out from Egypt, and has covered the face of the earth, and this one sits beside me; come now, therefore, and curse it for me, if perhaps we may be able to strike it and drive it out." And God said to Balaam: "you shall not go with them, nor shall you curse the people; for it is blessed."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There are many things that remained over for us when we were expounding the reading about Balaam and his donkey; and since it is a discourse bound by time, held in the church for the sake of edification, it did not have space enough for us to set forth each single word of Scripture in such a way that nothing at all should be left undiscussed, and to apply an explanation to each point, since indeed a style of this kind belongs rather to commentaries. Therefore those matters that seem worthy of inquiry we take up again, and, discussing them, we shall attempt to treat them with what explanation we can and to bring them into the open. But there is a further difficulty in the explanation of the history itself, namely how, when it is said that God came by night to Balaam first and asked who the men were that had come to him, and Balaam had answered that they had been sent by Balak, the son of Zippor, saying, "Come, and curse for me the people," God answered him, "You shall not go with them, nor shall you curse the people; for it is blessed"; yet again a second time it is said that God came to him by night and told him to go with them, but to observe this, that the word which God should give in his mouth, this he should speak; and again a third time, as he was going, an angel of God met him, to whom his journey seemed so far from proper or fitting that he even wished to kill him, had not the donkey, seeing the angel whom Balaam could not see, turned aside. And nevertheless, after he is blamed by the angel for having wished to go, he is again permitted by that very angel to go; only that he should keep the word which God should give in his mouth, so as to bring forth this alone and nothing further. All these things, then, have a difficult explanation; yet, as we have already said above, we shall give you in a few words occasions of understanding, so that you too may do what is written: that when these things are heard the wise may become wiser, and, "Give occasion to the wise, and he will be wiser." But before we come to the matter, we shall not even omit this, which, attending rather curiously, we observed in this place. In the letters of the Hebrews the name of God, that is God or Lord, is said to be written differently; for one thing is written for any god whatever, and another for God himself, of whom it is said: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God, God is one." This God of Israel, then, the one God and creator of all, is written with a certain fixed sign of letters, which among them is called the Tetragrammaton. Whenever, therefore, God is written in the Scriptures under this sign, there is no doubt that it is said of the true God and creator of the world. But whenever it is written with other, that is, common, letters, it is held uncertain whether it is said of the true God or of one of those of whom the Apostle says: "although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, as there are many gods and many lords; yet for us there is one God the Father, from whom are all things, and we through him." Those, then, who read the Hebrew letters say that in this place God is not set down under the sign of the Tetragrammaton; concerning which let him inquire who can. But also, as to what God said to Balaam, as if asking who those men were, it is inquired why he seems to be ignorant; and again, as to what he says: "you shall not curse the people; for it is blessed," whether it can be so understood as if he had said: "you shall not curse my people."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Here a deeper question arises, and I do not know whether it is fitting to lay bare a matter of such profound mystery and to bring it forth to the crowds—and those crowds who come to the hearing of the word of God only for a few days and immediately depart, nor tarry longer in the meditation of the word of God; yet for the sake of those who are studious and thirst to hear and are able to grasp the spiritual sense, we shall say a few things out of many. Something of this sort, then, can be objected. Suppose Balaam invokes the demons, suppose he curses the people, suppose the invoked demons do what they can: can God not defend the people from the demons and destroy their power in doing harm? What need was there, then, that he himself should come to Balaam and forbid the accustomed demons to approach, lest they even attempt or endeavor to wish to injure his people? To these things, then, although not all that can occur are to be brought forth, nevertheless we shall say in part that God does not wish to condemn the race of demons before the time. For the demons themselves also know that the present age contains their time. For this reason, in fact, they even begged the Lord that he would not torment them before the time, nor send them into the abyss. And on account of this he has not removed the devil from the principality of this age, because there is still need of his work for the perfection of those who are to be crowned; there is still need of his work for the exercises of the contests and the victories of the blessed. So, then, neither does he wish to draw away the rest of the demons violently, before the time, from the intention of their purpose; and therefore from the beginning he did not permit them to be invoked through Balaam, lest perhaps, being invoked, they should be destroyed before the time and be done away with, while God defended his people. For it is one thing if a demon requests from God someone to tempt, as in the case of Job, and receives power over him with a certain distinction—for example, that it be said to him: I give you all his goods into your power, but do not touch him himself; or again: I give you power over him, but guard his soul. And it is another thing if, at a magician's demand and with certain adjurations extorting it, the demons rage without any restriction; in which case, if freedom of will be preserved for them, they will give the people of God over to destruction; but if freedom of will be taken away, this would be to have condemned the rational creature and to have brought judgment before the time and to have hindered all those who, contending against them in the contest, could be crowned. For if freedom of will be taken from the demons, no one further will assail the athletes of Christ; but with no one assailing, there will be no contest, and with the contest removed there will be no reward, no victory. For this reason, therefore, God uses such a way, so that both the people, still untrained and who had newly begun to be drawn away from the worship of demons, may not be handed over to the demons, and responses may be delivered to the invoking magician, and the race of demons may not be stripped of the power of free will. And therefore God comes beforehand and forbids Balaam to go and to invoke the demons for cursing—if only he had ceased from his cupidity. But because he persists in the desire for money, God, indulging the freedom of will, permits him to go again, yet puts his word into his mouth, forbidding the curse to be made through the demons, so that he might give place to blessings, and in place of curses he makes Balaam bring forth blessings and prophecies, which could edify not only Israel, but also the rest of the nations. For if his prophecies have been inserted by Moses into the sacred volumes, how much more were they written down by those who dwelt then in Mesopotamia, among whom Balaam was held magnificent, and of whose art it is established that they were disciples? From him, in fact, the race and institution of the magicians is said to flourish in the regions of the East, who, having written down among themselves all the things that Balaam had prophesied, had this also in writing: that "a star shall arise out of Jacob, and a man shall spring up out of Israel." These things the magicians had in writing among themselves, and therefore, when Jesus was born, they recognized the star and understood the prophecy to be fulfilled—they, rather than the people of Israel, who despised to hear the words of the holy prophets. Those, then, from these things alone which Balaam had left in writing, recognizing that the time was at hand, came and, seeking him out, straightway adored him and, that they might declare their faith to be great, venerated a small child as if a king.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: This Balaam, as we said above, was a diviner, foreknowing things to come sometimes by the ministry of demons and by magic art. He is asked by King Balak to curse the people of Israel; envoys come, they carry instruments of divination in their hands, the nations stand astonished and anxious, awaiting what Balaam may answer, of whom they were persuaded that he was held worthy of divine conversations. See now how wisdom makes this vessel, prepared unto dishonor, to profit unto the usefulness not only of one nation, but of almost the whole world, and to this man, to whom demons were accustomed to appear, God appears, forbidding the journey of the evil work. Balaam is amazed and marvels at the authority of the one forbidding; for it was not usual for evil to be displeasing to demons. But meanwhile he sends back the envoys, saying that he cannot do anything except the word which God should give in his mouth. The envoys return again, again he inquires, again he is troublesome, again he desires to hear; for one who is greedy does not easily lack an eye to reward. What, then, does he hear a second time from God? "If these men came to call you," he says, "arise and go with them." In which indeed God yields to the will of his greed, that what is written may be fulfilled: "he let them go according to the desire of their heart, they shall go in their own wills," yet nevertheless the counsel of the divine dispensation is fulfilled; for it is said to him: "the word, whatever I shall give in your mouth, this you shall speak." If Balaam had been worthy, God would have placed his word not in his mouth, but in his heart. But now, since in his heart there was the desire of reward and the greed of money, the word of God is placed not in his heart, but in his mouth. For a wondrous and great dispensation was being carried out, that, since the words of the prophets, which were contained within the court of Israel, could not reach the nations, through Balaam, in whom faith was held by all the nations, the secret mysteries concerning Christ might become known also to the nations, and he might carry a great treasure to the nations, borne not so much by heart and understanding as by mouth and speech. But that we may not delay over each point—for there is no time for all things to be resolved—Balaam, having mounted his donkey, went along the way; an angel met him, that one without doubt who was present with the sons of Israel. He opens the mouth of the donkey, that Balaam may be reproved through her, and that he who seemed a diviner and wise might be confuted by the voice of a dumb beast.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us return to the subject. Balaam is troublesome to God and almost extorts that it be permitted him to go to curse the sons of Israel and to invoke the demons, to whom God had already come. He mounts the donkey; there meets him the angel who kept watch on behalf of Israel, concerning whom it is written, the Lord saying to Moses: "my angel will go with you." To him, then, pressing on to go, it is granted; on the way he is crushed by the donkey; but the magician sees the demons, he does not see the angel; the donkey, however, sees it. Not because she was worthy to see the angel, just as neither was she worthy to speak, but so that Balaam might be confuted and, as Scripture says in a certain place, a mute animal, answering with human voice, might rebuke the madness of the prophet. But since many things have now been said concerning the history, let us touch also on some things concerning the allegory at the end. If you see the contrary power assailing the people of God, you understand who it is that sits upon the donkey; and if you consider men, how they are cast headlong by demons, you understand what the donkey is. For thus in the Gospel too you will understand Jesus sending his disciples to the donkey, which was tied, and to its colt, that the disciples may loose her and lead her, that he himself may sit upon her. And perhaps this donkey—that is, the Church—formerly bore Balaam, but now Christ, from the time when she was loosed by the disciples and, released from the bonds by which she had been bound, that the Son of God might sit upon her and with her might enter into the holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the Scripture might be fulfilled which says: "rejoice, daughter of Zion; proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem: behold, your king comes to you, meek and sitting upon a beast of burden." By the beast of burden—that is, the donkey—he means, without doubt, those who believe from among the Jews, and by the young colt those, surely, who from among the nations believe in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But after these things it now seems fitting to touch also on something of allegory. This Balaam, who is interpreted "a vain people," seems to me to bear the person of the scribes and Pharisees of the Jewish people. But Balak, who is interpreted "exclusion" or "devouring," is himself also to be understood as bearing the person of some one of the spiritual contrary powers of this world, which desires to exclude and devour Israel—not that Israel which is according to the flesh, but that which is according to the spirit. This contrary power, then, wishing the spiritual Israel to be destroyed and utterly extinguished, uses no other ministers than the chief priests and scribes and Pharisees; it invites these, to these it promises rewards and prizes. But they, just as this Balaam does, feign that they refer all things to God and act with zeal for God; for they say: "search the Scriptures and see that a prophet does not arise out of Galilee"; and again they say: "we have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God." Through each of these things the scribes and Pharisees indeed seem to have zeal for God, but a feigned one. But the donkey on which Balaam sat, since Scripture says: "men and beasts you will save, O Lord," can be understood as that part of the believers which, whether for foolishness or for innocence, is compared to animals. For thus also the Apostle says: "consider your calling, brothers, that not many among you are wise, not many powerful, not many noble; but the foolish things of the world God has chosen, that he may confound the wise." These, then, such as they are—as the deeds that were done in the parables in the Gospel signify—were held in a manner subjected and bound by those most evil masters, the scribes and Pharisees, but they are loosed by the Lord, not indeed through the Lord himself, but through his disciples; for he himself says to the disciples: "go into the village that is opposite you; and you will find a donkey tied and her colt; loose them and bring them." As, therefore, in the Gospel not the Lord himself, but the disciples loose the donkey, so also here the mouth of the donkey is opened not by God himself, but by an angel; and as in the Gospels those who do not see reprove those who see, so also here those who were dumb reprove those who speak. And this is what the Lord said: "Father, I give you thanks, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and have revealed them to little ones." The scribes, therefore, and Pharisees were they who sat upon this donkey and held her bound. Against these, then, the angel is angry, and, but for a certain foresight of things to come, he would indeed have destroyed them, but would have saved the donkey, who saw and reverenced him who came to the vineyard and stood among the vineyards. Yet he crushed the feet of the one sitting upon her against the wall, and therefore perhaps that ancient rider of hers cannot walk, nor come to him who says: "come to me all you who labor and are burdened." Yet the donkey comes, led by the disciples, and on her, on whom then sat Balaam greedy for reward, now Jesus sits. And do not marvel if you see him, whom we said bears the form of the scribes and teachers of the people, prophesying about Christ; for we read that Caiaphas also did this, who said: "it is expedient for you that one man perish for the whole people"; but this, it says, because he was high priest of that year, he prophesied. Balaam therefore also prophesies about Christ, and therefore let no one be exalted, even if he prophesy, even if he deserve foreknowledge, but let him return to the saying of the Apostle, who, looking to these things, says: "whether prophecies, they will be abolished; whether tongues, they will cease; whether knowledge, it will be destroyed." And what, then, is it that remains? "Faith," he says, "and hope and charity; but the greater of these is charity." And "charity alone," he says, "is that which never falls." Therefore above prophecy, above knowledge, above faith, above even martyrdom itself, as Paul teaches, charity is to be held and charity is to be cultivated, because both God is charity and Christ his Son is charity, who may deign to grant us the perfection of charity. To him be glory unto ages of ages. Amen.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: I even think those birds blessed, which were offered for the birth of the Lord; and just as I marvel at Balaam's ass and heap up her happiness, because she was worthy not only to see the angel of God, but also, with her mouth unlocked, to break forth into human speech, so much more do I proclaim and exalt these birds, that they were offered for our Lord and Savior before the altar.
source_title: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 14

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Although the order of the readings which are recited demands rather that we speak of those things which the reader has set forth, nevertheless, since some of the brethren earnestly ask that rather those things which are written concerning the prophecy of Balaam be brought forward for the discourse of our discussion, I have thought it right to satisfy not so much the order of the readings as the desires of the hearers. First of all, then, let us inquire concerning Balaam himself, why in the Scriptures he is set forth now as blameworthy, now as praiseworthy. For he is blameworthy when, though forbidden by God to come to the king, he persists in coming, and, greedy for reward, consults God again, again inquires, until he is left to his own desires and goes in his own wishes. He is culpable when he builds altars and places victims upon them for demons and by magical apparatus seeks divine counsels. He is culpable when he gives that most wicked counsel, that the people be deceived through the Midianite women and the worship of idols. Again he is shown to be praiseworthy, when the word of God is placed in his mouth, when the Spirit of God comes upon him, when he prophesies concerning Christ, when he foretells to Jews and Gentiles the future mysteries concerning the coming of Christ, when instead of curses he bestows blessings upon the people and exalts the name of Israel above visible glory with mystical utterances. Since, then, divine Scripture indicates concerning him things so diverse and so varied, it seems very difficult to me to determine with any definiteness his person, to whom not only this diversity may suit, but to whom that also may be fitted which he himself, as though prophesying, says concerning himself: "Let my soul die among the souls of the righteous, and let my seed be as the seed of the righteous." But also through the prophet Micah the Lord gives such a testimony concerning him, where he says: "My people, what have I done to you? Answer me; for I called you back from the land of Egypt, and from the house of bondage I freed you, and I sent before your face Moses and Aaron and Miriam. My people, remember what Balak king of Moab plotted against you, and what Balaam son of Beor answered him from the ropes even to Gilgal, that the righteousness of the Lord might be known." He shows, then, through these words that, in order that the righteousness of the Lord might be recognized, for this reason Balaam son of Beor answered to king Balak all those things which are reported as written in the books. And who, do you think, will be found of such a kind as to be able to show from Balaam's very answers that the righteousness of God is made manifest in them? For truly, if the word of God has been placed in his mouth, and the Spirit of God has come upon him, and the righteousness of God is recognized and made manifest from his answers, then in every way the things which are said by him must be believed to be nothing other than prophetic and divine. And yet we scarcely read anywhere written that the Spirit of God came upon any of the prophets; but rather "the vision which he saw," or "the taking up of the word of God," or "the word of God came to" this one or that one, and certain other such things we read concerning the prophets. But that the Spirit of God came upon any of the prophets, I do not for the present recall to have read, except that concerning David I remember it thus written: "And the Spirit of God appeared," or "shone forth, upon David from that day and thereafter"—yet the Spirit of God was not "made" upon David. But concerning Saul I remember it thus written: "And the Spirit of the Lord shall fall upon you, and you shall prophesy with them, and you shall be turned into another man"; and again concerning the same it is said: "And the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord confounded him"; and again: "And it came to pass, when the evil spirit was upon Saul, David took up the psaltery and played with his hands, and struck it, and it was well with him, and the evil spirit departed from him." These things I have noted because that which is written, "and the Spirit of God came upon him," can seem to be something intermediate. Wherefore we too, according to what we had understood in the earlier treatise, shall now also attempt to explain this same Balaam under the person of the Pharisees and scribes and those like them. But come now, let us look at the words of his prophecy, which he is written to have spoken when he had taken up his parable. "From Mesopotamia," he says, "Balak king of Moab has called me, from the mountains of the East." By Mesopotamia he means the land which lies between the rivers of Babylonia, concerning which it is written: "Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, while we remembered Zion." If, then, anyone is among these rivers of Babylon, if anyone is flooded by the streams of lust and washed about by the heats of wantonness, he is said not to stand, but to sit; and therefore those who were caught there said: "Upon the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept, while we remembered Zion." But they cannot even weep before, except when they have remembered Zion; for the remembrance of good things makes the causes of evils to be lamented. For unless a person remembers Zion, unless he looks upon the law of God and the mountains of the Scriptures, he does not begin to weep for his own evils. From these rivers, then, Balaam is called, and from these mountains of the East he is invited. These mountains are not those holy mountains, concerning which it is written: "Its foundations are in the holy mountains," and again: "Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose sharing is together in one": "Mountains are round about it, and the Lord is round about his people." The mountains of Mesopotamia, then, are not such, but rather those of which it is said: "dark mountains," and again, of which it is said: "Behold, I am against you, O corrupt mountain." These are the mountains in which is "every height lifting itself up against the knowledge of God." From these mountains, then, this Balaam too is summoned. And of what kind these mountains are, such also is their East; for he too who "transforms himself as an angel of light" has the rising of his own light; he has that light concerning which it is written: "The light of the ungodly shall be extinguished."
