But if, as we taught above, grossness is held blameworthy, on the contrary fineness is to be held praiseworthy, since the "spirit of wisdom" too, which is called intelligible and holy and only-begotten and manifold, is likewise reported to be subtle. "And with his darts he shall shoot the enemy." His darts are his words, by which he either conquered the devil or overcomes and transfixes even now all his enemies and those who contradict him; for everyone who sins is his enemy, while he sins. But if he hears the words of God and, recognizing his sins, is transfixed by them and pierced with compunction and turns to repentance, having been bored through by the word of truth, he too will be said to have been transfixed by his darts. But after these things he also mentions the very dispensation of the passion and says: "Lying down he rested like a lion and like the whelp of a lion; who shall rouse him up?" He rested like a lion when, placed upon the cross, he stripped off the principalities and powers and triumphed over them on the wood of the cross; but like the whelp of a lion, when he rises from the sleep of death. And that he is compared at once to a lion and to the whelp of a lion can still be understood also on this account, that in those who are perfect he is named a lion, but in those who are beginners and untrained, the whelp of a lion. But as to his saying: "Who shall raise him up?"—this is because at one time he is said to be raised up by the Father, and at another he himself says that he will raise up the temple of his body after three days; and rightly in this the disposition, as it were, of one asking is indicated. "Those who bless you are blessed, and those who curse you are cursed." It is certain that those who bless Christ are blessed and taken up into the communion of the Father's blessing; but those who curse him are cursed. For if you look to that people which curses Christ, it is found, even lamentably, to be cursed. For what else could befall those who curse wisdom, who curse truth, who curse life, except that they should lie banished and exiled from all these good things? For all these things are Christ; and he who curses Christ, as one cursing all these, is condemned to perpetual malediction. Yet I think that not only he curses Christ who utters against him a cursing word, but also he who under the name of Christian acts wickedly and lives basely and, by his dishonest words or deeds, makes his name to be blasphemed among the nations; just as, on the contrary, not he who blesses the Lord with words alone is to be thought to bless, but he who by his deeds and life and manners makes the name of the Lord to be blessed by all. And in these it will be more fully accomplished, that which the third prophecy of Balaam designates, that those who bless Christ shall be blessed and those who curse him shall be cursed. Wherefore let us in every way take heed lest through our works and acts the name of Christ be blasphemed, but rather let us so act that we may deserve to be partakers of his blessings. To him be blessing and glory unto the ages of ages. Amen.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We now take up in hand the fourth of these prophecies which Balaam spoke in the word of God, wishing to open up, concerning this one too, whatever God may grant. To this prophecy, however, there were prefixed in the introduction things similar to those above. For it says: "And Balak was angry with Balaam, and clapped his hands together; and Balak said to Balaam: I called you to curse my enemy, and behold, blessing you have blessed him three times. Now therefore flee to your own place; I said: I will honor you, and now the Lord has defrauded you of honor." In these words he shows that Balak too understood that Balaam was no longer being deceived by the ministry of demons, but was being carried over to better things by the power of God, and therefore he says: "The Lord has defrauded you of honor." But passing quickly over these things, which are plain, let us come to what follows. "And Balaam said to Balak: Did I not also speak to your messengers whom you sent to me, saying: If Balak should give me his house full of silver and gold, I shall not be able to transgress the word of the Lord, to do it, whether good or evil, of my own accord? Whatever God shall say to me, this I shall speak. And now behold I return to my place." Balaam, knowing that responses were not brought to him through the accustomed ministers, but from Him who has power over all, rightly is seen to have protested that he could not transgress the word of the Lord and do it, whether small or great, of his own accord. For the one who spoke to him was not one who could be changed by sacrifices and gifts, but was one with whom there is no change nor shadow of change. And therefore the prophet cannot be altered by a fee, where God is not moved by gifts. Yet as he is about to depart, Balaam begins again to prophesy, and says: "Come, I give you counsel, what this people shall do to your people in the last days." And taking up his parable he said. But before we come to the explanation of the things which have been prophesied, I would like to inquire what this sense is, or what the order of the words is, in that he says: "Come, and I give you counsel." And indeed he seems to give no counsel, but says what this people is about to do to your people in the last days, whereas it would surely have seemed more fitting if it had said: "Come, I prophesy to you what this people is about to do to your people in the last days"; and it would surely follow as a consequence that Balaam would seem to prophesy about those things which the people of Israel were about to do to the people of Balak or to the rest of the nations, and that he would do it in power, so as to leave none of the cities of Moab that would be saved.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the prophecy also, nonetheless, which he joins to it in what follows concerning Christ, saying: "A star shall arise out of Jacob, and a man shall rise up out of Israel, and he shall lay waste the princes of Moab," would seem fittingly placed if it had been written: "Come, and I prophesy to you." But now what shall we say to this, that it is written: "Come, I give you counsel, what this people shall do to your people"? Let us therefore inquire how it ought to be understood, this that is written: "I give you counsel," concerning which, often inquiring within myself, I could find no outcome for the meaning, if we suppose that this which he says, "I give you counsel," is said in the common and ordinary way. But I saw that this rather is fitting, that what he says, "I give you counsel," is to be understood as though he had said: The divine counsel, which is to be fulfilled in the last days, now revealed to me I open and make manifest to you, that you may know what this people shall do to your people. And in this way it seemed to me able to stand, this that he says: "I give you counsel, what this people is about to do to your people," that is: I announce and make manifest to you the counsel of God. Indeed, as I inquired whether perhaps somewhere in the divine Scriptures some similar saying under this expression might occur, it seemed that this also was similarly to be noted, which the Apostle says: "For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?" For here "who" is taken not for "no one," but for "rare" or "exceptional." For how did his Only-begotten not know the mind of God, who says: "No one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son shall will to reveal him"? What else, then, is it to know the Father, except to know both his counsel and his mind? But also the Holy Spirit, who searches even the deep things of God, what does he do but recognize his mind? Therefore both the Son and the Holy Spirit recognize the mind of the Lord, and those to whom the Son shall will to reveal it. But if the Son recognizes the mind of God, then he is also his counselor. But "counselor" is not to be taken as though the Son or the Holy Spirit gives counsel to him as to one ignorant of what he is doing; but in that the Son and the Holy Spirit are partakers of, and knowing in, his counsel and will. In a similar way, then, Balaam too, because he was making Balak a partaker of, and acquainted with, the counsel which God had revealed to him, says: "Come, I give you counsel," as one who truly sees and has truly heard the words of God, as he says in what follows: "Balaam, the son of Beor, said, the man who truly sees, hearing the words of God, knowing the knowledge of the Most High, and seeing the vision of God in sleep, his eyes uncovered." Of all these things we have already spoken above, since in the introduction of the third prophecy the same things were written. This alone in the present passage seems added, that he says: "knowing the knowledge of the Most High." For this was not said of Balaam in the earlier passages; which indeed I have found not easily written of any one of all the holy prophets.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Whence also I greatly marvel how this was written of Balaam, to whom it was not even granted to say what is customary among the prophets: "Thus says the Lord," but he says: "Balaam said, the man who truly sees said." Then further, how will it be worthy that so much be understood of Balaam, that he knows the knowledge of the Most High—he who even taught King Balak how to send a stumbling-block before the children of Israel, that they might eat things sacrificed to idols and commit fornication? For scarcely will anyone find it said of the holy prophets or Apostles that they know the knowledge of the Most High. Although Paul said that he heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for men to utter, yet he did not profess to have the knowledge of the Most High. On which account let us attend more diligently, in case perhaps God may deign to reveal something worthy to us upon this expression. In the book which among us is usually held among the volumes of Solomon and is called Ecclesiasticus, but among the Greeks is named the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach, it is written: "All wisdom is from God." Which perhaps we might so understand, as though from God were also that wisdom of this world, which is said to be destroyed, and of the princes of this world, and if there is any other by which false knowledge is commended; were it not that in the same little book it says in what follows: "For the discipline of wickedness is not wisdom." By which surely he teaches that every discipline which asserts anything false, even if it seem forceful and plausible and such as can hardly be overthrown, yet by no means ought knowledge of this kind to be applied to the title of wisdom. What then is it that he says: "All wisdom is from God"? He seems to me to have meant this: that every skill which is held necessary for human use in regard to any art, or the knowledge of any matter whatever, is said to be wisdom given by the Lord. In short, in Job it is written: "Who gave to women the wisdom of weaving and the discipline of embroidery?" But also in Exodus: "The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Behold, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the divine spirit of wisdom and understanding and discipline, that he may have understanding in every work, and be an architect to work silver and gold and bronze and stones for setting and all works of craftsmanship, and in wood, that he may work according to all the works to which I have appointed him. And also Oholiab the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan; and I have put understanding into the heart of everyone who is prudent, that they may make all the things which I have appointed you." Consider therefore from all these things how the craftsman's wisdom is from the Lord, whether in gold or in silver or in any other material whatever, or even the wisdom of weaving; and see that of all these it can rightly be said that the knowledge of them is from the Most High. But if the craftsman's knowledge is declared to be from the Most High, how is not also geometry, from which surely this knowledge, which Scripture names architectonic, is derived? Indeed, in Zechariah too a geometric line is mentioned, with which an angel measures Jerusalem, and therefore I do not think it seems absurd if this knowledge too is said to be of the Most High. But what shall we say of music, all the skill of which the most wise David had so grasped, and had gathered the disciplines of all melody and rhythm, that from all these he might discover sounds by which he could, by playing, even soothe the king when troubled and vexed by an evil spirit? Whence I do not think anyone of right sense would deny, in the knowledge of all these things, that all wisdom is from God. But now concerning the knowledge of medicine I do not think there can even be a doubt; for if there is any knowledge from God, what will more be from him than the knowledge of health, in which even the powers of herbs and the qualities and differences of juices are discerned? Therefore from all these things it is gathered that even this knowledge of Balaam, for the sake of which he was summoned from the mountains of Mesopotamia in the east to curse Jacob, has indeed its beginnings and origin from the Most High, and thence too is the discernment by which he had learned either the natures of animals or the movements of birds or the differences of voices, but that the things which he had received unto the knowledge of good things, he had turned to the use of evil ones. This seems to me similar to as if one who had learned medicine and come to know the powers of herbs and their tempering—given by God to men doubtless for the sake of healing—should wish to reverse his purpose and use all this knowledge, which was granted for the health of bodies, unto evil, and become a poisoner instead of a physician, bringing diseases instead of remedies, deaths instead of healings. But that we may understand still more fully that the wisdom of all knowledge draws its origin from God, but that by men of evil purpose, or even by demons mingling in certain corruptions of the wisdom of God, it is turned aside to evil, let us reread the things which are written in Daniel concerning Daniel himself and his three friends, whom King Nebuchadnezzar handed over to be instructed for three years, wishing them to become most learned in their own—that is, the ancestral—wisdom of the Babylonians. There, then, it is written that: "The Lord gave them knowledge and understanding and prudence in every grammatical art; and to Daniel he gave understanding in every word and vision and dreams; and they were before the king, and in every word and prudence and discipline concerning which the king inquired of them, he found them tenfold more than were the sophists and philosophers who were in all his kingdom." And these things indeed are found in the copies of the Seventy translators; but in the codices of the Hebrews I found something even more forceful, which, although we do not use them, yet for the sake of acknowledgment we shall state, what we read there also: "God gave them," it says, "understanding and prudence in all grammatical wisdom; and Daniel had understanding in every vision and dreams," and after a few words: "and they stood," it says, "in the sight of the king, and in every word of wisdom and discipline concerning which the king inquired of them, he found them tenfold above all the enchanters and magicians who were in all his kingdom." From all these things, then, it can be understood how Balaam too said of himself: "who knows the knowledge of the Most High," namely, that it may be understood that the origin of all knowledge took its beginning from him, but that by the fault of human malice, with demons also breathing upon and stealing in, those things were turned to destruction which were granted for usefulness. Let these things concerning that which he said, "knowing the knowledge of the Most High," have been discussed by us according to our powers.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After these things he says: "seeing the vision of God in sleep, his eyes uncovered." Of these things it has been sufficiently discoursed in the third vision, and it is idle to repeat the same things. Let us therefore see what it is that he says in what follows: "I will show him, and not now; I bless him, and he does not draw near." In other copies indeed it reads: "I will see him, but not now"; which, if it be accepted, will be thought to be understood more easily, so that he says that Christ, of whom he speaks in what follows: "A star shall arise out of Jacob, and a man shall rise up out of Israel," is to be seen, but not now, that is, not at that time at which he was saying these things; for in the last days, when the fullness of times came, God sent his Son. But if it is to be read according to what we have in our copies, that is: "I will show him, and not now; I bless him, and he does not draw near," it refers not to this Balaam, through whom these things are said, but to those whose person we have said is represented in this. For those teachers of the law and scribes will show Christ prophesied in the law and the prophets, but not now, that is, not at the time at which he came, but when the fullness of the nations shall have entered in, and all Israel shall begin to be saved—then they will show him and then they will bless him whom they now blaspheme. But this time, in which these things are to be, does not draw near; for it is far off and to be hoped for at the very end of the age. And therefore he says: "I will show him, and not now"—"to him," that is, to the people who will then be saved. After these things: "A star," he says, "shall arise out of Jacob, and a man shall rise up out of Israel." Of these things we spoke also in the earlier passages, that it is evidently prophesied of the star which appeared to the Magi in the east; with which as their guide they came to Judea seeking him who was born, the King of Israel, and having found him, offered gifts and adored him. But it moves me that concerning that very star, after it was said in the Gospel that it went before the Magi as far as Bethlehem, and coming, stood above where the child was, nothing further was said, that either it departed thence or vanished or was taken up, or that the Gospel narrative indicated anything at all about this, but it said only this: that it came and stood above where the child was. Lest therefore perhaps, just as at the time of the baptism, when Jesus, having been baptized, ascended from the Jordan, the heavens were opened to him and John saw the Spirit of God descending as a dove and remaining upon him, and heard a voice from heaven saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased," so also this star, which came above where the child was and stood there, likewise remained upon Christ, just as the Holy Spirit too is said to have come in the appearance of a dove and to have remained upon him. And just as we understand that the Spirit of God came upon him and remained upon him in such a way that the Spirit of God never departed from him, so also the star, which came and stood over him, I think is to be understood to have so stood over him that it was never moved thence. And therefore I am of the opinion that that star was an indication of his deity. Whence also the order of the prophecy shows these same things consequently, when concerning his deity indeed it says: "A star shall arise out of Jacob," but concerning his human nature: "and a man shall rise up out of Israel," so that in both, according to deity and according to humanity, Christ may evidently appear to have been prophesied. "And he shall lay waste the princes of Moab." Moab indeed is a nation, whose princes we understand to be none other than the spiritual wickednesses and those principalities against whom is our wrestling. These, then, that man out of Israel shall lay waste, when he shall strip off the principalities and powers, and shall fasten them to his cross. For he could not save the Moabites and lead them to the knowledge of God, unless he had laid waste those princes who had held the dominion of impiety over them. "And he shall despoil all the sons of Seth." Seth is the son of Adam, of whom Eve said, when he was born: "For God has raised up for me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew." This, then, is Seth, from whom the whole human race in this world is said to descend; for of those who had been born of Cain, they perished in the flood. The sons of Seth, therefore, are all men who are in this world. And when it is said: "he shall despoil all the sons of Seth," take "spoil" as we interpreted it in the earlier passages, where it is written: "he shall eat the nations of his enemies," and where he is compared to a lion's cub and to a lion. Here too, then, he takes as spoil all the sons of Seth. When the adversary demons are conquered, Christ leads the men who were held under their dominion as, so to speak, the spoil of his victory, and carries off the plunder of salvation, just as it is written of him also elsewhere that: "ascending on high he led captivity captive"; that captivity, namely, of the human race, which the devil had taken to perdition, this one in turn led captive and recalled from death to life. Would then that Jesus might always hold me too captive and lead me as his spoil, and that I might be held bound by his chains, so that I too might deserve to be called a prisoner of Christ Jesus, just as Paul too glories of himself.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And Edom shall be an inheritance, and Esau his enemy shall be an inheritance." Edom is the same as Esau. He according to history indeed is the enemy of Israel, but at the coming, he says, of Christ, he too shall be his inheritance, that is, he shall be received unto the faith and shall not be excluded from the inheritance of Christ. But if we consider it spiritually, Edom is understood as the flesh, which is opposed to the spirit and is its enemy. At the coming, then, of Christ, when the flesh shall have been subjected to the spirit, through the hope of resurrection it too shall come to the inheritance. For not the soul alone, but also the flesh, which once had been an enemy, through the obedience of the spirit shall become a sharer of the inheritance to come. "And Israel did it in power." This is what he says: that then Edom or Esau, that is, the nature of the flesh, shall be called into the fellowship of the inheritance, when Israel, namely the soul, shall have been made to be in power and shall have been fittingly filled with virtues. For if the soul does not come to the virtues, but perseveres in sloth, neither shall the flesh come to the inheritance, but to the judgment of him who can destroy both soul and body in gehenna.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And there shall rise up one out of Jacob, and he shall destroy him that is delivered from the city." That one, he says, who shall rise up as a star out of Jacob, shall destroy him that is delivered from the city. Not in this alone, but in almost every prophetic style, the things that are said are said in speech quite involved and obscure. For it did not please the Holy Spirit, who willed these things to be written, that these should be set plainly and, so to say, to be trodden under the feet of the unskilled, but he so provided that, while they seem to be held publicly, yet, hidden by the obscurity of the words, they should be kept covered in mysteries and in secrets. And now, then, this that he says: "he shall destroy him that is delivered from the city," unless you look to the prophetic custom, of which it is said: "all prophecy cannot stand by its own solution," the understanding will seem far more difficult. Let us see, however, whether perhaps in this way it can be explained. Let us understand "the city" here as the world, just as also in the Gospels it is said of the prodigal son, who squandered the substance of his father, that "he went," it says, "to a certain chief man of the city in that region," by whom, being received, he is sent into the field to feed swine. And here too, then, the city, of which that man was chief, is understood as this world. Therefore him that is delivered from this city, that is, whom Christ delivers from this world, he destroys him. For he says to him that: "he who shall destroy his soul for my sake, shall make it safe." By a saving destruction, therefore, Jesus shall destroy him whom he shall have delivered from the city of this world. And so we too, if we wish to come to salvation and to be delivered from this world, ought to destroy our souls with a useful and necessary destruction. For he destroys his soul according to Christ who curbs its desires, who cuts back its cravings, who chastises its luxury and dissoluteness, and in nothing at all does his own will, but the will of God; and through these things the soul is said to perish. For its former life perishes and it begins to lead a new life, which is in Christ. Similar to this saying is also that: "if we die together, we shall also live together," and that: "but if you are dead to the elements of the world, how, as though living in this world, do you make decrees?" Necessarily, therefore, in these too it is declared that he destroys his soul in this world who dies with Christ, and he who has thus destroyed it shall find it there, without doubt, where the Apostle says that "your life is hidden with Christ in God," to whom be glory unto the eternal ages of ages. Amen.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: This fifth and likewise final vision of Balaam is now to be examined by us, concerning which, just as in the others, let us beseech the Lord that at the end He may not forsake us, so that we may be able to grasp the meaning of this vision too not far from the truth. Its beginning, then, is in these words: "And when Balaam saw Amalek," it says, "taking up his parable, he said: The beginning of the nations is Amalek, and their seed shall perish." It seems necessary to me to search out in the divine Scriptures in what places or at what time the name of Amalek is written, and from what stock that nation descends. For what is sought will be more easily recognized if it is brought forward from the several places that are written about the same matter. Therefore in the reading of Genesis, where five kings assembled to make war upon the four kings who were reigning in Sodom, after some space it is thus reported: "And returning," it says, "they came to the fountain of judgment, this is Kadesh, and they slew all the princes of Amalek and the Amorites, who were dwelling in Hazazon." In these places I first find Amalek named. But perhaps it may be asked whether there are two nations of the same name, since indeed in the catalogue of the sons of Esau and of the leaders who had descended from his stock Amalek is also mentioned. For it is thus written: "Now these are the generations of Esau, the father of Edom, in mount Seir. And these are the names of the sons of Esau: Eliphaz the son of Adah, the wife of Esau, and Raguel the son of Basemath, the wife of Esau. And the sons of Eliphaz were: Teman, Sophar, Gatam, Kenaz. And Timna was the concubine of Eliphaz, the son of Esau, and she bore Amalek to Eliphaz himself; and these are the sons of Adah, the wife of Esau." And after a little: "And these," it says, "are the leaders from the sons of Esau. The sons of Eliphaz, who was the firstborn of Esau: leader Teman, leader Omar, leader Sophar, leader Kenaz, leader Korah, leader Gatam, leader Amalek." This Amalek, therefore, was the son of Eliphaz the firstborn son of Esau, born of a concubine named Timna. But let us return to the first mention of Amalek, where those who returned and came to the fountain of judgment, which is called Kadesh, slay all the princes of Amalek. For Kadesh is interpreted "sanctification" or "holy"; but Amalek is interpreted "one who licks up the people" or "one who turns the people aside." Therefore those who return to the holy and turn themselves to sanctification slay and destroy Amalek, namely that one who licks up the people or turns the people aside. But who else is it who turns the people aside from God, except the adverse power and the spiritual wickednesses? Who then are the princes of these? Those principalities, without doubt, against whom the saints have their wrestling. For against the principalities and powers and the rulers of this world are their struggles; yet they will not be able to overcome them unless they turn to holiness. Yet in that very holiness, which is Kadesh, is the fountain of judgment. For everyone who turns himself to holiness has always before his eyes the fountain of judgment. For he looks ahead to the day of judgment, and with a purified heart he beholds both the punishments of the wicked and the blessednesses of the pious; and doing these things he lays low and casts down all the princes of the Amalekites. But if any do not turn themselves to Kadesh, that is, to holiness and the fountain of judgment, nor think upon the coming day of judgment, these are subjected to the princes of Amalek; for he licks up and consumes this people, and such a people he turns aside from God. Let these things be referred to that first Amalek. But now let us look also at this Amalek, the son of Eliphaz the firstborn of Esau, whom Timna his concubine bore to him; whose father is Eliphaz, which is interpreted "God has scattered me," but his mother Timna, who herself too is first of all base-born, and then is interpreted "commotion of failing"; and of necessity, indeed, whoever is begotten of such as these is an enemy of Israel, licking up or turning aside the people. For he himself first attacked the Hebrews, when they had gone out from Egypt, in battle at Rephidim, then when Moses said to Joshua: "Choose for yourself men, and go out, and fight with Amalek tomorrow; and behold, I stand on the top of the hill, and the rod of God shall be in my hand." And Joshua did as Moses said to him, and fought with Amalek; but Moses and Aaron and Hur went up to the top of the hill. And it came to pass that, when Moses lifted up his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he let down his hands, Amalek prevailed. And after a little it is again written that Joshua put Amalek to flight and cast down his people with the sword, then when the Lord said to Moses: "Write these things for a memorial in a book, and deliver them into the ears of Joshua, for wiping out I will wipe out the memory of Amalek from under heaven." And Moses built an altar and named its name: "The Lord is my refuge," and said: "For with a hidden hand the Lord makes war upon Amalek from generation to generation." Understand from this more evidently who ought to be understood as Amalek, whom God is said to make war upon with a hidden, that is, an invisible hand, from generation to generation. But also in Deuteronomy it is thus written: "Remember how much Amalek did to you on the way, when you had gone out of Egypt, how he opposed you on the way and cut off your tail, all who were toiling behind you, while you were hungry and toiling, and you did not fear God." Observe therefore in these things also how Amalek opposed Israel on the way, but nevertheless was not able to cut off its head, but only the tail: that is, he was able only to seize those who were set in the rear, who followed last, and who, not forgetting the things that were behind, did not stretch themselves toward the things that are ahead. And for this reason I think the Lord gave the precept in the Gospels, saying: "No one putting his hand to the plow and looking back is fit for the kingdom of God." And rightly; for if anyone be found behind in the tail, Amalek will cut him off. But we will bring forward yet another history concerning Amalek as well, so that from more places of Scripture what we seek may be more clearly perceived. In the first book of Kingdoms, Samuel says to Saul: "The Lord sent me to anoint you king over His people Israel, and now hear the voice of the words of the Lord. Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have called to mind all that Amalek did against Israel, how he smote him on the way, when he was coming up out of Egypt. Now therefore go and smite Amalek and put under the ban all that he has, and do not spare, but slay all, from man to woman, and the little ones and the sucklings and the bulls and the flocks of sheep and the camels and the asses." And Saul commanded the people, and reviewed them in Gilead, two hundred thousand foot soldiers, and three thousand men of Judah. And Saul came to the city of Amalek, and set an ambush in the valley. And Saul said to the Kenite: "Go you and depart out of the midst of Amalek, lest perhaps you too be added together with him. For you did mercy with all the sons of Israel, when they were coming up out of the land of Egypt." And the Kenite departed out of the midst of Amalek. And Saul smote Amalek from Havilah as far as Shur, which is over against the face of Egypt. And he took Agag the king of Amalek alive, and put all his people under the ban by the mouth of the sword. And Saul and the people spared king Agag, and preserved everything that was good of the sheep and oxen, and also the fruitful ones of all the good cattle, and would not utterly destroy them; but everything that was contemptible and despised, this they put under the ban. And the word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying: "It repents me that I anointed Saul as king." Here too, then, observe how God through the prophet commands king Saul to make war upon Amalek and to spare none of them, and, because he spared Agag the king of Amalek, he incurs an offense that cannot be expiated, so that he moved God to this point, that, contrary to what that nature admits, He said: "It repents me that I anointed Saul as king." It is not expedient for us, therefore, to spare that one who turns the people aside or licks up and devours; that invisible Amalek, namely, who resists on the way those who wish to come up out of Egypt and to escape from the darkness of this world and to press on to the land of promise, and assails us, and, if he finds us weary and worn out and looking back and set among the last and in the tail, cuts us off and destroys us. And for this reason we must always press forward, and hasten to the things that are ahead, nay rather even ascend to the top of the mountain, and always lift up our hands to heaven in prayers, so that at last in this way Amalek may be conquered and fall. But do you wish to know that one does not cross over to the holy land nor arrive at the kingdom unless Amalek be first conquered? Although David had waged many wars and there had been for him most sharp and frequent conflicts against the Philistines, nevertheless he is not written to have obtained the kingdom until he had first subdued Amalek. For the Scripture says: "And David returned, after Amalek had fallen, and received the kingdom of Saul," though Amalek himself is described as having first made many slaughters among the people of Israel and burned very many of their cities. For truly, before the coming of the true David, of Him who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, the Amalekites, who are the adverse powers, made many spiritual slaughters among the people of Israel. But also, it says, they took captive both the wives of David himself. I think the first is called the Jewish and the second the Gentile people; for it is established that both Jews and Gentiles were all shut up under sin. But the outcome of things did not remain in this state; for hear what David, coming, does. "And David found," it says, "the Amalekites scattered, eating and drinking, and exulting over the plunder which they had carried off; and he smote them," it says, "from the first night until the evening of the next day." And after this slaughter of the Amalekites he returned and received the kingdom.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: This Amalek, therefore, seeing him, Balaam the son of Beor, a man truly seeing and hearing the words of God, who knows the knowledge of the Most High and sees the visions of God, having taken up his parable as is written in the earlier visions also, says: "The beginning of the nations is Amalek, and their seed shall perish." As for what he says: "The beginning of the nations is Amalek," it is certain that it can in no way be referred to that Amalek who then existed in the flesh, for neither was he first in the antiquity of origin, but it is better referred to the invisible Amalek, who from turning the peoples aside from God and making Gentiles out of the worshipers of God is named Amalek. And therefore he is rightly called the beginning of the nations, as being a certain such adverse power which first gave the beginning for men to become Gentiles, by changing the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man and of birds and of four-footed beasts and of serpents, and by serving the creature rather than the Creator. For just as among the people of God it is written that the beginning is Christ, so on the contrary among the people who turns aside from God and becomes Gentile, the beginning is Amalek. "And their seed shall perish." Their seed is the persuasion and teaching by which they taught men to turn aside from God. This evil seed, then, and this worst teaching shall perish, not they themselves in whom it was sown. For they themselves, when they groan being converted, shall be saved. And see whether such an exposition may not also fittingly stand against those who accuse the God of the law as of harshness and cruelty, in that He pronounces that not only the nation of Amalek but also its seed shall perish; when indeed the nation is referred to the spiritual wickednesses, but its seed is expounded as the teaching of the superstitions of the Gentiles and the worship of idols and every sect which persuades the people to turn aside from God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the prophecy makes mention of the Kenite after Amalek, saying: "And seeing the Kenite, taking up his parable, he said: Strong is your dwelling, and if you set your nest in the rock, and if Beor be to you a nest of cunning, the Assyrians shall lead you captive." It seems to me that he names the Kenite not very blameworthily; for he is the one to whom in the earlier passages Saul also said: "Depart out of the midst of Amalek, and I will not smite you, because you did mercy in Israel, when it was coming up out of Egypt." Of this one, therefore, it is now said also that his dwelling is strong, if he sets his nest in the rock. The rock is Christ. If therefore he sets his nest in the rock, his dwelling is strong, provided that Beor does not become for him a nest of cunning. Beor is the father of Balaam, who can be taken in the person of the heretics; so that this seems to be said, that the Kenite can be saved if he sets his nest in the rock, that is, if he places his hope in Christ and does not surround and circumscribe him with the cunning of the heretics. For if this should happen, it will profit him nothing that he seems to be set in the rock, which is Christ; for he will be led captive by the Assyrians, that is, by the malignant powers, which lead captive and take into their power those whom heretical error has enveloped. It seems indeed, according to this exposition which we have set forth concerning the Kenite, that the conjunction "and" also disturbs the sense. But it must be known that it is a native property of the Hebrew tongue to use the conjunction "and" frequently in such a way that at times it is superfluous and, as appears in our language, seems inserted among unnecessary things. This certainly must be received with indulgence; for each language has something of its own property which among other languages may seem faulty. And here therefore the conjunction "and" is to be held as, so to speak, superfluous and redundant. Let the Kenite, therefore, who is interpreted "possessing," beware — let him beware, I say — even if he possesses and earns this grace, that he be in the Church of Christ, lest perhaps the cunning of Beor circumvent him and turn him aside to depraved and perverse doctrines and for this cause he be handed over to the Assyrians. For those who blaspheme, being set within the Church, are handed over to Satan, as Phygelus and Hermogenes, of whom Paul says: "Whom I handed over," he says, "to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme." Therefore for this reason he who has turned aside into heretical blasphemy is handed over to the Assyrians, because the Assyrians are interpreted "directing"; and for this cause those who are handed over are handed over to these, not that they may perish, nor that they may utterly be destroyed, but that they may be directed and corrected and, as Paul himself says: "that they may learn not to blaspheme."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But after these things Balaam concludes the discourse of his prophecy in these words, saying: "And having taken up his parable, he said: Oh, oh, who shall live, when God shall do these things? And he shall come forth out of the hands of the Kittim, and they shall afflict Asshur, and they shall afflict the Hebrews, and they themselves shall likewise perish." That Balaam is said to speak through each detail by way of a parable strikes shame into the reader, lest in these things that are said he should think anything said not as in a parable, but according to the letter. He says, then: "Oh, oh, who shall live, when God shall do these things?" Here he names not this common life, but that life which is according to God, and this is what he says: that, when all these things shall come to pass, when a star shall arise out of Jacob, and a man shall rise up out of Israel and shall destroy Amalek and shall bring his seed to perdition, that is, when Christ shall come and shall destroy the worship of idols and shall subject the power of all the demons, who shall be so blessed, so happy, as to see these things? that is, who shall perceive and understand and believe that God has done these things thus? "And they shall come forth out of the hands of the Kittim, and they shall afflict the Assyrians." The Kittim are interpreted "the stroke of the end." These, therefore, who, being converted to the Lord and instructed by Christ, escape the stroke which shall come upon the impious at the end of the age, they themselves shall afflict the Assyrians, that is, these, for whom, being set in the contest of piety, God shall crush Satan under their feet, they themselves shall afflict the Assyrians, namely the nation of demons. For they shall tread upon serpents and scorpions, and upon all the power of the enemy, and shall afflict them. "And they shall afflict the Hebrews, and they themselves shall likewise perish." The Hebrews are interpreted "those passing over." This same people, therefore, is also called Hebrew, because it passes over from Egypt to the land of promise, from darkness to light, from death to life. But since these things, as we have said, cannot be obtained without a contest nor without a great struggle, as one set in the contest he now afflicts, now is afflicted, and now smites the adversary, now is himself beaten by the adversary. Therefore the Assyrians themselves also shall afflict the Hebrews, that is, the people of God, just as they are afflicted by them; but they themselves, that is the Assyrians, when they shall have done these things and when they shall have poured out all their strength upon afflicting the Hebrews, immediately they themselves also shall perish. As for what he says, then: "And they shall afflict the Hebrews, and they themselves shall likewise perish," it is not to be taken as though the Assyrians shall perish together with the Hebrews; but "likewise," that is, immediately as they shall have done these things, as they shall have afflicted the Hebrews, they themselves also shall perish; for the Greek word puts "likewise" for "immediately." This, therefore, shall be the end of all things, that even Asshur, to whom were handed over those who were transgressing from the people of God, either unto the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit might be saved, or that they might learn not to blaspheme, shall himself also perish at the hands of Him who has the power to destroy in Gehenna. For it shall be said to them by the just judge: "Go into the eternal fire, which God prepared for the devil and his angels." There, therefore, Asshur shall perish. And indeed one sheep too out of the hundred sheep once perished, but this sheep the good shepherd, leaving the ninety and nine in the mountains and descending to this valley of ours, the valley of tears, and seeking it, found it and, having laid it upon his shoulders, carried it back and joined it to that number which in the passages above remained saved. But this Asshur, who is said to be about to perish at the end of all things, I know not whether he can ever either be sought or be found; for he perishes not by error, but by judgment, nor moved by a lapse, but hardened by perseverance. For as to what is written: "I will kill and I will make to live, I will lead down into hell and I will bring back," I know not whether it looks generally to all or only to those whom the deception of the devil caused to be led down into death. Let these things too concerning the last prophecy of Balaam be said by us according to our strength, which, because of the difficulty of the passages, it has seemed good to unfold rather with the pen of one explaining than of one delivering a formal discourse. For what does it matter, provided that all things be said unto edification and all things be done unto the glory of God? Who is blessed unto the ages of ages. Amen.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Yet far more execrable is that general fornication in which every kind of sin is alike contained. Now it is called general fornication when the soul, which has been admitted into fellowship with the Word of God and in some manner joined to Him in matrimony, is corrupted and violated by some other — namely by one foreign and hostile to that Husband who betrothed her to Himself in faith. The bridegroom, then, and husband of the pure and chaste soul is the Word of God, who is Christ the Lord, as the Apostle also writes: "I wish to present you all as a chaste virgin to one husband, Christ; but I fear lest perhaps, as the serpent seduced Eve by his cunning, your senses be corrupted from the simplicity which is in Christ Jesus." As long, therefore, as the soul clings to her bridegroom and hears his word and embraces him, without doubt she receives from him the seed of the word; and as he said: "From fear of you, Lord, we have conceived in the womb," so also she says: "From your word, Lord, I conceived in the womb and travailed and brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth." If, therefore, the soul thus conceives from Christ, she makes sons, for whom it may be said of her that: "She shall be saved through the bearing of children, if they continue in faith and charity and holiness with sobriety" — even if the soul may seem first, like Eve, to have been seduced. And so the offspring is truly blessed where there has been an intercourse of the soul with the Word of God and where they have given embraces to one another. Thence a noble progeny will be born, thence chastity will arise; thence righteousness, thence patience, thence gentleness and charity, and the venerable offspring of all the virtues will follow. But if the unhappy soul forsakes the holy nuptials of the divine word and, deceived by the enticements of the devil and of other demons, gives herself over to adulterous embraces, she will without doubt beget sons even from that, but those of whom it is written: "The sons of adulterers shall be imperfect, and from the unjust bed the seed shall be exterminated." All sins, therefore, are sons of adultery and sons of fornication. Whence it is shown that through each single thing which we do, our soul gives birth and generates sons — namely the thoughts and works which it does. And if indeed what it does is according to the law and according to the word of God, it brings forth the spirit of salvation, and therefore it shall be saved through the bearing of children; and these are the sons of whom the prophet says: "Your sons like young olive-shoots round about your table." But if what it does is against the law and is sin, without doubt from the conception of the contrary spirit it begets a wicked offspring; for it brings forth sons of sin. And these are the accursed generations, in which by some of the saints even the day on which they were born is cursed. There is therefore never a time when the soul does not give birth; the soul always gives birth, always generates sons. But that generation indeed is blessed which, conceived of the word of God, is generated, and this is the bearing of children through which she shall be saved. But if, as we have said, she conceives from the contrary spirit, it is certain that she bears sons of wrath fitted for destruction. And perhaps to both these generations of the soul that refers which was said: "For when they were not yet born, nor had done anything good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works but of him who calls, it was said that the greater shall serve the lesser, as it is written: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." For such generations of the soul, even before they do anything good — if indeed they are generated of the Holy Spirit — are already loved; but if they are of the evil spirit, even before they accomplish anything of evil in work, yet by this very thing, that the soul has brought forth a will of this kind, the execrable conception of the evil will is worthily hated in her. Therefore perhaps, as a figure of this sacrament, even the boy Canaan is cursed before he was born. For Ham his father had sinned, and Noah, prophesying, when he was signing out each best thing to each of his sons, when it came to Ham, said: "Cursed be the boy Canaan." Ham sinned, and Canaan his offspring is cursed and was cursed. And therefore we must apply ourselves more sharply and look ahead, lest perhaps the soul generate something worthy of a curse; even if it has not yet accomplished it in work, yet in its very will and purpose there will be an accursed progeny of this kind. And if perhaps this should ever happen — for who will easily be found who is held immune from such generation, that is, from the will to sin? — if therefore anything of the sort should happen, let us seek from the divine volumes what remedy is given. We find, then, written in the Psalms concerning this: "O wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who will repay you the repayment which you repaid to us; blessed is he who will hold and dash your little ones against the rock." Even if this conceived Babylonian has not yet performed any work in us, while it is still a little one, do not pity it nor spare it, but at once kill it — for it is hateful — destroy it, slay it, dashing it against the rock. And the rock is Christ. Who then is so great and such a man that he will not by any means wait until the Babylonian offspring grows within him and the works of confusion are increased within him, but at the very first beginnings, when they have begun to be born and to grow strong from the motions of the will, and, so to speak, when the pernicious desires conceived by the inspiration of the evil spirit have begun to bring forth their head from the womb of the soul, will at once seize them and dash them against the rock — that is, bring them to Christ, so that, placed in the sight of His fearful judgment, they may wither away and perish? These things have been said by us concerning the general fornication, which has very many species, of which one is this which, in common usage, on account of bodily debauchery is called fornication. But I, reading the Apostle, when I had come to that place in which he says: "He who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit," and: "He who joins himself to a harlot is one body," was inquiring whether there is anything else in between besides this — that either one is joined to the Lord or to a harlot; and, examining according to my strength the sufficiently deep and hidden sense in these words, I beheld the meaning of the Apostle, who thus defined that every soul is either joined to the Lord or to a harlot, and I understood that by the Lord he meant the virtues, which are Christ, that is, the word, the wisdom, the truth, the righteousness, and the rest of this kind, but by the harlot all the contrary species of malice. This I understand to be said also in Solomon in that which he says of the harlot, that: "She looks out through the windows into the streets, and if she sees any of the foolish young men and one lacking in senses passing by the corners of her house and speaking in the evening darkness, when there is the silence of night or the gloom of night, a woman meets him, having the appearance of a harlot, who makes the hearts of young men fly away." This, then, which is called a harlot, is malice itself, and he who joins himself to this harlot becomes one body of malice. As, therefore, he who joins himself to the Lord joins himself to wisdom, joins himself to righteousness, joins himself to piety and truth, and with all these becomes one spirit, so also he who joins himself to this harlot joins himself to unchastity, to impiety, to iniquity, to falsehood, and at once to all the evils of sins, with which he becomes one body.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The reading recited today contains, first, a piece of history about the fornication of an Israelite man and a Midianite woman, and second, about the visitation of the people, in which it is commanded that they again be numbered by the precept of the Lord, the former number having, of course, been made void on account of the sins which those had committed who had earlier been enrolled under the reckoning of the number. Therefore the number that had been written down is cancelled and rendered void because of sins, and offenses have such power that not even this profits a man — that he had been counted in the number in God's sight — once he has turned aside. But, as Scripture reports, even the limbs of those who withdrew from God fell in the desert. There are, then, two histories that have been recited; but we, for the present, will speak of the first, which describes the fornication of the people, if the Lord shall deign to grant any grace as you pray; and if He Himself shall grant it, we shall venture also to touch upon something of the second. "And Israel sojourned at Shittim," it says, "and the people was defiled, and committed fornication with the daughters of Moab. And they invited them to the sacrifices of their idols, and the people ate of their sacrifices and worshipped their idols, and was consecrated to Baal-peor; and the Lord was angry with fury against Israel." In these words is shown that which we have often recalled, namely that Balaam, after he had been so constrained by the power of God that he was not permitted to curse Israel, yet wishing to please King Balak, said to him, as it is written: "Come, I will give you counsel." And what counsel he gave did not appear there, but it is reported as written in the later parts of the book of Numbers itself. Yet more fully in the revelation of John, where it is contained thus: "You have there," it says, "the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling-block in the sight of the sons of Israel, that they should eat things sacrificed to idols and commit fornication." From this, therefore, it appears that Balaam used wickedness and gave counsel to the king, saying to him something of this sort: "This people conquers not by its own strength, but by worshipping God and by preserving chastity. If you wish to conquer it, first cast down their chastity, and they will be conquered of their own accord. But against these we must fight not with the strength of soldiers, but with the beauty of women, not with the rigor of armed men, but with the softness of females. Away, far away from here remove the band of armed men, and gather a choice display of maidens; let them go dancing with their feet and clapping with their hands; beauty conquers armed men, loveliness takes the sword captive, they will be conquered by beauty who are not conquered in battle. But when the Moabite women perceive that they have surrendered to lust and bowed their necks to sin, let them not offer themselves to their desirers before the men have agreed to taste of the sacrifices of the idols, so that, driven by lust, they may obey the counsels of the women and be first consecrated to Baal-peor, which is the idol of shamefulness." These were the counsels of Balaam; having received them, King Balak at once prepares an army composed not with the strength of arms, but with feminine elegance, kindled not with warlike fury, but with the flame of lust. Shame restrains none, modesty forbids none. Love of country and the vice of the nation conspire alike into wantonness, and to deceive, upright behavior turns to depravity. O the wickedness! scarcely is lust checked by the threats of laws, scarcely repressed by the terror of the sword! What crime would it not commit, when a woman believes that by her outrage she will please the king and secure the safety of her country? So the Israelites are taken captive not by iron, but by luxury, not by valor, but by lust, and they commit fornication with the Midianite women, and the wrath of God rises up over them. There are indeed in these things certain mystical matters and secrets of a deeper understanding; but let first the very text of the history edify us, and let us learn from it that fornication wars against us, that the darts of luxury are hurled against us. But if we do not lack the arms with which the Apostle bids us be armed, darts of this kind will not be able to pierce us, if we have the breastplate of righteousness, if we have the helmet of salvation and the sword of the spirit and above all the shield of faith and our feet are shod in the preparation of the gospel of peace. These are the arms which defend us in wars of this kind. But if we cast away such arms, at once we give place to the diabolical wound, and the whole chorus of demons leads us captive; and on account of this the wrath of God will rise up over us, and we shall be punished not only in the present age but also in that to come. Therefore that which makes us conquer in these battles which the devil stirs up against us is chastity and righteousness and prudence and piety and the other virtues. But those things which make us be conquered are luxury and lust, avarice and impiety and every malice. These, then, are the things which the text of the history has taught us. But since John in his revelation brings the things which are written according to the history in the law up to divine mysteries and teaches that certain sacraments are contained in them, it seems necessary that we too, according to what he perceived, should follow the rule of exposition given by him, and first recall those things which, writing to the angel of a certain church, he says: "You have there certain persons who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling-block in the sight of the sons of Israel, that they should eat things sacrificed to idols and commit fornication." Therefore in the times of the Apostle John there were some in that church to which he was writing who taught the teaching of Balaam. Do you suppose it is to be taken thus, that there were in those days people who said that they taught the things which Balaam taught, and who professed themselves to be teachers of his doctrines and traditions? Or ought we rather to note this, that, if anyone does the work which Balaam did, he is seen to teach the teaching of Balaam? Just as also concerning the teaching of Jezebel it is mentioned in the same revelation, not that anyone teaches from the disciplines of Jezebel the things which she handed down, but that if anyone, for example, either persecutes the prophets of God, as she did, or deceives some toward idols, or destroys the innocent by false frauds, this one is said to hold the teaching of Jezebel. So therefore, if anyone by evil counsels generates stumbling-blocks for the people of God and provokes divine offense and heavenly wrath against the people, either by communicating in the sacrifices of idols or by serving debaucheries and lust, this one is to be said to hold the teaching of Balaam. Even the fornication of the body, then, is execrable. For what is so execrable as to violate the temple of God and to take away the members of Christ and make them members of a harlot?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "But Israel sojourned at Shittim." In the interpretation of Hebrew names we find that Shittim, in our language, is said to mean "answer" or "refutation." Israel, then, sojourned at "answer" or "refutation." It did not sojourn well. See, finally, what it ran into, placed in this station. It committed fornication with the Midianite women and was refuted by God, because not only did it commit fornication, but it was also consecrated to the idols of the nations and ate of those things which had been sacrificed to idols — things which are altogether execrable in God's sight. For what agreement has the temple of God with idols? Indeed I have also greatly wondered at those things which the Apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying: "But if anyone sees you, who have knowledge, reclining in an idol's temple, will not his conscience, since it is weak, be built up to eat things sacrificed to idols?" For he seems to pronounce not so much the matter itself grievous as the offense of that one who, seeing these things, is provoked by a like example, since he is not fortified by like knowledge — so that he shows that the one who, having knowledge, reclines in an idol's temple is made guilty not so much of his own harm as of another's. But see whether perhaps this alone was not being done among the Corinthians, that they reclined in an idol's temple and ate things sacrificed to idols. But perhaps, since they were men zealous for Greek letters and lovers of philosophy, they were still held by desire for their old studies and ate the doctrines of the philosophers as though sacrificed to idols; which, however, perhaps could not harm those who had received the full knowledge of the truth. But these, who had less learning in Christ, if they imitated them, reading such things and still giving attention to those studies, could be wounded and entangled in the various errors of diverse doctrines. So then it came about that another was harmed, whereby he who had the full knowledge of the truth could not be harmed. But since charity does not seek what is useful to itself, but what is useful to many, one must take care to receive such food of the word as not only builds us up and delights us, but also does not offend or harm those who see. There is, therefore, a thing sacrificed to idols not only in foods, but also in words. And I think that, just as every discourse which teaches piety and righteousness and truth is consecrated to God and sacrificed to God, so also every discourse which looks toward unchastity or injustice or impiety is sacrificed to idols, and he who receives it eats, as it were, things sacrificed to idols. "The people, therefore, ate of their sacrifices, and worshipped their idols." Not only did they eat, but they also worshipped. See the order of evil: first concupiscence deceived the servants of the Lord, then the gluttony of the belly, and last impiety took them captive. And the wage of impiety that is paid out is fornication. If you read again the things that are written concerning Solomon, you will find that he, and indeed although he was most wise, inclined his loins to many women, though the law of God says: "You shall not multiply women for yourself, lest perhaps they make you commit fornication away from your God." He, then, although he was most wise and of enormous merits before God, yet because he gave himself over to many women, was deceived. I think that "many women" is the name for many doctrines and the diverse philosophies of many nations. And when, as a most learned and most wise man, he wished to recognize and thoroughly examine each of these, he could not hold himself within the rule of the divine law, but Moabite philosophy deceived him and persuaded him to sacrifice to the Moabite idol, and likewise of the Ammonites, and also of the remaining nations, whose women he is said to have received and to have built temples or sacrificed to their idols. It is, then, a great thing and truly a work of God to be mingled with many doctrines as with women, and yet not to turn aside from the rule of truth, but constantly to say: "There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and young maidens of whom there is no number; yet my dove is one, my perfect one is one; she is the only one of her mother, the only one of her that bore her." But these worshipped idols and were consecrated to Baal-peor. Baal-peor is the name of an idol which among the Midianites was worshipped especially by the women. In the mysteries of this idol, then, Israel was consecrated. Yet when we inquired rather carefully into the interpretation of the name itself among the Hebrew names, we found only this written: that Baal-peor is a species of shamefulness. He was unwilling, however, to declare which or what sort of species, or of whose shamefulness — consulting, I believe, for decency, the one who interpreted, so as not to pollute the hearing of the listeners. Therefore, since there are many species of shamefulness, one particular species out of many of shamefulness is called Baal-peor. Whence it is to be known that everyone who commits anything shameful and turns aside into any species of shamefulness is consecrated to Baal-peor, the demon of the Midianites. But also through the individual sins which we commit — especially if we now sin not by some stealthy surprise, but with zeal and affection — we are without doubt consecrated to that demon whose care it is to work out that sin which we have committed. And perhaps it will befall us to be consecrated to as many demons as we commit sins, and in each and every offense we receive, as it were, the mysteries which they call of this or that idol. And perhaps on account of this the Apostle said: "For already the mystery of iniquity is at work." The evil spirits, therefore, go about and seek how they may deceive each one and, through the enticement of sin, consecrate him to their mysteries, and, without his perceiving or understanding, they bring him — for example, through the sin of fornication — to the demon of the Midianites and consecrate him to Baal-peor, consecrate him to shamefulness. Likewise also, through the other sins, as we have said, men are consecrated to other demons. But do you observe carefully what is written, and "stand in the ways and ask which are the eternal ways of the Lord and which is the good way, and walk in it," and do not approach the doors of the house of malice. But if you perceive an evil spirit speaking in your heart, so as to lead you to some work of sin, understand that it wishes to lead you in order to consecrate you to some demon, it wishes to lead you in order that you may receive the diabolical mysteries, the mysteries of iniquity. And this is, I think, what the Apostle writes: "But when you were gentiles, going after the form of idols, according as you were led." By whom, or by what, were you led? By the evil spirits, surely, you were led to the works of sins. Hearing these things, every watchful hearer will perhaps say: "What, then, shall we do? If the evil spirits go about each one of us and lead and drag us to sin, but there is no other who draws to righteousness, who invites and leads to chastity, to piety: how will it not seem that the way lies wide open indeed toward perishing, but that nowhere is any access given toward salvation?" Nay rather, consider more carefully, if you can with the eye of the heart opened consider with me the inner mysteries, and you will see how much greater care is exercised in the secrets of our salvation than opportunity is afforded for deceiving. There is present to each one of us, even to the least who are in the Church of God, a good angel, an angel of the Lord, who guides, who admonishes, who governs, who for the correcting of our acts and the seeking of mercies daily sees the face of the Father who is in heaven, as the Lord indicates in the gospels. And again, according to those things which John writes in the Apocalypse, over each church generally an angel presides, who is either praised for the good deeds of the people or also blamed for its offenses. In which too I am moved with wonder at the astounding mystery, that God's care for us is so great that He allows even His angels to be blamed and confuted on our behalf. For just as, when a boy is handed over with a tutor, if perhaps he appears imbued with less worthy disciplines and not according to his father's nimbleness, at once the blame is referred to the tutor, and the boy is not reproved by the father as the tutor is — unless the boy be too obstinate and have spurned the tutor's admonitions and, prone to wantonness and insolence, have despised his salutary words, obeying rather those who counsel luxury and provoke to wantonness. And learn from the voices of the prophet what befalls that soul: "The daughter of Zion," he says, "shall be left like a booth in a vineyard, and like a watchman's hut in a cucumber field, like a city that has been stormed"; and again: "Its wall shall be taken away and it shall be for a trampling, and all who pass along the way shall plunder it, and the solitary wild beast shall feed upon it." These things it will suffer, if it does not acquiesce in the admonitions of the angel who is placed for its salvation. For the soul is of its own free will, and it is free for it to incline to whichever part it wills; and therefore the judgment of God is just, because of its own accord it obeys either good or the worst counselors. Do you wish that I show you still further and more from the divine scriptures how much greater is God's care for the salvation of men than the devil's care for their destruction? Was not the diligence of the angels enough against the snares of the demons and against those who draw men to sinning? The Only-begotten Himself, the Son of God Himself, I say, is present, He Himself defends, He Himself guards, He Himself draws us to Himself. Hear how He Himself says: "And behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age." Nor does it suffice Him to be with us, but in a manner He does violence to us, that He may draw us to salvation; for He says in another place: "But when I shall be lifted up, I will draw all things to myself." You see how He not only invites the willing, but also draws the hesitating. Do you wish to hear how He draws even the hesitating? He did not grant it to the one who wished to go and bury his father, nor did He give him a space of time, but said to him: "Let the dead bury their dead, but you follow me." And elsewhere He says: "No one putting his hand to the plow and looking back is fit for the kingdom of God." But if you wish to know still more about this sacrament, I will show you from the scriptures that even God the Father Himself does not neglect the dispensation of our salvation, but He too not only calls us to salvation but also draws us. For thus the Lord says in the gospel: "No one comes to me unless my heavenly Father draws him." But also the householder, who sends his servants to invite friends to the wedding of his son, after those who were first invited had excused themselves, says to the servants: "Go out to the roads and lanes, and whomever you find, compel them to come in." So then we are not only invited by God, but also drawn and compelled to salvation. But neither indeed is the Holy Spirit lacking in dispensations of this kind; for He too says: "Separate for me Paul and Barnabas for the ministry to which I have taken them"; and again He forbids Paul to go into Asia, and again compels him to go to Jerusalem, foretelling him that bonds and prisons await him there. But if the angels of the Lord encamp round about those who fear Him, to rescue them, if God the Father, if the Son, if the Holy Spirit not only exhort and provoke, but also draw us — how is not far greater care taken for us toward salvation than is procured by our adversaries toward death? And let these things be said on account of the fact that the people was consecrated to Baal-peor.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: I might say that those who deny Christianity on oath at the tribunals or before they have been put on trial do not worship but only bow down to idols when they take "God" from the name of the Lord God and apply it to vain and lifeless wood. Thus the people who were defiled with the daughters of Moab bowed down to idols but did not worship them. Indeed, it is written in the text itself, "They invited them to the sacrifices of their idols, and the people ate of their sacrifices, and they bowed down to their idols, and performed the rites to Baal Peor." Observe that it does not say "and they worshiped their idols"; for it was not possible after such great signs and wonders in one moment of time to be persuaded by the women with whom they committed fornication to consider the idols gods.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And the Lord," it says, "was angry with fury against Israel. And the Lord said to Moses: Take the chiefs of the people and display them to the Lord before the sun, and the anger of the Lord's fury shall be turned away from Israel." I do not know whether, in discussing these things, we may not offend some; but even if we do offend, it is more fitting to obey and serve the word of the Lord than the favor of men. Israel sinned, and the Lord said to Moses that he should take all the chiefs and display them to the Lord before the sun. The people sins, and the chiefs are displayed before the sun — that is, they are brought forth to be examined, that they may be reproved by the light. You see what the condition of the chiefs of the people is: they are reproved not only for their own offenses, but they are also compelled to render account for the sins of the people, lest it be their fault that the people transgressed — lest perhaps they did not teach, lest perhaps they did not admonish, nor were solicitous to reprove those who gave the beginning of the fault, so that the contagion might not be scattered among the many. For it is incumbent upon the chiefs and the teachers to do all these things. For if, when they do not do these things nor bear solicitude concerning the people, the people has sinned, they themselves are displayed and they themselves are brought forth to judgment. For Moses — that is, the law of God — reproves them as negligent and slothful, and the wrath of God will be turned upon them and will cease from the people. If men considered these things, they would never desire nor strive after the chieftainship of the people. For it is enough for me if I am reproved for my own offenses; it is enough for me to render account for my own self and my own sins. What need is there for me also to be displayed for the sins of the people, and to be displayed before the sun, before which nothing can be hidden, nothing obscured? But perhaps even in this there is some hidden and secret sense which teaches something more than this common exposition seems to have. For perhaps this too can be referred to those chiefs of the people of whom we spoke a little above. For the angels too will come to judgment with us and will stand for us before the sun of righteousness, lest perhaps something of the cause of our transgression should have been from them too — lest perhaps they expended less of work and labor toward us, whereby they might have recalled us from the stain of sins. For unless there were something also in them which should seem blameworthy in the cause of ours, the discourse of Scripture would never say to the angel of this or that church that "you have, for example, certain persons holding the teaching of Balaam," or that "you have forsaken your former charity" or "your patience," or other things of this kind which we have already mentioned above, for which in the Apocalypse the angels of each church are blamed. For if the angel — for example, who received me sealed to him from God — hopes for a reward for those things which I did well, it is certain that he will also expect to be blamed for those things which were not done well by me. And therefore they are said to be displayed before the sun, without doubt so that it may appear whether the sins were committed through my disobedience or through his negligence, by which I was consecrated either to Baal-peor or to any other idol, according to the quality, that is, of the sinning. But if my chief — I mean the angel who is sealed to me — was not lacking, but admonished me of good things and spoke in my heart, at least insofar as my conscience recalled me from sin, but I, despising his admonitions and spurning the restraint of conscience, burst headlong into sins, my punishment will be doubled, both for the contempt of my admonisher and for the outrage of the deed committed. And do not indeed be surprised if we say that the angels come to judgment with men, since Scripture says that: "The Lord Himself will come to judgment with the elders of the people and with its chiefs." The chiefs, then, are displayed, and if the fault is in them, the wrath of God ceases from the people. There ought, therefore, to be a keener solicitude for us concerning our acts, knowing that not only shall we stand before the tribunal of God for our acts, but the angels too shall be brought to judgment for us, as our chiefs and leaders. For on this account Scripture also says: "Obey your overseers and submit to them in all things; for they keep watch, as those who will render account for your souls."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After these things it is reported that, when Phinehas the son of Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest had seen a certain Israelite man go in to a Midianite woman, he snatched up a lance in his hand, entered the brothel, and pierced them both through their very shameful parts. And for this, it says, the Lord said to Moses: "Phinehas the son of Eleazar the son of Aaron has quieted my anger." Let these things have edified the former people; but you, who have been redeemed by Christ, and from whose hands the bodily sword has been taken away and the sword of the spirit given, snatch up this sword; and if you see an Israelite thought whoring with Midianite harlots — that is, wallowing with diabolical thoughts — do not spare, do not dissemble, but at once strike, at once destroy. The very womb also — that is, discerning and penetrating the secrets of nature — cut away that very kindling of sin, lest it conceive further, lest it generate further and the accursed offspring of sins contaminate the camp of Israel.
