For if you do this, you will straightway quiet the wrath of the Lord; for you have anticipated the day of judgment, which is called the day of wrath and fury, and, with the kindling of sin — which now is called the womb of the Midianite woman — exterminated from you, you will come secure to the day of judgment. And therefore, rising up, let us pray that we may find this sword of the spirit always ready, through which both the seeds themselves and the receptacles of sins may be exterminated, and that God may become favorable to us through the true Phinehas, our very Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And lest we seem to you to bring these things forth rather from our own understanding than from the authority of divine Scripture, return to the book of Numbers and recall what Phinehas the priest did, who, when he had seen a harlot of the Midianite nation clinging in impure embraces with an Israelite man before the eyes of all, filled with the anger of divine zeal, seized a sword and drove it through the breast of both. Which work was reckoned to him by God unto justice, the Lord saying: "Phinehas has assuaged my fury, and it shall be reckoned to him unto justice." This earthly food of anger, then, becomes our food, when we use it rationally unto justice.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: These are the numbers we are reading, and in the earlier reading we were shut out by time from saying anything about the second numbering; but it is fitting now to render what was omitted or left out. Therefore by the Lord's command the people was first numbered, but since those who had first been enrolled fell on account of their persistence in sins, a second people now, which succeeded into the place of the fallen by a revived generation, is called to the numbering, and what had not been said of those former ones is said of these. For after the number was gathered by tribes and peoples and houses and families, the Lord says to Moses: "To these the land shall be distributed by lot according to the number of names. To the more numerous more shall be given by lot, and to the small you shall give a small inheritance." If it had been said of the former ones that "to these the land shall be distributed by lot," it would surely have been false, because they fell in the desert on account of their sins. What therefore was not said to the first is said to the last, for whom also all the things that are promised were fulfilled. But I would not have you think this is confined to the text of the mere history; these are mysteries which are set down through the image of the law. For the former people, which is in circumcision, is rejected, and a second is brought in, which is gathered from the nations; and it is this people that obtains the paternal inheritance. And from whom does it obtain it? Not from Moses, but from Joshua. For Moses, even if he gives an inheritance to some, does not give it within the Jordan nor does he cross the Jordan at all, but he gives land beyond the Jordan — not land flowing with milk and honey, but land suited to cattle and better at nourishing dumb animals and irrational beasts than rational men. But my Joshua, the land which he gives to the second people is a land flowing with milk and honey — nay rather, it is a honeycomb beyond every land. And Moses indeed does not give an inheritance by allotment nor distribute it by lot, nor is he able to weigh out by divine lot the merits of individuals according to peoples and houses and families and names; this Joshua alone does, to whom the Father has handed over all judgment; he knows how to dispense to his people, not only by tribes and families and houses, but even by names, to each one a worthy and fitting dwelling. Yet there are some among these who rise above the condition of the lot and are not brought to the lot at all. All the Levites, that is, all who remain intently and unceasingly in the ministry of God and keep ever-watchful guard in his service, do not receive a lot among the rest; but neither is their lot at all in the land, but the Lord himself is said to be their lot and inheritance. Through these there seem to me to be indicated those who, dulled by no obstacles of bodily nature, but having risen above the glory of all visible things, have set the practice and exercise of their living in the wisdom of God and his Word alone, who require nothing bodily, nothing foreign to reason. For they have desired wisdom, they have desired the knowledge of the secret things of God, and where their heart is, there also is their treasure. These therefore have no inheritance on earth, but they rise above the highest heights of heaven, and there they will ever delight in the Lord, ever in his Word, ever in wisdom and in the pleasure of his knowledge. This will be their food, this their drink, these their riches, this their kingdom. Such therefore will they be, and among these will be those for whom the Lord himself will be the inheritance. But those who are lower and have not reached this summit of advancement will receive an inheritance of land, though of some more sublime and more powerful land. For the land of the living is promised, which is surely called the land of the living for this reason, that it knows no death. And these indeed are great and these are blessed, but more blessed are those who now will see God no longer through a mirror and in a riddle nor in bodily substances, but face to face, radiant with the illumination of wisdom and made capable of pure divinity through purity of heart, and having their portion not in the creature but in the Creator, who is God over all, blessed forever.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: He says therefore: "According to the number of names, to the more numerous more shall be given by lot, and to the small you shall give a small inheritance; to each, as he has been counted, his inheritance shall be given." This is what the history teaches, that if any tribe is held to be more numerous among the peoples, it should obtain by lot larger tracts of land; but if any is reckoned with a smaller number of men, it should be content with a smaller possession. But since we say that the division of this land and the earthly inheritance holds the appearance and shows the image and form of those future goods, of that heavenly inheritance which is hoped for by the faithful and the saints, I inquire, in that inheritance which is to be hoped for, who are the many and who are the few, and I find that there the few are held more blessed than the many. For those who travel their journey by the broad and spacious way that leads to destruction are called many; but those who go by the strait and narrow way that leads to life are called few. And again in other places it is said: "How few are they who are saved!" and again in others: "Where iniquity is multiplied, the charity of many"— not of few —"shall grow cold." Moreover in the ark, which was built by Noah, where the measurements are given from heaven, in the lower parts a length of three hundred cubits is set and a breadth of fifty; but where its structure rises to higher parts, it is drawn into a narrow space and gathered into the enclosure of few cubits, so that its top is finished in the space of a single cubit — for this reason, that in the lower parts, where broad and spacious places were had, either beasts or cattle were placed, but in the upper parts the birds, and in the topmost parts, which were narrower and more confined, there the rational man is placed. But the very peak is gathered into one cubit; for all things are brought back to the monad, which nevertheless in the number of three hundred cubits designates the mystery of the Trinity, and next to this mystery man is placed, as being rational and capable of God. But from this too let us gather the tokens of what is the difference between the few and the many. Set down the whole number of the human race and from all the nations choose the faithful: without doubt they will be fewer than are the whole. Then next from the number of the faithful choose the better: it is certain that a much smaller number will remain. And again from those very ones whom you have chosen, choose again the more perfect: you will surely find fewer. And the further you proceed in choosing, the more scanty and the fewest you will find, until at last you come to some one man who may confidently say: "I have labored more than all those." These therefore, who in this manner are the many, will receive more land and more of the bodily inheritance; but the few will obtain some scanty thing of land, because they have more in the Lord; but others will receive nothing at all of earthly inheritance, if any are worthy to be priests and ministers of God; for of these the Lord himself will be wholly the inheritance. And who is so blessed as either among the few to receive a scanty portion of land, or among the chosen priests and ministers to deserve to receive by lot of inheritance the Lord alone? Although these too on account of their beasts of burden receive something of land, but of that land which is contiguous to the cities and adjoins the towns. Yet this saying which says that "to the more numerous the inheritance shall be multiplied" can still be understood in another way also. For one just man, according to this — that he is accepted by God — is counted for many. Finally it is also written: "By one wise man a city shall be inhabited, but the tribes of the wicked shall be made desolate." And one just man is reckoned for the whole world, but the wicked, even if they are many, are counted scanty and for nothing before God. There is therefore also a praiseworthy multitude, as we see said also to Abraham, when he led him outside and said to him: "Look to heaven, if you can number the stars; so shall your seed be." In this consider also this: how the just man is within and always stands in the inner parts, because within, in secret, he prays to the Father, and all the glory of the king's daughter, that is, of the royal soul, is within; but nevertheless God leads him outside when the matter requires it and the account of visible things demands it. In this way too, therefore, for those many who are as the stars of heaven in multitude the inheritance can be multiplied, and for those scanty ones — namely those who, even if they are many in number, are yet held scanty by the unworthiness and vileness of their life — a scanty inheritance may be set.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "By lot," he says, "shall the distribution of the inheritance be made." This indeed is commanded, but when I come to the Scriptures, I see that Moses himself, to whom these things are entrusted, does not use the lot in the division of the inheritance of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh. And Joshua too gives an inheritance to the tribe of Judah and to Caleb apart from the lot, and gives one apart from the lot also to the tribe of Ephraim and to the half-tribe of Manasseh. In the rest the lot is cast, and the first lot comes forth for Benjamin, and thereafter for the remaining tribes. Whence I think that in that blessed inheritance of the kingdom of heaven also there will be some who do not come to the lot nor are numbered with the rest, although they are holy; but there will be a certain outstanding and exceptional inheritance for them, as there was for Caleb of the tribe of Judah and for Joshua himself the son of Nun. For just as, for example, when after a battle the provinces and the spoils are apportioned to the victors, each of the outstanding and exceptional warriors is not brought to the lot along with the rest of the soldiers in the division of the spoils, but the best and most excellent things are awarded to them by the merit of their valor, while the rest use the lot solely by the right of victory, so it seems to me that my Lord Jesus Christ also will do; for to certain ones, whom he knows to have labored more abundantly than the rest and whose magnificent deeds and lofty virtues he himself knows, to those he awards the choicest and most exceptional honors and glories, and, if I may dare so to say, honors like his own. Or does it not seem to you that he confers something like his own blessedness upon his dearest disciples, when he says, "Father, I will that, where I am, these also may be with me," and when he says again, "You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel," and again, "As you, Father, in me, and I in you, that these also may be one in us"? All these things do not come down by lot, but are granted by the prerogative of election by him who alone sees the hearts and minds of men — who may deign to bring us also, even if not among the exceptional and the elect and those who are above the lot, yet into the lot of the saints; to whom be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There were five daughters, whose names too are recorded in Scripture, born of a certain Israelite named Zelophehad, who died in the desert leaving behind no male offspring. These daughters of Zelophehad therefore approach Moses and demand a share of their father's inheritance, saying: let not the name of their father be blotted out from the midst of his people, because no son was born to him. On this matter Moses refers the question to God. But the mercy of Almighty God does not spurn or despise a consultation offered by young women, and not only deigns to give an answer, but so approves and embraces their words that from them he establishes eternal laws for men, to be observed for all ages. For the Lord says, speaking to Moses: the daughters of Zelophehad have spoken rightly; you shall give them a possession in the midst of their father's brothers, and you shall give the inheritance of their father to them. And you shall speak to the children of Israel, saying: if a man dies and has no son, you shall give his inheritance to his daughters; but if he has no daughter, you shall give his inheritance to his brother; but if he has no brothers, you shall give his inheritance to his father's brother; but if his father has no brothers, you shall give the inheritance to the kinsman who is nearest to him from his own tribe, and he shall take his inheritance. And this shall be for the children of Israel a statute of judgment, as the Lord appointed to Moses. What force these things have according to the historical sense is plain to all who know that these laws are kept not only among the children of Israel, but among all men who live by laws at all. From which it appears that the freedom of the daughters of Zelophehad conferred an inheritance not only upon themselves, but also gave perpetual laws of living to the world. You see how great is the usefulness even of the historical account itself in the law of God. Who can ever dissolve these laws which the whole world employs? But nevertheless let us seek how we too may be edified spiritually. For it can happen that I have neither daughters according to the flesh nor any land whose inheritance could be received. What then? Will this law accomplish nothing in the case of such a person, and will what has been sanctioned by the divine voice be idle for anyone? Let us therefore inquire, even in the spiritual law, who these five daughters are, who, even if their father has died for some sin, may themselves receive an inheritance from the word of God. In earlier passages, when we were treating of spiritual sons, we taught that the virtues of the soul and the perceptions of the mind are called sons. It seems, without doubt, a consequence and fitting that daughters too should be understood as works, which are accomplished by the ministry of the body. And therefore too the number five is assigned to them; for there are five bodily senses, by which every work is accomplished in the body. These five daughters, then — that is, the perfection of works — even if they are bereaved of their father and remain orphans, are nevertheless not cast out from the inheritance nor excluded from the kingdom, but receive a portion of the inheritance in the midst of the people of God. But now let us see who is their father who is said to have died to them. Zelophehad, it says. Now Zelophehad is interpreted "a shadow in his mouth." The father of works is understanding. It often happens, then — and there are not a few among our brothers — in whom there is no higher or deeper understanding, but in whom the perception is dead, as is written of a certain man: and his heart died within him. This man, therefore, even if he has no taste for spiritual understanding, but is dead, nevertheless, if he begets daughters — that is, works of ministry, works of obedient service, works of the commandments of God — will obtain an inheritance in the land with the people of the Lord. He will not indeed be able to be numbered among those whose portion is the Lord, whose inheritance is God; he will not be able to be received into the number of the ministers and priests; yet in the order of the common people he will receive an inheritance of the land of promise: for many are called, but few are chosen. Yet the cause is also shown from the interpretation of the very name, why this Zelophehad could not beget sons but daughters; for it is interpreted, as we have said, "a shadow in his mouth." You see, then, that if anyone has the shadow of the law in his mouth and not the very image of the realities, this man, because he can perceive nothing spiritual, nothing of deep understanding, but there is only a shadow of the law in his mouth, cannot beget living and spiritual perceptions, yet can beget works and acts, which are the ministries of a simpler life. And therefore in these the mercy of God shows that the more innocent, even if they are deficient in understanding, yet have good works, are not excluded from the inheritance of the saints. Rightly, therefore, have the daughters of Zelophehad spoken.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After this the law of God concerning succession is set down, that first the son, second in place the daughter, third the brother, fourth the father's brother should succeed; but the fifth degree does not designate any definite person, but whoever is nearer out of the whole family, that he should succeed. In these things the sense of the history is so whole and perfect that it seems to require nothing from outside. Yet if anyone is well instructed in the spiritual laws and irradiated with the fuller light of knowledge, he can understand these various degrees of successions, and how the first degree of attaining the heavenly inheritance is by the merit of teaching and knowledge, which is the male son; the second by the prerogative of works, which is the daughter; the third of some compassion and imitation, on account of which he is named a brother. For there are some who indeed do nothing of their own accord and by their own understanding, yet placed among the brothers by imitation of the rest they seem to do the same things which those also do who are moved by their own understanding. To these also, therefore, is given a third degree of inheritance under the title of the fraternal name. But the fourth, whom he names the father's brother, can perhaps be understood as that order of men who, having heard things from the fathers and having received the narration of the ancients, endeavor to fulfill them, and, moved not so much by their own perceptions nor stirred by the admonitions of present teaching as instructed by the tradition or the custom alone of the ancients, nevertheless do something good. The last degree, then, is written as that man who by any means whatever has been nearest to these; as if he should say, whether by occasion or by the truth of teaching, if anyone has done something good, the reward of the good work will not perish, but by the Lord's bounty he will receive a place of inheritance. These things, indeed, may perhaps seem to have been boldly presumed by us and brought forward into the open; yet it will not be absurd if, setting forth spiritual things to the spiritual, we make them zealous and desirous of a more secret understanding.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After this a history is related, both marvelous in its narration and magnificent in its meaning. For it is set down how God said to Moses that he should go up onto the mountain, and there, when he had looked out from it and gazed upon the whole land of promise, there he should die. But he, who bore the care of the people more than of himself, prays to the Lord that he provide a man to rule the people: let not this congregation, he says, become like sheep which have no shepherd. See therefore, first of all, how he who is perfect and blessed dies not in a valley nor on any level of ground nor on some hill, but on a mountain — that is, in a high and steep place. For the consummation and perfection of his life was held in the height. And he is commanded also to behold with his eyes the whole land of promise, and diligently to survey all things from an eminent station. For it was fitting that to one about to attain the summit of perfection nothing should remain unknown, but that he should have knowledge of all things that are seen and heard; for this reason, I believe, that of all things which, placed in the flesh, he had grasped by bodily sight, being made in the spirit and with a bare mind, hastening to the audience-halls and discipleship of wisdom, he might swiftly attain their reasons and causes. For what usefulness would seem to appear in this, that to one departing from the world and about to receive forthwith the end of this life there should be shown lands and places of which he would neither undergo the labor nor receive the benefit? The saying which follows truly terrifies me and renders me timid and trembling to speak, in that concerning that great Moses, servant and friend of God, to whom God spoke face to face, through whom signs and wondrous powers were wrought, things so grave, so perilous are related. For what does God say to him? And you shall be gathered, he says, to your people, even you, as Aaron your brother was gathered on Mount Hor. And as though setting forth the cause of his death, he says: because you transgressed my word in the desert of Zin, when the congregation resisted, so that it did not sanctify me. You did not sanctify me at the water before them. Is then Moses too at fault? He too incurs the charge of transgression; he too was made under sin. For this reason, I believe, the Apostle said with confidence: death reigned from Adam until Moses; for it came even unto Moses and did not spare even him. And therefore, I think, he said: sin entered into this world, and through sin death, in that all sinned; and again: God has shut up all under sin, that he may have mercy on all. But thanks be to our Lord Jesus Christ, who freed us from the body of this death, so that, where sin abounded, grace might more abound. For how could Moses have freed anyone from sins, when it is said even to himself: you transgressed my word in the desert of Zin, and you did not sanctify me at the water before the children of Israel? — so that it may be manifest to all that he alone must be sought who alone did no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But meanwhile let us see the greatness of Moses. About to depart from the world, he prays to God that he provide a leader for the people. What are you doing, O Moses? Have you not sons, Gershom and Eleazar? Or if you doubt anything about them, are there not the sons of your brother, a great and excellent man? Why do you not pray to God for them, that he may set them as leaders over the people? But let the princes of the churches learn to mark out for themselves as successors not those who are joined by blood-kinship, nor those who are allied by nearness of flesh, by testament, nor to hand down the headship of the church as an inheritance, but to refer it to the judgment of God, and not to choose him whom human affection commends, but to leave the whole matter of the successor's election to the judgment of God. Could not Moses have chosen a prince for the people, and chosen him by true judgment and by right and just verdict — Moses, to whom God had said: choose elders for the people, whom you yourself know to be elders, and he chose such men in whom the Spirit of God straightway rested, and they all prophesied? Who then could so choose a prince of the people as Moses could? But he does not do this, he does not choose, he does not dare. Why does he not dare? Lest he leave to posterity an example of presumption. But listen to what he says: let the Lord God of spirits and of all flesh provide, he says, a man over this congregation, who may go out before their face and who may go in, and who may lead them out and who may bring them back. If then so great and such a man as Moses does not entrust to his own judgment the choosing of a prince of the people, the appointing of a successor, who will there be who would dare — whether from the common people, who, often stirred by clamors to favor or perhaps to a price, are wont to be moved, or even from the priests themselves, who will there be who would judge himself fit for this — unless it be revealed by the Lord to one who prays and asks? As also God says to Moses: take to yourself Joshua the son of Nun, a man who has the Spirit of God in himself, and you shall lay your hands upon him; and you shall set him before Eleazar the priest, and give him commands in the sight of the whole congregation, and give charge concerning him before them; and you shall put your glory upon him, that the children of Israel may hear him. You hear the ordination of a prince of the people so plainly described that it scarcely needs exposition. Here there is no acclamation of the people, no reckoning of blood-kinship, no consideration of nearness of relation. To the near kinsmen let the inheritance of fields and estates be left; let the governance of the people be handed over to him whom God has chosen — namely, to such a man who has, as you have heard written, the Spirit of God in himself and the precepts of God are before his eyes, and who is well known and familiar to Moses — that is, in whom there is the brightness of the law and knowledge — that the children of Israel may be able to hear him. But since all things are filled with mysteries, we cannot omit the things that are more precious, even if these things which are commanded according to the letter seem necessary and useful. Let us consider, then, what is the death of Moses: the end, without doubt, of the law, but of that law which is spoken according to the letter. But what is its end? The interruption, namely, of the sacrifices and of the other things which are commanded with like observance in the law. When these things, then, receive their end, Jesus takes up the headship: for the end of the law is Christ unto righteousness to everyone who believes. And as it was said of those of old that: all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, so let it also be said of Jesus that: all were baptized into Jesus in the Holy Spirit and water. For it is Jesus who crosses the waters of the Jordan, and in them, in a certain manner, even then baptizes the people; and it is he who divides the land of inheritance, the holy land, among all — not to the former people, but to the second; for the former people, on account of its transgression, fell in the desert. Of the times of Joshua it is said that: the land rested from wars, which could not be said of the time of Moses. But this is said of my Lord Jesus, not of that son of Nun. And would that my land might cease from wars! And it could cease, if I served faithfully as a soldier under Jesus my prince. For if I obey my Lord Jesus, my flesh will never rise up against my spirit, nor will my land be assailed by hostile nations — that is, by the various lusts — provoked against it. Let us pray, therefore, that Jesus may reign over us and that our land may cease from wars, may cease from the assaults of carnal desires; and when these things have ceased, then each one will rest under his own vine and under his own fig tree and under his own olive tree. For under the covering of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit will the soul rest which has recovered within itself the peace of flesh and spirit. To him, the eternal God, be glory unto the ages of ages. Amen

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: If the observance of the sacrifices and the legal ordinances, which were given to the people of Israel as a figure, could have stood firm right up to the present time, they would without doubt have shut out the faith of the Gospel, through which, from the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, the nations are converted to God. For there was in those things which were then observed a certain magnificent religion, full of every reverence, which even at the very first glance would astonish the beholder. For who, seeing that which was called the sanctuary or holy place, and gazing upon the altar, and upon the priests standing by to complete the sacrifices, and beholding the whole order by which all these things were carried out, would not have supposed this to be a most complete rite by which God the Creator of all ought to be worshipped by the human race? But thanks be to the coming of Christ, who, tearing our souls away from this spectacle, has brought them over to the consideration of the heavenly and to the contemplation of spiritual things, and has indeed destroyed those things that seemed great upon the earth, and has transferred the worship of God from the visible to the invisible and from the temporal to the eternal. But in truth the Lord Jesus Christ himself requires both ears that may hear these things and eyes that may see them. Hence we too, now having in our hands the law given through Moses, and wishing to show that it is a spiritual law, require from you such ears and such eyes as look not to those things that have been destroyed, but that seek these things there where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God, and that savor the things which are above, not the things which are upon the earth. Let it suffice, then, that these things have been set forth by us in the place of a preface for the things that are to be said.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But now let us come at last to the things that are written. "And the Lord spoke to Moses," it says, "saying: Command the children of Israel, and thou shalt say to them: My offerings, my gifts, my victims, for an odor of sweetness, observe to offer them to me on my feast days. And thou shalt say to them: These are my victims, which you shall offer to the Lord." No one offers anything of his own to God, but what he offers is the Lord's, and a man does not so much offer his own things as render back to Him the things that are His own. Therefore, wishing to write laws concerning the sacrifices and gifts to be offered to Him by men, the Lord first of all discloses the true nature of those very things that were to be offered, and says: "My offerings, my gifts, my sacrifices, for an odor of sweetness, observe to offer to me on my feast days." "These offerings," He says, "concerning which I am about to command you that you offer them to me on my feast days, are my gifts," that is, they are given to you by me; for from me the human race receives all that it has. Therefore, lest anyone in offering gifts should believe that he confers some benefit upon God, and through this become impious in the very act in which he seemed to worship God — for what is so impious as for a man to think that he bestows something upon God as upon one in need? — of necessity, as we have said, He first teaches man, so that he may know that whatever he offers to God he rather renders back to Him than offers. But let us also see how He says: "which you shall offer to me on my feast days." Does God, then, have His feast days? He does. For to Him human salvation is a great festivity. I think that through each and every one of the believers, through each one who is converted to God and advances in faith, a festivity arises for God. How greatly, do you think, does it gladden Him when he who had been unchaste becomes chaste, and he who had been unjust cultivates justice, and he who had been impious is made pious? All these conversions of each individual generate festivities for God. Nor is there any doubt that our Lord Jesus Christ also, who for our salvation poured out even his own blood, keeps the greatest festivity when He sees that it was worth the labor that He humbled Himself and, taking the form of a servant, became obedient even unto death. The Holy Spirit likewise keeps festival, when He sees more temples prepared for Himself in those who are converted to God. For what shall I say of the angels, to whose festivity of rejoicing all are said to draw near who are converted to the Lord? Or is it not for them a great festivity, when they rejoice in heaven over one sinner doing penance more than over ninety-nine just who have no need of penance? The angels therefore also keep a feast day, rejoicing over those who, fleeing the fellowship of demons, hasten through the exercises of the virtues to associate themselves with the angelic fellowships. Perhaps it may seem wonderful, what I wish to say: we, it appears, give to God and to the angels causes for festivity and gladness; we, placed on earth, furnish to heaven an occasion of joy and exultation, when, walking upon the earth, we have our conversation in the heavens, and through this without doubt generate a feast day for the heavenly powers. But just as our good acts and the progress of the virtues beget joy and festivity for God and the angels, so I fear lest our evil conversation bring in lamentations and mournings not only to the earth but also to heaven, and perhaps human sins strike even God Himself with grief. Or is not that the voice of one mourning, when He says: "It repenteth me that I made man upon the earth"? And likewise that word of our Lord and Savior in the Gospel, where He says: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, that stonest the prophets and killest those sent to thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and thou wouldst not!" And do not think that it was said only of the men of old that they stoned the prophets: I too today, if I do not hear the words of the prophet, if I spurn his admonitions, stone the prophet and, as far as in me lies, kill him, whose words, namely, I do not hear, as though he were dead. But that too is the voice of God lamenting the human race, in which it is said through the prophet: "Woe is me, for I am become as one who gathers stubble in the harvest and as gleanings in the vintage, for there is no ear of corn nor cluster of grapes to eat of the firstfruits! Woe is me, O my soul, for the reverent man has perished from the earth, and there is none among men to set them right!" These are the voices of the Lord mourning the human race. For He came to gather the harvest and found stubble instead of a harvest, and He came to gather the vintage, but found few clusters instead of a vintage — the Apostles, namely, whom unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us as a seed, and unless the grain of wheat had fallen into the earth to bring forth much fruit, we should have become as Sodom and been made like to Gomorrah. To the angels of God also, as we said above, there comes joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance. It is certain that where joys are held for good things, there mourning is held for the contrary; if therefore they rejoice over the one converted, they must needs mourn over the one sinning. Therefore, because Jerusalem sinned a great sin, according to what is written in the Lamentation, she is become an object of commotion, and all her festivities and her solemn days have perished, because in the holy place and on the day of festivity they killed my Lord Jesus Christ. And therefore He says to them: "Your new moons and your sabbaths and your feast days my soul hateth." Here indeed, where the command is about the offerings, where as yet there are no sins, He says "my feast days"; but where there is sin, the Lord says not "my," but "your" feast days. All these things, however, in which God is said to mourn or rejoice or hate or be glad, are to be understood as spoken by Scripture figuratively and after the manner of men. For the divine nature is far removed from every affection of passion and change, ever abiding, immovable and unshaken, upon that summit of blessedness.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Since, therefore, we have in our hands the laws of the feasts, and the discourse is now about them, let us inquire more diligently what the order of the festivals is, so that from the very orders and the rite of the sacrifices we may be able to gather how each one, out of his own acts and holy conversations, may be able to prepare a festivity for God. The first, then, of God's festivals is that which is called "unceasing"; for the command is about those things which are to be offered unceasingly and without any interruption at all in the morning and evening sacrifices. Therefore, in commanding the rites of the festivals, He did not come first at once to the festival of the Passover, nor to that of the unleavened bread, nor to that of tabernacles and the others concerning which He gives command, but He set this one first, in which He commands the unceasing sacrifice to be offered — so that whoever wishes to be perfect and holy may recognize that a festivity is not to be kept to God sometimes and sometimes not, but the just man ought always and unceasingly to keep a feast day. For the sacrifice which is commanded to be offered unceasingly, both in the morning and in the evening, indicates this: that in the law and the prophets, which show the morning time, and in the evangelical teaching, which shows the evening, that is, the coming of the Savior at the evening of the world, one should persist with unceasing attention. Such festivals, then, the Lord calls His own: "And you shall observe my feast days." It is therefore the Lord's feast day, if we offer Him sacrifice unceasingly, if we pray without intermission, so that our prayer ascends like incense in His sight in the morning, and the lifting up of our hands becomes to Him the evening sacrifice. The first solemnity, then, is that of the unceasing sacrifice, which by the worshippers of the Gospel ought to be fulfilled in the manner we have expounded above. But since, as the prophetic word has fully taught, the feast days of sinners are turned into mourning and their songs into wailing, it is certain that he who sins and keeps days of sin cannot keep a feast day; and therefore on those days on which he sins he cannot offer the unceasing sacrifice to God. But he can offer it who unceasingly keeps justice and preserves himself from sin. But on whatever day he interrupts this and sins, it is certain that on that day he does not offer the unceasing sacrifice to God. I am afraid to say something which is given to be understood from the Apostolic discourses, lest perhaps I seem to sadden some. For if the prayer of the just man is offered like incense in the sight of God, and the lifting up of his hands is the evening sacrifice, but the Apostle says to those who are in marriages: "Defraud not one another, except perhaps by consent for a time, that you may have leisure for prayer, and return again to the same," it is certain that the unceasing sacrifice is hindered for those who serve the necessities of marriage. Hence it seems to me that it belongs to him alone to offer the unceasing sacrifice, who has devoted himself to unceasing and perpetual chastity. But there are also other feast days for those who perhaps cannot unceasingly immolate the sacrifices of chastity.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The second festival, then, after the festival of the unceasing sacrifice, is set the sacrifice of the sabbath, and every holy and just man ought to keep also the festival of the sabbath. But what is the festival of the sabbath except that of which the Apostle says: "There remaineth therefore a sabbath-keeping," that is, an observance of the sabbath, "for the people of God"? Leaving aside, therefore, the Jewish observances of the sabbath, let us see of what sort the Christian's observance of the sabbath ought to be. On the sabbath day one ought to do no work out of all the works of the world. If, therefore, you cease from all secular works and do nothing worldly, but have leisure for spiritual works, come together to the church, lend an ear to the divine readings and expositions, think upon heavenly things, take thought for the hope to come, keep the judgment that is to come before your eyes, look not to present and visible things but to invisible and future things — this is the Christian's observance of the sabbath. But these things the Jews too ought to observe. Finally, even among them, if a smith, if a builder, and if any workman of this kind there be, he is idle on the sabbath day; but the reader of the divine law or the teacher does not cease from his work, and yet does not defile the sabbath; for so the Lord too says to them: "Have you not read that the priests too in the temple profane the sabbath and are without blame?" He therefore who has ceased from the works of the world and has leisure for spiritual acts, this is he who keeps the sacrifice of the sabbath and the feast day of the sabbaths. Nor does he carry burdens on the way; for every sin is a burden, as the prophet also says: "Like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me." Nor does he kindle a fire — that fire, namely, of which it is said: "Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame which you have kindled." On the sabbath each one sits in his own place and does not go forth from it. What, then, is the place of the spiritual soul? Justice is its place, truth, wisdom, sanctification, and all that Christ is, is the place of the soul. From which place it ought not to go forth, that it may keep the true sabbaths and fulfill the feast day in the sacrifices of the Sabbaths, as the Lord also said: "He who abides in me, and I in him." But as to what we called the true sabbaths, if we seek out more deeply what the true sabbaths are, the observance of the true sabbath is beyond this world. For that which is written in Genesis, that "the Lord rested on the sabbath day from his works," we do not see either to have been done then on the seventh day or to be done even now. For we always see God working, and there is no sabbath on which God does not work, on which He does not bring forth His sun over the good and the evil and rain upon the just and the unjust, on which He does not bring forth on the mountains hay and grass for the service of men, on which He does not smite and heal, lead down to hell and bring back, on which He does not kill and make alive. Hence the Lord too in the Gospels, when the Jews laid down a rule for Him about working and healing on the sabbath, answered them: "My Father worketh until now, and I work," showing by these words that on no sabbath of this world does God rest from the dispensations of the world and from the provisions for the human race. For He indeed made the creatures from the beginning and brought forth substances, as many as He knew, being the Founder of things, could suffice for the perfection of the world, but until the consummation of the age He does not cease from their provision and dispensation. There will be, therefore, a true sabbath, in which God will rest from all His works — the age to come, then, when grief and sadness and groaning shall flee away, and God shall be all and in all. On which sabbath may God grant us too to keep a feast day with Him and to celebrate festivals with His holy angels, offering the sacrifice of praise and rendering to the Most High our vows, which here our lips have set apart. Then perhaps also the unceasing sacrifice, of which we expounded above, will be better offered. For then the soul will better be able unceasingly to stand before God and to offer the sacrifice of praise through the great high priest, who is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The third festival is set as the day of the new moon, on which a victim also is offered. Now "neomenia" means the new moon. This too, then, is a festival, when the moon is renewed. And it is called "new" when it has been made nearest to the sun and very closely joined to it, so that it hides beneath its brightness. But perhaps it may seem wonderful, indeed superfluous, that the divine law should command this. For what does it profit religion to observe as a festival the new moon, that is, when it is joined to the sun and cleaves to it? If these things are considered according to the letter, they will seem not so much religious as superstitious; but the Apostle Paul knew that the law does not speak of these things, nor did the Holy Spirit command that rite which seems to be observed by the Jews; and therefore he said to those who had received the faith of God: "Let no one therefore judge you in food or drink or in respect of a feast day or of a new moon or of a sabbath, which are a shadow of things to come." If, therefore, the sabbath, of which we expounded above as best we could, is a shadow of things to come, and the new moon is a shadow of things to come, it is certain that the other festivals likewise are shadows of things to come. But now let us look at the new moon. We said that the festival is called the new moon when the moon has begun to be renewed and to be made nearest to the sun and wholly joined to it. The Sun of justice is Christ; if the moon, that is, His Church, which is filled with His light, be joined to Him and cleave wholly to Him, so that, according to the word of the Apostle, "he who joins himself to the Lord becomes one spirit with Him," then it keeps the festival of the new moon; for then it is made new, when it has cast off the old man and put on the new, who is created according to God, and thus deservedly keeps the solemnity of renewal, which is the festival of the new moon. And it is then, finally, when it can neither be seen nor comprehended by human sight. For when the soul has wholly allied itself to the Lord and has wholly withdrawn into the splendor of His light, and thinks nothing at all earthly, seeks nothing worldly, nor is eager to please men, but has surrendered itself wholly to the light of wisdom, wholly to the warmth of the Holy Spirit, made subtle and spiritual — how can it be discerned by men or apprehended by human sight? For the animal man cannot understand and discern the spiritual man. And therefore most worthily will it keep the feast day and will slay to the Lord the victim of the new moon, as one renewed through Him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In the fourth place among the festivals of God is set the solemnity of the Passover, in which festival the lamb is slain. But do you look to the true lamb, the Lamb of God, the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world, and say: "Our pasch, Christ, is sacrificed." Let the Jews in a carnal sense eat the flesh of the lamb, but let us eat the flesh of the Word of God; for He Himself said: "Unless you eat my flesh, you will not have life in yourselves." This which we are now speaking is the flesh of the Word of God, provided at least that we do not offer, as to the weak, herbs, or, as to children, the nourishment of milk. If we speak perfect things, if strong, if mighty, we set before you the flesh of the Word of God to eat. For where mystical discourse, where doctrinal discourse, filled with the faith of the Trinity, is brought forth solid, where, the veil being removed, the spiritual mysteries of the letter of the law of the age to come are laid open, where the hope of the soul, torn away from the earth, is cast into the heavens and set among those things which eye has not seen nor ear heard nor have they ascended into the heart of man — all these are the flesh of the Word of God; and he who can feed on them with perfect understanding and a purified heart truly immolates the sacrifice of the festival of the Passover and keeps a feast day with God and His angels.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After this, indeed joined continuously to it, follows the festival of the unleavened bread, which you will rightly celebrate if you drive out every leaven of malice from your soul and keep the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. For it is not to be supposed that Almighty God writes laws for men about leaven, and for that reason commands the soul to be exterminated from the people, if perchance it is found to have had in its house any little bit of this leaven from the sprinkled flour; and that such care was a matter of great concern to the divine Majesty, that He should say Himself so greatly offended on account of this leaven, that He commands the soul which He Himself made to His own image and likeness to be exterminated and overthrown on this account — this does not seem to me an understanding worthy of the divine laws; but rather it is this, at which God shudders and rightly shudders, if the soul be leavened with the spirit of malice, of anger, of wickedness, and swell up to shameful deeds. These God does not wish to be in the soul, and unless we cast out such leaven from the house of our soul, we shall deservedly be exterminated. But do not despise it, even if you see a small malice being leavened within you, because a little leaven corrupts the whole lump; and therefore do not be negligent even of a small sin, since from one sin another too is generated. For just as from justice justice is generated, and from chastity chastity — for if anyone first begins to be chaste in a slight degree, having received the leaven of chastity he becomes daily more chaste — so also he who has once stored up within himself even a small leaven of malice becomes daily more wicked and worse than himself. And therefore, if you wish to keep the festival of unleavened bread with God, do not suffer even a small leaven of malice to remain within you.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After this follows the sixth festival, which is called of the "new fruits," that is, when the firstfruits of the new produce are offered. For when the field has been sown and diligently cultivated, and the crop has come to maturity, then in the perfection of the fruits the festival of the Lord is kept. If, therefore, you too wish to keep the feast day of the new fruits with God, see how you sow or where you sow, that you may be able to reap such fruits from which you may make God glad and keep a feast day. This you will not be able to fulfill otherwise, unless you hear the Apostle saying: "He who sows in the spirit, of the spirit shall reap life everlasting." If you so sow and so reap, you will truly keep the feast day of the new fruits. Finally, therefore, the prophet also admonishes, saying: "Renew for yourselves new tillage, and do not sow upon thorns." He therefore who renews his heart and his inner man from day to day, this man renews for himself new tillage and sows not upon thorns but upon the good earth, which renders him fruit thirtyfold or sixtyfold or a hundredfold. This, then, is he who sows in the spirit and gathers the fruits of the spirit. And the first of all the fruits of the spirit is joy. And he rightly keeps the feast day of the new fruits who reaps joy, especially if together he reaps also peace and patience and goodness and gentleness; and if he gather the other fruits like to these, he will most worthily keep the festival of the new fruits to the Lord.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After these, in the seventh month other solemnities are kept. On the "first day of the month" the new moon of the trumpets, as it says in the Psalm: "sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month". But on the "tenth day of the seventh month" is this solemnity of atonement. "On this" day alone the high priest is clothed with all the priestly garments, then he is clothed with "manifestation and truth", then he enters into those inaccessible places, whither it is permitted to approach only "once in the year", that is, into the "holy of holies". For "once in the year" the high priest, leaving the people, enters into that place where is the "propitiatory" and above the "propitiatory" the "cherubim", where is also the "ark of testimony" and the "altar of incense", whither it is lawful for no one to enter except the high priest alone.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then next follows the festival of the sevenths. For just as among the days every seventh day is observed as a sabbath and is a festival, so also among the months every seventh month is the sabbath of the months. There is therefore kept in it the festival which is called the sabbath of sabbaths, and on the first day of the month there is made the memorial of trumpets. But who is it that keeps the festival of the memorial of trumpets, except he who is able to commit to memory the prophetic and evangelical and apostolic scriptures, which sound forth like a certain heavenly trumpet, and to store them up within the treasury of his heart? He therefore who does this, and meditates on the law of God day and night, this man keeps the festival of the memorial of trumpets. But also, if anyone is able to merit those graces of the Holy Spirit by which the prophets were inspired, and to say, singing psalms: "Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the day of its notable solemnity," and he who knows how to make a joyful noise in the psalms, he worthily keeps to God the solemnity of the trumpets.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There is still also another festival, when they afflict their souls and humble themselves, celebrating festivals to God. O wondrous festival: the affliction of the soul is called a feast day! "For this," He says, "is the day of propitiation, on the tenth day of the seventh month." See, therefore, if you wish to keep a feast day, if you wish that God rejoice over you, afflict your soul and humble it. Do not permit it to fulfill its desires, nor grant it to wander off into wantonness, but as far as can be done, afflict and humble it. Finally, both the festival of the Passover and that of the unleavened bread is said to have the bread of affliction, nor can anyone keep a feast day unless he has eaten the bread of affliction, and has eaten the pasch with bitterness. "For you shall eat," He says, "the unleavened bread with bitterness," or with bitter herbs. You see, therefore, of what sort the festivals of God are; they admit no bodily sweetness, they wish nothing relaxed, nothing voluptuous or luxurious, but they demand affliction of the soul and bitterness and humility, because "he who humbles himself shall himself be exalted" before God. This, then, the day of propitiation too demands; for when the soul has been afflicted and humbled in the sight of the Lord, then God is made propitious to it again, and then there comes to it He whom God set forth as a propitiator through faith in His blood, Christ Jesus, its Lord and redeemer.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But now let us see what is the last feast day of God, on which God rejoices in man. "Tabernacles," He says. He rejoices, then, over you when He sees you dwelling in this world in tents, when He sees you not having your mind and purpose fixed and founded upon the earth, nor desiring the things that are earthly, nor reckoning the shadow of this life as your own perpetual possession, but as though set in transit and hastening to that true fatherland of paradise, whence you came forth, and saying: "I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, as all my fathers." For the fathers too dwelt in tents, and Abraham dwelt in little huts, that is, in tents, with Isaac and Jacob, coheirs of the same promise. When, therefore, you have been a sojourner and a pilgrim on the earth, and your mind is not fixed and rooted in the desires of earthly things, but you are ready to pass over quickly and ready to stretch yourself always to the things that are before, until you arrive at the land flowing with milk and honey and receive the inheritance of things to come — if, I say, God sees you set in these things, He rejoices in you and will keep a feast day over you. These things indeed in the present; but as for the future, if you wish to consider how the feast days are kept there, lift up your senses a little, if you can, from the earth, and forget for a while these things that are held before your face. Describe to yourself how heaven and earth pass away, and how all this fashion of the world passes away, and a new heaven and a new earth is founded. Remove from your sight even the light of this sun, and give to that world which is to come a sevenfold light of this sun; nay rather, according to the authority of Scripture, give to it the Lord Himself as its light. Set the angels of glory standing by, set the virtues, powers, thrones, dominions, and every name of the most illustrious and heavenly powers, not only that which is named in the present age but also that which is named in the age to come. Among all these, consider and conjecture how the feast days of the Lord may be kept, what festivity there is there, what joys, what magnitude of gladness. For concerning those spiritual festivals of which we spoke above, even though they are great and true, especially when they are kept spiritually in the soul, yet they are in part, not in whole; for just as the Apostle said: "We know in part and we prophesy in part," so it follows that we keep a feast day in part. But that you may know that this is so, let us return to that very discourse of Paul which he set forth about feast days and new moons, and see how observantly he said: "Let no one therefore," he says, "judge you in food or in drink or in respect of a part of a feast day." Attend, therefore, more diligently how he did not say "on a feast day" but "in respect of a part of a feast day." For in part and not in whole do we, set in this world, celebrate the feast day; for we are interrupted, even against our will, by the burden of the flesh, we are beaten by its concupiscences, and are bored through by cares and anxieties. For "the corruptible body," as the most wise man says, "weighs down the soul and depresses the mind that ponders many things." In part, therefore, in this world do the saints keep the feast day, because in part they know and in part they prophesy. But when the things that are perfect shall have come, those things which are in part shall be destroyed. For just as this which is in part gives way to perfect knowledge, and this which is in part gives way to perfect prophecy, so also this festival which is in part gives way to the perfect festival. For neither can this world receive that which is perfect, where, as we have said, the necessity of the body now suggests food, now drink, now sleep, now also stirs up as much anxiety of the present life as is necessary; all of which without doubt interrupt the continuation of the festival of God. But when that shall have come which was said concerning those who shall be restored into the holy places — if indeed we too may be counted worthy to be among those who are to be restored, who shall neither hunger nor thirst nor slumber nor labor, but shall be ever-wakeful, as the life of the angels is said to be ever-wakeful — when they shall be counted worthy to be restored into that order, then there will be a true and incorrupt festival, of which festival the prince and bridegroom and lord will be Jesus Christ Himself, our Savior, to whom is glory and dominion unto ages of ages. Amen!

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: All who are to be trained in the higher disciplines regard the labor of the rudiments as burdensome, so long as they do not know what the end and fruit of that discipline is to which they are being introduced. But when, having been led through in order, the perfection of the discipline has been attained, then it will be a delight to have endured the burdens of the rudiments. There are, therefore, also in holy and divine matters certain first rudiments, by which those are introduced who strive toward the perfection of blessedness. This the servant of God clearly indicates in the song of Exodus, saying: "Bringing them in, plant them on the mountain of your inheritance, in your prepared dwelling, which you have prepared, O Lord." Paul the Apostle also, knowing that there are certain first beginnings of instruction, and that then afterward, in the course of time, one comes even to perfection, writing to certain persons said: "For indeed, when you ought already to be teachers by reason of the time, you again need to be taught what are the elements of the beginning of the words of God, and you have become such as have need of milk, not strong food. For everyone who is fed on milk is inexperienced in the word of righteousness; for he is a little child. But solid food is for the perfect, who according to their capacity for receiving have their senses trained to the discernment of good or evil." And again elsewhere he recalls that the letter of the law and every writing of this kind are the elements of the world. And so now those things which pertained to those who were being instructed in the first elements seem burdensome to us at first hearing; for when each of the hearers wishes to learn about those things which pertain to salvation, and there is recited to them about the sacrifices of rams and goats and calves, they judge that writings of this kind confer no benefit upon them, so far as concerns the hearing itself. But if there be found anyone who can remove the veil which is placed upon the reading of the Old Testament, and thence search out what are the true sacrifices which purify the people on the festal days, then he will see how wonderful and magnificent are the things which are indicated through these, which by the ignorant are held to be superfluous and superstitious. But these things indeed Paul, and any who are like him, will have come to know more fully and more perfectly from Wisdom herself and from the Word of God; but we, so far as we can gather from their own writings, in which they have given us certain indications as it were through shadow and image, will attempt to discuss summarily, for the common edification, some things concerning the rite of the sacrifices. At the festival of Passover a lamb is written to be that which purifies the people, in others a calf, in others a goat or a ram or a she-goat or a heifer, as you have learned from those things which have been recited. One therefore of these animals which are taken to purify the people is the lamb. And this lamb is said to be our Lord and Savior himself. For thus understood John, who is greater than all the prophets, and he indicated concerning him, saying: "Behold, the Lamb of God, behold, him who takes away the sin of the world." But if the lamb which was given to purify the people is referred to the person of our Lord and Savior, it seems to follow that the other animals also, which are appointed to these same uses of purification, ought likewise to be referred to certain persons who confer something of purification upon the human race. See therefore whether perhaps, just as our Lord and Savior, led like a lamb to the slaughter and offered as a sacrifice upon the altar, granted remission of sins to the whole world, so perhaps also the blood of the other saints and just ones, which has been shed from the blood of Abel the just even to the blood of Zechariah the prophet, who was slain between the temple and the altar — the blood of one poured out as of a heifer, of another as of a goat or a she-goat or of one of these — was shed to expiate the people for some part. Whether therefore these things are to be seen as referred to the persons of the just and the prophets who were slaughtered in this world, or of those who say: "For your sake we are put to death all the day long, we are counted as sheep for the slaughter," or even to the higher powers to whom the care of the human race has been given, who would easily dare to affirm? For these animals are to be thought referred to this or that person not by species, but by figure. For the Lord Jesus Christ himself is not called a lamb as though he had been changed and turned into the species of a lamb. Yet he is called a lamb because his will and goodness, by which he propitiated God toward men and gave pardon of sins, was such, being to the human race as it were the immaculate and innocent victim of a lamb, by which the divine powers are believed to be appeased toward men. So therefore perhaps also, if there is any of the angels and heavenly powers, or if any of the just men or even of the holy prophets and Apostles who intervenes more earnestly for the sins of men, he can be taken as having been offered a sacrifice for the divine propitiation, like a ram or a calf or a goat, to obtain purification for the people. Or does not Paul seem to have offered himself as a whole-burnt-offering like a ram or a goat for the people of Israel, when he said: "I myself indeed was wishing to be anathema from Christ for my brethren, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh"? And do you wish to know that Paul offers himself as a victim to be slaughtered? Hear him saying also in another place: "For now I am being sacrificed, and the time of my dissolution" — or, as we read in the Greek codices, "of my return" — "is at hand." So therefore it can be seen figuratively that one is offered for the festival of the new moons, another for the festival of the sabbath, another for the festival of tabernacles, like a goat or a calf or a ram, to reconcile God to men. For so long as there are sins, it is necessary that victims also be sought for sins. For suppose, for example, that there had been no sin; if there had been no sin, it would not have been necessary for the Son of God to become a lamb, nor would there have been need for him, placed in the flesh, to be slaughtered, but this would have remained, which in the beginning was God the Word; but since sin entered into this world, and the necessity of sin requires propitiation, and propitiation does not come about except through a victim, it was necessary that a victim be provided for sin. And since the qualities of sin itself were diverse and various, the victims of diverse animals are commanded, without doubt such as would suit the varieties of sins. So therefore it comes about that one of the saints — whether of angels, as we have said, or of men — is a calf, who intervenes at that festival for the transgressions of the people, and another is a ram at another festival; by whose intercession purification is made for sins. But if men can be purified from sins and be purer, the victims also are diminished. For if the victims are for sins, and for the multitude of sins they are without doubt multiplied, so also for the smallness of sins they are diminished. And of this matter we have indications in the present passages of Scripture, that is, in the last festival of the setting-up-of-tents, when for eight days victims are commanded to be offered. And on the first day indeed, as though still in an abundance of sins, fourteen calves are commanded to be offered. But on the second day, the sins as it were being diminished, the victims also are diminished, and thirteen calves are offered. On the third day twelve, and after this eleven, and thus, as the multitude of sins fails through the days by the purifications, the number of victims also is consequently diminished. So therefore understand also, for the dispensation of the whole world, the account of purification; for not only the things which are on the earth need purification, but also the things which are in the heavens. For destruction threatens the heavens also; for thus says the prophet: "The heavens shall perish, and all shall grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you shall roll them up and they shall be changed." Behold therefore the purification of the whole world, that is, of the heavenly and the earthly and the infernal; see how many victims all these need, how many calves they require, how many rams, how many goats. But in all these there is one lamb, who could take away the sin of the whole world; and therefore the other victims have ceased, because this victim was such that it alone sufficed for the salvation of the whole world. For the others remitted sins by prayers, this one alone by power; for he said: "Son, your sins are forgiven you." So therefore the world is first instructed to seek remission of sins through diverse victims, until it comes to the perfect victim, to the consummated victim, the perfect yearling lamb, who takes away the sin of the whole world; through whom it may keep spiritual festivals, not to the satiety of the flesh, but to the advancement of the spirit, spiritual sacrifices being offered by the purification of the mind. For it is fitting that there be immolated to God the victim of the heart and the sacrifice of a contrite spirit, not of flesh and blood to be slaughtered, because even though we have known Christ at one time according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus, and therefore let us keep the festal day in the spirit and let us slaughter spiritual sacrifices. Let these things be discussed by us, according to our strength, concerning the diversity of the sacrifices, the clear understanding of which he knows to whom all things are bare and revealed, nor is there any creature invisible in his sight.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After these things the law of vows is set down, and Moses uses a new beginning in this legislation; for he says: "A man, a man, whoever shall vow a vow to the Lord." What is the reason for this repeating of the name? As though it did not suffice to have said: "A man who shall vow a vow to the Lord." What is it therefore that he says, "a man, a man," and what this doubled naming of "man" means, does not seem to me to be passed over in silence. The Apostle teaches that there is one inner man and another outer, and that the former is he who is renewed from day to day according to the image of him who created him, but that the latter is the visible one, who is corrupted. When therefore one comes to that advancement, that the law of God may be received and vows offered to the Lord — and no one can offer vows to the Lord except him who has something within himself and in his own substance which he may offer to God — this outer man does not suffice to receive the law of God nor to offer vows alone, for he cannot have anything worthy of God, but it is that inner man who rather has in himself what he may offer to God; for in him is the dwelling of the virtues, in him all understanding of knowledge, in him is the renewal of the divine image. And when he has recovered his form, by which he was made from the beginning by God, and by the restoration of the virtues has received back the beauty of his former shape, then he can now offer vows to God, and then he will now be called not "man" only, but "man, man." For he who does not cultivate the inner man, who takes no care of him, who does not equip him with virtues, does not adorn him with morals, does not exercise him in divine instructions, does not seek the wisdom of God, does not expend labor on the knowledge of the scriptures — this one cannot be called "man, man," but only "man," and an animal man, because that inner one, to whom the name "man" more truly and more nobly belongs, is lulled to sleep in him by carnal vices and overwhelmed by the cares and anxieties of this world, so that not even the naming of his name can be had. Wherefore each of us must strive earnestly that, if perhaps he sees the inner man in himself lying oppressed with the filth of sins and the rubble of vices, he may more quickly remove from him all uncleannesses, more quickly rescue him from every defilement of flesh and blood, be converted at last to repentance, recall to himself the memory of God, recall the hope of salvation. For these things are not to be sought from somewhere outside, but within us is the occasion of salvation, as the Lord also said: "For behold, the kingdom of God is within you." For within us is the faculty of conversion; for when, being converted, you shall have groaned, you shall be saved, and then you will be able worthily to render your vows to the Most High and to be called "man, man." Now a vow is when we offer something of our own to God. God therefore wishes first to receive something from us, and so himself to bestow upon us, that he may be seen to bestow his gifts and rewards upon the deserving and not upon the undeserving. But what is it that God wishes to receive from us? Hear the sentence of Scripture: "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, but that you fear the Lord your God, and walk in all his ways, and love him with your whole heart and with your whole soul and with all your strength?" These therefore are the things which God asks of us. And if we do not first offer them, we shall receive nothing from him. We read also in another place: "Give glory to God," and: "Give magnificence to God." If you give glory, you will receive glory; for thus God himself says: "Those who glorify me I will glorify." But I say that, if we also offer him our righteousness, we shall receive from him the righteousness of God; and if we offer him our chastity, that is, of the body, we shall receive from him the chastity of the spirit; and if we offer him our understanding, we shall receive from him his own understanding, as the Apostle also said: "But we have the mind of Christ." And when we have offered to God the things which are in us, and he has bestowed upon us the things which are his, then truly we shall now be called not "man" only, but "man, man"; for each man is fittingly adorned with the perfection of his name. These therefore are the vows which he ought to pay who is called "man, man." I know that diverse vows are related in the scriptures. Hannah indeed vowed to God the fruit of her womb and consecrated Samuel in the temple. Another vowed to God whatever should meet him returning after victory, and, his daughter meeting him, paid his vows with tears. Others offer to God calves or rams or houses or other vows of this kind lacking reason. But he who is called a Nazirite devoted himself to God; for this is the vow of the Nazirite, which is above every vow. For to offer a son or a daughter or cattle or an estate — all this is outside of us; but to offer oneself to God, and to please him not by another's labor but by one's own, this is more perfect and more excellent than all vows; and he who does this is an imitator of Christ. For he gave to man the earth, the sea, and all that is in them; he gave them for his service, and he granted heaven, the sun also and the moon and the stars, to the ministry of men; rains, winds, and all whatsoever is in the world, he bestowed upon men. But after all these things he gave himself; for thus God loved the world, that he gave his only-begotten Son for the life of this world. What great thing therefore will man do if he offers himself to God, to whom God himself first offered himself? If therefore you take up your cross and follow Christ, if you say: "But I live, now not I, but Christ lives in me"; if our soul desires and thirsts to return and to be with Christ, as the Apostle also said, and is not delighted with the allurements of the present age; and if he spiritually fulfills all the law which was given concerning the Nazirites — then he has offered himself, that is, his soul, to God. He who lives in chastity has vowed his body to God, according to him who said: "But the virgin considers how she may be holy in body and spirit." For this very thing which he said, "holy," looks to this; for those are called holy who have vowed themselves to God. Whence also a ram, for example, if it is vowed to God, is called holy, and it is not lawful to shear it for common uses. But a calf also, if it has been devoted to God, is nonetheless called holy, and it is not lawful to yoke it for common work. From these things therefore let us gather what it is for a man to vow himself to God. If you vow yourself to God, the calf is to be imitated by you, which is not permitted to serve human works — to do nothing which pertains to men and to the present life. But whatever pertains to the soul and to the observance of divine worship, this is both to be done and to be pondered by you.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But meanwhile the present reading contains certain distinctions among vows. For if it be a man who vows, he is said to be free in his vows and subject to no one. But if a woman vows, then, if indeed she be in her father's house, her vow hangs upon her father's judgment; and if he refuses it, she is released; but if he does not refuse it, both he and the daughter are held liable. But if, after the father has not refused, she does not fulfill the vow, the daughter's sin remains upon him. And in like manner it is decreed also concerning the husband, that, if a wife has vowed something in her husband's house and the husband on hearing it does not refuse, he is guilty of the vow equally with his wife; but if he refuses, then the wife is as free as the husband; but if he keeps silent, both, as we have said, are held guilty. These indeed are the things that are written; but we must pray to God that he may deign to give an understanding worthy of himself, whereby we may be able to perceive these things as it is fitting they be understood concerning the words of God. All of us who live under the law of God and are counted in his Church, some pass our life under fathers, some under husbands. And if the soul is a little one and has its beginnings in the divine instructions, this soul is to be believed to conduct itself under a father. But if it has already become more grown up, so that it is capable of a husband for conceiving the seed of the word of God and of receiving the secrets of spiritual teaching, this soul is said to be placed under a husband. For thus also Paul said concerning the Corinthians: "I wish to present you all as a chaste virgin to one husband, to Christ." But those who are more perfect and more eminent than these, of them it is not said that they are under a husband, but hear how Paul pronounces concerning himself and those like him: "until we all," he says, "come together into the perfect man, into the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ." Over this soul, then, which comes together into the perfect man, no one is master in vows, but it has power over its own things and freedom of its vows. But if the soul be still of the feminine kind, over which either a husband or a father is master in vows, the fault is not always in the soul itself, but sometimes it returns upon the husbands or the parents. Concerning these, although it be difficult to apply, nevertheless the things that, by the Lord's bounty, have been able to occur to us we will set forth.
