We have often said that the care and management of the souls which are in the Church of God is exercised through angels, and we have shown that these too come to judgment along with men, so that in that divine scrutiny it may be established whether men have sinned through their own sloth or through the negligence of their admonishers and guardians. It seems to me, therefore, that in this passage also the same thing is designated and shown under a mystery, namely that some souls dwell under these as daughters, others as wives, according to the things which we distinguished above. If, therefore, any of these desires to offer something and to vow it to God, then, if what she vows is over-hasty and less fitting, it belongs to him—namely to the angel, as her guardian and admonisher—to check and beat back the boldness of her who vows. But if, on hearing it, he does not check it, does not admonish, the soul indeed is freed from fault, but he himself will remain liable to the vow. This indeed is to be taken as happening with regard to any of the lower sort; but with the more perfect God himself is present, as it is written concerning the people of Israel: "But the Lord himself led them." But after they had transgressed and had made themselves lower than themselves, they are handed over to an angel. Whence Moses too said: "Unless you yourself come with us, do not lead me up hence." But also concerning another he says: "I am with him in tribulation," and elsewhere he says: "Do not fear to go down into Egypt, for I will be with you." To the just, therefore, and the elect God himself is present, but to the lower angels are present, governing and caring for them according to the things we said above, sometimes transferring their vows to themselves, but sometimes leaving them upon those very persons. But we ought to strive that we may come together into the perfect man, into the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, that we may use the freedom of vows and so hasten to cleave to the Lord that with him, rather than with an angel, we may be one spirit, so that he himself may abide in us and we in him, and that nothing feminine, nothing of little age, may be found in us, nor be it necessary for us to be left under guardians and stewards by the father, but let us hasten to hear from our Lord and Savior that voice in which he says: "the Father himself loves you." To him be glory unto the ages of ages. Amen!

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: In the passages above, the sons of Israel committed fornication with the women of the Midianites, and this was a stumbling-block to the sons of Israel, in which they offended the Lord and provoked to anger the Holy One of Israel. Now therefore, after Israel had suffered what it suffered, "the Lord spoke," it says, "to Moses, saying: Avenge the vengeance of the sons of Israel upon the Midianites, and afterward you shall be added to your people." Therefore, as for the stumbling-blocks that had befallen the Israelites, since they had befallen them through the treachery of the Midianites — for they themselves had suborned the women who were to deceive them, so that they might sin before the Lord — those men indeed suffered punishment for their sin, yet more moderately and more sparingly, whereas these, who were the cause of their sinning, are subjected to a far more severe vengeance. Whence we are taught that it is far graver to furnish others the occasion of sin than for each one himself to sin, just as the Lord also indicates, when He says that: "It were better for a man not to have been born, or that an ass's millstone be tied about his neck and that he be cast into the depth of the sea, than that he should scandalize one of these little ones." And at the same time it must be noted that the name of "scandal" is improperly assumed by some — that a scandal is said to be there, where for one walking on the straight road some deception toward sin is contrived and the cause of sinning is put beneath him, just as also the Midianites, for the Israelites walking in the law of the Lord and keeping chastity, suborned the women who were to deceive them into sinning. Therefore to furnish the cause of sin, this is to scandalize. And yet punishment is given, but far graver upon those who scandalized, who furnished the cause of sin, than upon those who sinned. At the same time observe also that which He added to these things: "but at the last," He says, "you also shall be added to your people." If ever we have discourse with the Samaritans, since indeed they deny the resurrection of the dead and do not accept the faith of the age to come, let us press them hard from these words, in which the Lord says to Moses that he is to be added to his people. For no one is added to those who do not exist. Whence it is established that there is some people to which Moses is said to be joined after the departure from this life. Since therefore the Samaritans do not believe the prophets, from whom the faith of the resurrection of the dead could be more amply proved, at least from these books of Moses, which they receive and whose authority they confess, they are to be convicted and cured — if indeed even Babylon ought to be cured. This passage, then, is one that evidently shows the resurrection of the dead. For it indicates that there is a people to whom Moses is to be joined after his death, and to whom he is to be transferred according to his merits.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After these things Moses spoke to the people, saying: "Arm men of yourselves and make war against Midian, to render vengeance from the Lord upon Midian; a thousand from a tribe and a thousand from a tribe; from all the tribes of Israel send men to make war." Attend to the reading; for the mind must be directed not only to the hearing of words, but to the consideration of the realities. Recall the things past, hear the things present, mark the things that follow. Compare the earlier things with the later, and contemplate the magnificence of the divine powers. The sons of Israel some time ago had been six hundred thousand armed men who had gone forth against Midian, and all these were conquered, because sin was in them. But now the Midianites, the victors, who had put to flight six hundred thousand, are conquered by twelve thousand, that you may know that Israel conquers not in a multitude nor in the number of soldiers, but there is righteousness and piety in those who conquer. Therefore, finally, it is also said in their blessings that, if they keep the law of the Lord, one of them shall pursue a thousand and two shall put ten thousand to flight. You see, then, that one holy man praying avails much more than innumerable sinners doing battle. The prayer of a holy man penetrates heaven: how should it not also conquer the enemy on earth? And therefore we must strive in every way to seek first and to keep the righteousness of God. And if you obtain and keep it, it will subject all your enemies to you; if you are clothed, as the Apostle says, in the breastplate of righteousness and girded with truth, if you have taken the helmet of salvation and the sword of the spirit and above all the shield of faith, in which you can quench all the fiery darts of the evil one. For, equipped with such arms, you will put to flight all the camps of the devil and all his army, and with confidence you will sing: "If camps stand against me, my heart shall not fear; if battle rise up against me, in this will I hope."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Therefore twelve thousand engage against the Midianites, and "they slay," it says, "all their males; and their kings and Balaam, the son of Beor, they slew with the sword together with the rest of their wounded." That which in the passages above we were inquiring — how it could be proved from the Scriptures that the women of the Midianites, who deceived the sons of Israel into fornicating, had been suborned by the counsel of Balaam — this present passage of Scripture evidently shows, saying that he was slain by the sword as the author of the scandal that was brought upon the sons of Israel. And it is said of him in what follows still more evidently in this way: "and Moses said to them: why have you preserved every woman alive? For it is they who, according to the word of Balaam, made the sons of Israel apostates." And the kings of the Midianites are also slain, and those who were formerly conquered by the women now, expiation being had and repentance performed, conquer even the kings. From this let us understand how much conversion to God avails, how much the amendment of sins profits. Every male, all the kings of the Midianites, are conquered and destroyed by those who through the correction of the Lord and through the repentance for their deeds were corrected and amended. Five kings of the Midianites, therefore, are reported to have been overcome by the Israelite soldiers.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the divine Scripture was also careful to record their names. "Evi," it says, "and Rekem and Zur and Hur and Reba." These are they who reign among the Midianites, whom everyone who serves God as a soldier ought to overcome and utterly to destroy. For Evi is interpreted "beastly" or "wild." And how will you be able to please Him who has approved you, if you do not cut off from yourself and utterly destroy beastly and wild ways? How will you be able to attain to the beatitude of the meek, unless first you slay Evi and hand over to death the wildness of all anger? I think that the divine Scripture did not narrate these names for the sake of history, but fitted them for the sake of causes and realities. For do you suppose there would have been anyone so foolish as to impose on his son the name "Beastly"? But I judge rather that the divine word looked to the instruction of souls, wishing to show us that we ought to make war against vices of this kind and to drive them from the dwellings of our flesh, to put these kings to flight from the kingdom of our body; which the Apostle more evidently indicates, saying: "Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body." But do you wish to see that not only among the saints are names fitted to realities, but also among the Gentiles and Barbarians? Concerning the saints indeed it is known why Abram was called Abraham, and Sarah Sarra, and Jacob Israel. But let us show that this custom is held also among the Barbarians. Had not one of the sons of Israel received from his parents the name Joseph? But when he passed into Egypt and stood before Pharaoh, he changed his name and from Joseph surnamed him Zaphenath-paneah, which Pharaoh in his own tongue composed from the revelation of secrets or of dreams. And not only is a name fitted to Joseph from the reality before Pharaoh, but Daniel too in Babylon is named Belteshazzar, and Hananiah and Azariah and Mishael are called Shadrach, Meshach, Abednego. You see, then, that both the names of Israelite men and even of barbarian men are fitted in the law not by chance, but for the sake of realities and causes. Therefore Moses called the king of the Midianites as he himself judged he should be called. "It is a beastly wildness," he says, "that reigns among the Midianites, and not that alone, but there is also among them another king by the name of Rekem, which in our tongue is 'emptiness.'" Emptiness, then, also reigns among the nation of the Midianites; for there is in truth much emptiness and vanity in this world — nay, "vanity of vanities, and all is vanity" — which the soldier of God ought to overcome and conquer. But he conquers emptiness who does nothing emptily, nothing superfluous and that pertains not to the matter; who remembers that command of the Lord, in which He says that: "even for an idle word men shall render account in the day of judgment." But in this life almost everything men speak, everything they do, is idle and empty; for every act and every word is called empty in which there is not within something for God or for the commandment of God. There is also another king of Midian, Hur, and this is interpreted "provocation." You see what sort they are who reign among the Midianites, all of whom must be opposed, nay, whom it is fitting to be destroyed by those who follow God, and to be slain. For it is not so much the names of kings as of vices, which reign in men, that are reported in the law, and not so much the wars of nations as of carnal concupiscences, which do battle against the soul, that are described. Finally, those who reign in the vices are said to be five kings, that we may be most evidently taught that every vice which reigns in the body depends on the five senses. These five senses, then, are to be destroyed out of the kingdom of the Midianites, that no longer may vices reign over them, but righteousness, and that they may not look for a scandal at the things they see, but for edification. For among the Midianites these senses reigned unto scandalizing, that they might scandalize and deceive. And therefore the Lord commanded that, if your eye scandalize you, you pluck it out; if your hand or foot, you cut it off. You see, then, that He Himself commands the kings of those who scandalize to be cut off and destroyed. "It is better," He says, "for you one-eyed to enter into the kingdom of God, and maimed or lame, than with these to be cast into Gehenna." In which He by no means commands the eye of our body to be dug out, nor the hand or foot to be cut off, but He commands the sense that perceives carnal things and wantons in carnal concupiscences to be cut off, that our eyes may see right things and our ears hear right things and our taste taste the word of God and our hands handle and touch of the Word of life. And this is that in which, the kings of the Midianites being destroyed and the affections of scandal amputated, there reigns in us as righteousness our very Lord Jesus Christ, who was made for us righteousness from God, and peace, and redemption.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Therefore twelve thousand engage against the Midianites, and "they slay," it says, "all their males; and their kings and Balaam, the son of Beor, they slew with the sword together with the rest of their wounded." That which in the passages above we were inquiring — how it could be proved from the Scriptures that the women of the Midianites, who deceived the sons of Israel into fornicating, had been suborned by the counsel of Balaam — this present passage of Scripture evidently shows, saying that he was slain by the sword as the author of the scandal that was brought upon the sons of Israel. And it is said of him in what follows still more evidently in this way: "and Moses said to them: why have you preserved every woman alive? For it is they who, according to the word of Balaam, made the sons of Israel apostates." And the kings of the Midianites are also slain, and those who were formerly conquered by the women now, expiation being had and repentance performed, conquer even the kings. From this let us understand how much conversion to God avails, how much the amendment of sins profits. Every male, all the kings of the Midianites, are conquered and destroyed by those who through the correction of the Lord and through the repentance for their deeds were corrected and amended. author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Finally, in the present reading, Eleazar the priest is not written as speaking to all the people, but only to those who return from the battle. For it says: "and Eleazar the priest said to the men of valor, who were returning from the battle." You see, then, how the word of God speaks to the men of valor. For men of valor are they who go forth to war. But if anyone is unwilling to fight and to be a soldier, if anyone is unwilling to have the contest of divine studies and of abstinence, this man is unwilling to fulfill that which the Apostle said: "but he who contends in the contest is continent from all things." He, then, who does not contend in the contest and is not continent from all things, nor wishes to be exercised in the word of God and to meditate on the law of the Lord day and night, this man, even if he be called a man, cannot nevertheless be called a man of valor. But this one, of whom now the divine Scripture speaks, who brings back spoils from the enemy, is called a man of valor; for this is the mark of his praise, that Scripture says: "Eleazar the priest spoke to the men of valor, who were returning from the battle." Which of us is so prepared that he may go forth to war and fight against the adversaries, so that he too may be able to be called a man of valor? But as a continent life and the labor of abstinence and the struggles of contests make each one to be called a man of valor, so on the contrary a life relaxed and negligent and slothful makes a man to be called a man of sloth. If, then, you wish to be called a man of valor, clothe yourself with Christ the Lord, who is the power (virtus) of God and the wisdom of God, and in all things join yourself to the Lord so that you become one spirit with Him, and then you will be made a man of valor. For the time of war is for us in this world; the fight is against the Midianites, whether against the vices of our flesh, or against the contrary powers. The choir of angels and of the heavenly powers watches us; a devout expectation, therefore, hangs upon us as to when or how we may return from this battle, what each one of us may bring back of the spoils, and they look on more curiously and search more anxiously as to which of us bears from here more of gold, which also displays there a weight of silver, which too carries down precious stones. They inquire also, whether anyone bears down bronze or iron or lead, but also a wooden vessel, if perhaps anyone, or an earthen one, or another of this kind necessary for the uses of a great house. For in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and of clay. It is diligently inquired, therefore, when we shall have gone thither, what each one of us brings down, and according to the things he has brought down, according as his labor is proved by the contemplation of the spoils, the merit also of his abode will be reckoned to him. Yet all these things are tested — those through fire, by fire, and those through water, by water; for what sort each one's work is, the fire will prove.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Therefore it says: "This is the justification of the law which the Lord established for Moses: besides gold and silver and bronze and iron and lead and tin, every thing that passes through fire, pass it through fire and it shall be cleansed, but it shall also be purified in the water of purification; all things whatsoever that do not pass through fire shall pass through water. And you shall wash your garments on the seventh day, and you shall be clean; and after these things you shall enter into the camps." You see how everyone who has gone out of the battle of this life needs purification. And if this is so, that I may dare to say something according to the authority of Scripture, everyone who goes out of this life cannot be clean. For consider diligently what the text of the history indicates. These men went out to fight for the sons of Israel, they slew the Midianites; and in slaying them, as far as concerns the order of the history and the letter of the law, they pleased God — for they fulfilled the will of God. Yet by this very fact, that they slew the adversaries, they are said to have been made unclean, and therefore it is said to them: "and you shall wash your garments on the seventh day, and you shall be clean; and after these things you shall enter into the camps." Therefore those who fight, for this very reason that they touched the unclean enemies and that they engaged against them and had a contest with them, are polluted. And I too, therefore, even if I shall have been able to conquer the devil, even if the unclean and evil thoughts which he suggests to my heart I either repel as they come or slay them within me once they have entered, lest they come to effect — nay, even if I shall have been able to trample on the head of the dragon, yet by this very fact it is necessary that I be polluted and defiled, in that I strove to trample on him who is polluted and defiled. And I shall indeed be blessed that I was able to overcome him, yet I am unclean and polluted, who touched the polluted one, and on this account I need purification. Therefore, no doubt, Scripture also says that: "no one is clean from filth." All of us, then, need purification — nay, purifications; for many and diverse purifications await us. But these things are mystical and ineffable. For who will be able to narrate to us what are the purifications that are prepared for Paul or Peter or others like these, who fought so much, destroyed so many barbarous nations, laid low so many enemies, took so many spoils, so many triumphs, who return with bloodstained hands from the slaughter of the enemy, whose foot is dipped in blood, and who washed their hands in the blood of sinners? For they slew in the mornings all the sinners of the earth and exterminated their image from the city of the Lord. For they conquered and destroyed diverse nations of demons. For unless they had conquered these, they could not have taken captives from them — all this number of believers — and led them to the obedience of Christ and subjected them to His sweet yoke and laid upon them His light burden. Who, then, is so blessed as to succeed them in these battles and to slay all the Midianites and to be justified from their blood? For he is said to pour out the blood of demons who snatches away those over whom they hold dominion. And he shall be washed from this blood and purified in the kingdom of God, that, purified and made clean, he may be able to enter the holy city of God, Christ Jesus our Lord opening to him the door — nay, He who is the very door of that city of God, to whom is glory unto the ages of ages. Amen.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Therefore, by the command of the Lord, the wars against the Midianites were carried through by the sons of Israel; abundant spoils are brought back from them, an immense weight of gold and silver and of the other movable goods, a very great number of beasts and of captives. But since among the Israelites all these things are reckoned unclean, a purification suited to each several thing is applied; and those things indeed which consist of metals, fire purifies, but those which are more fragile and do not bear the fire are commanded to be purified by water. Therefore from all the spoils two equal parts are made, that one may be of those who had gone forth to war and the other of those who had remained in the camps. They are also commanded to offer from these into the gifts of God: those indeed who had gone forth to war, one head out of five hundred; but those who had remained in the camps, one out of fifty; and the number of all, collected together into one, is reported. This is the tenor of the history.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us see what the spiritual sense indicates in these things. In the people of God there are certain ones, as the Apostle says, who serve God as soldiers — those without doubt who do not entangle themselves in secular affairs; and these are they who go forth to war and fight against the enemy nations and against the spiritual wickednesses on behalf of the rest of the people and on behalf of those who are weaker, whether by age or by sex or by resolve. And these fight with prayers and fastings, with righteousness and piety, with meekness and chastity and all the virtues of continence, fortified as with weapons of war; and when they have returned to the camps as victors, even the unwarlike enjoy their labors, and those who either are not called to the fight or cannot go out. Yet it must be known that all things that are taken from these nations are unclean; and perhaps everything whatsoever is taken up in this world or captured in battle is unclean and needs purification; and certain of these things will pass through fire, but for others the purification of water will suffice. And there are taken up from the battle even men and beasts, when every understanding is taken captive to obey Christ. For unless we fight in the word of God, we shall not be able to take captive the understanding of those who think differently from Christ, and to lead them to the obedience of Christ. Yet few are they who can fight and carry through these battles; out of six hundred thousand and more armed men who seem to serve God as soldiers, only twelve thousand are chosen; the rest are left in the camps. Behold for me now the people of God that is in the Church, how many there are of those who can fight for the truth, who can resist those who contradict, who know how to handle the wars of the word. Blessed are these, who can fight for the whole people and defend the people of God and bring back abundant spoils from the enemy. Yet the remaining part of the people also, which seems unwarlike, if it reside quietly in the camps, if it act in silence and depart not from Moses but remain in the law of God, will itself also receive a part of the spoils. For an equal portion shall be made — not indeed by number, but as much as is given to all the rest of the people, so much also to those twelve thousand, by whose conquering the spoils were taken. Who, hearing these things, is not invited to the warfare of God? Who is not animated to fight for the Church and to resist against the enemies of truth — those, namely, who teach men either to oppose the doctrines of the Church, or to give their effort to pleasure and luxury? He, then, who overcomes these, and who destroys the vices either in himself or in his neighbors, this man will receive many spoils, multiplied fiftyfold beyond the others; for the quantity seems to be increased into so great a number, when twelve thousand are compared with six hundred thousand. Yet each part is commanded to offer to God. And those indeed who conquered, one out of five hundred; but those who remained at home, one out of fifty. And that the number of five hundred and of fifty is holy, Scripture testifies; whence also the Savior said in the Gospels: "A certain moneylender had two debtors; one of them owed five hundred denarii and the other fifty. When they had not the means to pay, he forgave both." But also seven weeks, a monad — that is, one — being added, make the fiftieth day, which is called the festival of Pentecost. Likewise also seventy weeks, the perfection of one decade being added, render the number of five hundred. But by as much as seventy weeks are more than seven, by so much is the number of five hundred more excellent and more perfect than fifty. Hence, finally, also in the parable of the Gospel, which we set forth above, our Savior declares that he loves more to whom the five hundred denarii which he owed were forgiven, than he to whom fifty were.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: That there are differences of progress and of merits among the people of the faithful, anyone who attends more carefully to the reading will discover in many places in the divine volumes. And we gather this no less from the present reading also, from what is written: "And there came to Moses all who had been appointed leaders throughout the tribes in the army, commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds. And they said to Moses: We your servants have gathered the sum total of our men of war, and not one of us was missing; and we have offered a gift to the Lord, each man whatever vessel of gold he found, a collar or a bracelet or a ring or an armlet or a little chain, to make propitiation for ourselves before the Lord." The chosen leaders, then, who had been appointed over the army, speak to Moses and, for their deeds well done, offer gifts to God, saying: "We are your servants, who have received the sum total of the warrior sons of Israel." Now by the sum total of the warriors they mean those twelve thousand men who were chosen out of all the tribes of Israel to do battle against the Midianites. There are, then, among the people of God many warriors, and there are also very many who are unfit for war; and again among the warriors there are certain ones who are called the sum total of the warriors, more eminent without doubt than those who are called warriors, just as the warriors too are more eminent than those unfit for war. And again there are some loftier than those who are called the sum total of the warriors, namely those who have been appointed leaders over them and set in command over each individual thousand of the chosen ones. There is, then, much diversity in that order which is called warriors. But even among those unfit for war there is nonetheless some difference; for not even they are all called unfit for war equally and in one and the same rank. For some are so unfit for war that they can never become warriors, as is old age and the whole female sex, and also the servile condition. But the age of boyhood is unfit for war in such a way that it holds a hope of one day becoming warlike; that is, when one shall have come to a perfect man, to the measure of the age, then they hope not only to become warriors out of boys, but also to come into the sum total of the warriors and to be chosen and to be numbered among the twelve thousand, or even to be preferred to these and to be leaders of the chosen ones.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Consider now the state of the present age, and see all things filled with wars and all human life hard pressed by invisible battles and by the assaults of demons, but that among the people of God there are certain ones so strong in faith and armed with virtues that against enemies of this kind they daily wage wars and, always standing ready in battle array, guard from the ambushes of the enemy not only themselves but also the rest who cannot fight, whether by reason of sex or of age or of the condition of servitude, fortifying them by the word of teaching and by the example of their life and by the diligence of their admonitions; provided, however, that faith be not lacking to them. For whether warriors or unfit for war, it is impossible to be saved without faith. Among the warriors themselves, however—those at least who serve as soldiers to God—consider that some are so ready and unencumbered that they entangle themselves in no worldly affairs at all, that they may be able to please him who has approved them, and also meditate on the law of God day and night. These, then, who are of this kind, are called the sum total of the warriors. Indeed it is not said of the common number of the warriors that no one among them was missing, but this is said of those who are named the sum total of the warriors. For among those who are such, there is no dissension, no discord. For these are they of whom it was said: "And the heart and soul of the believers was one, nor did any of them call anything his own, but all things were common to them." These, then, are the sum total of the warriors, among whom no one was missing. These are they who by fighting took a great abundance of gold, and offer to God all the gold and every ornament, whether of the head or of the arms or even of the fingers—that is, whatever they have in their understandings, whatever in their works—they offer to God. For they know that his gifts are his own, and therefore not even one among them dissents. For those set in dissension could not offer gifts to God. These, I think, are, according to the Gospel, those who diligently observe that precept which the Lord and Savior commands: "But if you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has anything against you, leave there your gift at the altar, and go, first be reconciled to your brother, and then coming you shall offer your gift"—namely, so that they may lift up their hands to God without wrath and dissension. These, then, are they who say: "We have gathered the sum total of our men of war, and not one of us was missing; and we have offered a gift to the Lord." Greatly, therefore, must we learn the discipline of concord; because, as in music, if the harmony of the strings has been fitted together in concord, it renders the sweet sound of a melodious song, but if there is any dissonance in the strings, a most disagreeable sound is rendered and the sweetness of the song is spoiled, so also those who serve as soldiers to God, if they have dissensions and discords among themselves, all things will be disagreeable and nothing will seem acceptable to God, even if they wage many wars, even if they carry off many spoils and offer many gifts to God. For it will be said to them: "Lay down your gift at the altar, and go, first be reconciled to your brother," that you too may be numbered among those who are the sum total of the men of war and may say that "not one of us was missing." I say even something further. Unless you are such that you dissent in nothing from the commandments of God nor differ in anything from the evangelical precepts, you will not be able to conquer the enemy, you will not be able to overcome the adversary. For in that very thing in which you dissent, you are already conquered; and by this very thing you are overcome by the devil, in which you are in discord with God. But if you wish to conquer the enemy and to be of the sum total of the warriors, cleave to God and be in concord with him, like the one who said: "Who shall separate us from the love of God? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or the sword?", and again: "Neither life nor death nor things present nor things to come nor height nor depth nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus." Such a one dissents in nothing at all; such a one is able to conquer the Midianites and to slay all the sinners of the earth and to destroy their image from the city of the Lord. And I too, then, ought to destroy the sinners from myself and from the land of my flesh, and to slay fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil concupiscence, and avarice. For these are the sinners of my land, whom I shall at last be able to exterminate and to slay if I do not dissent from the commandments of God; and then I shall truly be worthy to offer gifts to God. "Every vessel of gold," he says, "a collar or a bracelet or a ring or an armlet or a little chain." The collar is the ornament of wisdom. For in Proverbs it is said of wisdom that whoever acquires it may place a golden collar about his neck. The bracelet and the ring are ornaments of the hands, on which the tokens of works are marked; and likewise the armlet. But the little chains declare the connections of word and doctrine. "To make propitiation," he says, "of God for us." If we should say that God is made propitious to men on account of gold, see how absurd, indeed how impious, this is judged to be. For this is reckoned reprehensible even in a good man, if he is appeased by gold received from his inferiors. How much more, then, is it unfitting to think this of God? Whence I think that the rationale of this ecclesiastical exposition stands more firmly, which teaches that by the kinds of gold are signified the virtues of the soul and the deeds of good works, which alone are worthy to be offered to God by men, and for which alone it is fitting that God be made propitious to men. "And Moses and Eleazar the priest," he says, "took the gold from all the commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds, and brought it into the tabernacle of testimony, a memorial for the sons of Israel before the Lord." You see that the things which are said are referred not to visible sight but to the memory of the mind. For blessed is he who remembers that he has done some good work before the Lord and has offered gifts well-pleasing to God, the virtues of the soul and the ornaments of piety.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: That the going forth from Egypt is taken in two ways has already been said often, both by our predecessors and by us. For both when someone is led from the darkness of errors to the light of recognition and is converted from an earthly manner of life to spiritual institutions, he seems to have gone out of Egypt and to have come to the wilderness, namely to that state of life in which, through silence and quiet, he may be exercised by the divine laws and be imbued with heavenly utterances; instructed and directed by these, when he has crossed the Jordan, he may hasten all the way to the land of promise, that is, through the grace of baptism he may come all the way to the evangelical institutions. But we have said that there is also that figure of going forth from Egypt when the soul leaves the darkness of this world and the blindness of bodily nature and is transferred to another age, which is indicated either as the bosom of Abraham, as in Lazarus, or as paradise, as in the thief who believed from the cross; or even if God knows there to be any other places or other dwellings, through which the soul, passing and believing God and arriving all the way to that river which gladdens the city of God, may within it receive the lot of the inheritance promised to the fathers. Therefore, since in a twofold manner, as we have recalled, the going forth from Egypt is designated, and the passage to the desert, and thence the entry to the inheritance of the holy land, let us now see what Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh mean. The inheritance which is handed over through Moses and decreed beyond the Jordan, in the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel, by certain hidden and mystical reasons embraces the figure of the whole human race, or certainly of all men who have come to the recognition of God. Of these, then, some part obtains an inheritance beyond the Jordan through Moses, but a part receives its inheritance across the Jordan and in the land of promise through Joshua. And those indeed to whom the inheritance is decreed beyond the Jordan are the firstborn; although less noble, although not without blame, they are firstborn nonetheless. For Reuben is the firstborn of Jacob; although he defiled his father's bed, he is the firstborn nonetheless. And Gad also, although of a handmaid, yet he too is a firstborn. Manasseh also, whose half-tribe obtains beyond the Jordan, he too, although born of an Egyptian woman, is nevertheless the firstborn. All these, then, are firstborn, and therefore they designate the former people, who receive the lot of inheritance not through Joshua our Lord, but through Moses beyond the Jordan. But consider more diligently also the cause by which the former ones obtain the inheritance both beyond the Jordan and set apart from the rest. "We have," he says, "beasts and much cattle." This, then, is the cause by which the former people could not attain to the inheritance of that land which flows with milk, which abounds with honey, which is a honeycomb beyond every land, nor could it recognize the Word made flesh, because it had many beasts and much cattle. For the animal man could not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God, nor discern them spiritually, because "man, when he was in honor, did not understand; but was compared to the senseless beasts and was made like to them," for which it received its inheritance beyond the streams of the Jordan and made itself a stranger to the holy land. That people, then, received an inheritance through Moses; it received the land of two kings only. For Moses could slay no more than two kings, whose land he divided among peoples having many animals and much cattle. But to those who cross the Jordan, Joshua divides the land; although they too have animals, have cattle, yet not so much as to exclude them, so that they should not cross the Jordan, but together with their women and with their little ones they strive to cross the Jordan and to attain the promises of the fathers. But those, on account of their cattle and beasts and their women and little ones, could not cross the Jordan nor enter the faith of Christ, which is the land of promise.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After these things there follows the account concerning the inheritance of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh; concerning which, purposing to discuss some things, we wish first to alert the diligence of our hearers and to rouse their minds to the contemplation of spiritual understanding. All the things that are said must be weighed not only from the word itself which is spoken, but the person of the speaker also must be greatly considered. For example, if it is a boy who speaks, we fit our minds to the hearing of a boyish utterance, and we expect nothing more in the things that are said than in so far as a boy could perceive. But if he who speaks is a man, we straightway consider whether the things said are worthy of a man. And again, if that man who speaks is learned, we weigh the words also according to the view of his learning. But if he is indeed a man, yet unskilled and an untutored layman, we receive the things said in another way. So likewise, if it be an elder who speaks, and of much and proven skill, inasmuch as he has grown old in learning, there will be held in him a far greater expectation of his words. But why we have premised these things, wishing to expound the account of the inheritance of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, hearken. He who narrates these deeds which we read is neither a boy, such as we described above, nor any such man, nor an elder, nor any human being at all; and, to say something further, neither is he any one of the angels or of the heavenly powers. But, as the tradition of our forefathers holds, the Holy Spirit narrates these things. For whence could Moses narrate either the things that were done from the beginning of the world or the things that were to be done at its end, except through the inspiration of the Spirit of God? Whence could he have prophesied concerning Christ, except by the Holy Spirit speaking? For thus Christ himself renders testimony to him and says: "If you believed Moses, you would surely believe me also; for he wrote concerning me; but if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?" It is established, then, that these things were spoken through the Holy Spirit, and therefore it seems fitting that they be understood according to the dignity, or rather according to the majesty, of the speaker. But I judge it most apt to recall in this place also that, when Abraham heard that rich man set in torments beg him that he might be released and, coming, might admonish his brothers to live piously, lest they too descend into that place of torments, he answered him that "they have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them." He certainly did not mean any men set in the body as Moses and the prophets, but these things which were written through Moses at the dictation of the Spirit of God, these he named Moses. Let someone, then, say: since these things are thus written, if Abraham sends me to the words of Moses, that by reading them I may be able to escape that place of torments, what will it help me toward escaping Gehenna, if I read how the sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh receive an inheritance from Moses across the Jordan, because they had much cattle beyond the other tribes, and how Moses says to them: "See that you do not exasperate God, as did also those ten who were sent with Joshua and Caleb to explore the land," and who said that the land is such and such, and "we cannot take it"; and how to these things the sons of Reuben and the rest with them answered: "Give us this land and its inheritance, and we shall no longer seek within the Jordan a land of inheritance with our brothers, but here we shall leave our beasts and our baggage and our women and our little ones, but our men shall go along and shall cross the Jordan"; and how after these things Moses commends them to Joshua the son of Nun and to Eleazar the priest, the son of Aaron, under this condition, however, that they cross over with the sons of Israel and fight with them against the enemies who were across the Jordan, until the land be freed from them, and then they receive the land which they demanded, of King Sihon and King Og, and to them alone the inheritance beyond the Jordan is given through Moses, but to all the rest the inheritance within the Jordan through Joshua. Let someone, then, say: what do these things profit toward that which Abraham said: "They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them," namely so that those who read and hear these things may not come into that place of torments? Now we have said these things to arouse the minds of the hearers, that they may more vigilantly attend to the things that are read or said, and that in the writings of Moses, with the veil of the letter removed, they may so understand the things that are written that they may find in each and every one of them that things are said which, if they be understood and observed, the hearers may be able not to be led to that place of torment, whither that rich man, who scorned to hear these things which are written in secret, was carried off, but that they may go into the bosom of Abraham, where Lazarus reposes. Let us pray, therefore, to the Lord that the veil may be taken away from our hearts in the reading of the Old Testament, that we may be able to see the things that are hidden and concealed in the writings of Moses, according to the admonition of the prophet who says: "And unless you hear in secret, your soul shall weep." And indeed, that these things are mystical and contain some divine meaning, I think that no one can be in doubt from the things that have been asserted above, however insatiably he be given over to Jewish fables; yet, just as I think no one denies this, so what those things are which are indicated by these narratives, and what the face of realities is which is covered under this veil, to know clearly I think belongs to the Holy Spirit himself, who inspired these things to be written, and to our Lord Jesus Christ, who said of Moses: "For he wrote concerning me," and to the almighty God, whose ancient counsel is indicated to the human race not naked, but veiled in letters. But let us pray from the heart to the Word of God, who is his only-begotten and who reveals the Father to whom he wills, that he may deign to reveal these things also to us: for in these there are mysteries of the promises, which he promised to those who love him, that we too may know the things that have been given to us by God. But do you also help us in your prayers and diligently attend, not so much to us who speak as to the Lord who enlightens those whom he shall find worthy of his enlightenment. By the contemplation of these things may he deign to give a word to us also in the opening of our mouth. But come now, if you have lifted up your hearts to the Lord and have sought the illumination of his holy word, let us come to searching out the meaning of the things which seem to lie hidden.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Yet Moses rebukes them and says to the sons of Reuben and to the sons of Gad: "Your brothers shall go to battle, and will you sit here? And why do you pervert the hearts of the sons of Israel, that they should not cross into the land which the Lord gives them?" And when he had rebuked them with words of this kind, "there came," he says, "to him the sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad and said: We shall build sheepfolds here for our sheep and for our cattle, and cities for our encumbrances, and we, armed, will advance in the first company before the sons of Israel, until we lead them into their own place." And promising these things they mollified Moses, so that he himself commended them to Joshua and to Eleazar. For thus it is written: "And Moses brought them to Eleazar the priest and to Joshua the son of Nun and to the leaders of the families of the tribes of Israel. And Moses said to them: If the sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad cross the Jordan with you, every one armed for battle before the Lord, and you obtain the land in your sight, you shall give them the land of Gilead for a possession." The name of "land," placed in the divine Scriptures, we find with diverse significations; and first indeed this land which we inhabit was not from the beginning called land, but "dry"; and after this, that which had first been called "dry" received the name of land; just as this visible heaven too was not from the beginning called heaven, but first "firmament," and afterward it was named also by the term "heaven." Yet in the beginning of creation God is said to have made heaven and earth, and afterward the dry, and afterward the firmament. But do you wish to know that "dry" is one thing in the Scriptures, and "land" another? Hear the prophet Haggai saying: "Yet once more I will shake heaven and earth and the sea and the dry land." You see how the prophet places "land" as one thing, "dry" as another. But also in many places of Scripture we find "land" named praiseworthily, but "dry" we do not easily read placed praiseworthily. For Adam too is thrust down into this place, as one culpable after his sin, which was named "dry." For before that he was not in the dry, but in the land; for paradise is not in the dry but in the land. But also what the Lord promises to the meek in the Gospel is not the dry, but the land. "Blessed," he says, "are the meek, for they shall inherit the land." And likewise in the Gospel the seed which gives fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold is said to be land, not dry. And I think that there is a certain progress from the dry to coming to the land, just as there was also a certain progress that this land was called dry. For all of us, so long as we are unfruitful and bring forth no fruit of righteousness, none of chastity, none of piety, are dry. But if we begin to cultivate ourselves and to rouse our sluggish minds to the fruit of the virtues, we are made land out of dry, which, having received the seeds of the word of God, multiplies them with a glad harvest. There is, then, in the kingdom of God also a certain land which is promised to the meek, and a land which is named "of the living," and a land placed on high, concerning which the prophet says to the righteous man: "And he shall exalt you, that you may inherit the land." The inheritance, then, of this land, after it has gone forth from the Egypt of this world, the soul believing in God obtains; and in one place indeed those who lived under the law, but in another those who were dispensed through the faith and grace of Jesus Christ. Yet these who seem to be dispensed first and through Moses will not obtain the inheritance decreed to them until they too cross over with those whom Joshua dispenses, and fight with these against the enemies, and settle them in their seats, and thus they themselves shall obtain the inheritance which they merited with Moses as leader.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But unless these things be proved from the divine Scriptures, they will seem fables. Let Paul, then, be brought forward as a suitable witness of these things, who in the epistle to the Hebrews, where he describes all those fathers and patriarchs and prophets who by faith pleased God, after the enumeration of them all, in his final conclusion says thus concerning them: "And all these, having received the testimony of faith, did not obtain the promises, God providing something better for us, that they should not be perfected without us." As if those nine and a half tribes were to say concerning those two and a half tribes that for this reason they did not receive the promise of that land which was decreed to them beyond the Jordan through Moses, God providing something better for us, that they should not be perfected without us. Therefore for this reason they cross over with us armed for battle and help us in warring, in vanquishing the enemies. But those cross over who are armed, who are strong men and mighty; but all the rest, the cowardly and unwarlike band, remain beyond the Jordan. But if any among them are strong men, having left their animals and cattle and all their encumbrances, they fight against the enemy together with us, until our enemies be conquered, until we take the inheritance of the good land, the land of honey and milk. For who doubts that all the saints among the fathers both help us by their prayers and confirm us by the deeds they have done and exhort us by their examples, but also by their volumes, through those things which they have left written for our remembrance, teaching us and instructing us how we must contend against the hostile powers and how the struggles of the contests must be endured? They fight, then, for us, and they themselves advance first before us, armed. For having them as an example and seeing their brave deeds through the Spirit, we are armed for the spiritual battle and contend against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Thus, finally, those who serve as soldiers under Joshua as leader slay thirty and more kings and receive their lands by the lot of inheritance. For when the spiritual forces of wickedness have been driven out from the heavenly places, they receive the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, our Lord Jesus dividing it.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: There can be seen also yet a third mode of exposition, so that among the sons of Israel, that is, among the people of the Church, there are understood to be certain spiritual ones, who within the Jordan receive the inheritance of the land flowing with milk and honey, namely receiving the sweetness of wisdom and knowledge, whose land is surrounded and watered by the river of God, which is filled with the waters of divine understanding. But others are carnal, who abound in beasts and cattle, that is, in gross and dull senses; such as were those of whom the Apostle said: "Are you so senseless that, having begun in the Spirit, you now are perfected in the flesh?" and: "O senseless Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth?" But each one of us also, unless he arms himself and, having cast off the brutish and beastlike senses, hastens to spiritual understanding, will remain beyond the Jordan and will not be able to advance through the river of wisdom, which gladdens the city of God, that is, the soul capable of God; he will not attain the interior things of the Lord's utterances, which are "sweeter than honey and the honeycomb," but he will attain only that land in which the two kings were slain, where it is said to him: "I judged myself to know nothing among you except Christ Jesus, and him crucified." But he who has been able to cross the Jordan and penetrate to the interior things, there following Jesus our Lord will slay thirty and more kings—those, perhaps, of whom it is said: "The kings of the earth stood by and the princes gathered together into one against the Lord and against his Christ"—and when these kings have been driven out and cast down, he will recognize the more secret mysteries, until he come even to that place where the seat of God is and Jerusalem the city of the living God, not this one which serves with its sons on earth, but that heavenly one which is free and is the mother of us all; to whose inheritance may he deign to lead us, our leader and Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory unto the ages of ages. Amen.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But first of all, consider the meaning of the mystery, which anyone who observes it carefully will find in the Scriptures: that in the going out of the children of Israel from Egypt there were forty-two stations; and again, the coming of our Lord and Savior into this world is traced through forty-two generations. For thus the Evangelist Matthew recounts, saying: "From Abraham until David the king, fourteen generations, and from David until the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon until Christ fourteen generations." These forty-two stations of the generations, then, which Christ made in descending into the Egypt of this world, make up by the very same number the forty-two stations of those who go up from Egypt. And Moses set it down well and observantly, saying: "The children of Israel went up with their power." And what is their power, if not Christ himself, who is the power of God? He therefore who goes up, goes up together with him who came down to us from thence, so that he might arrive there whence that one descended not by necessity but by condescension, that the saying might be true which was spoken, that "he who descended is himself also the one who ascended." Therefore in forty-two stations the children of Israel arrive at the beginning of the taking of their inheritance. And the beginning of taking the inheritance was where Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh receive the land of Gilead. And so the number of Christ's descent through forty-two fathers according to the flesh, as though descending to us through forty-two stations, matches the ascent of the children of Israel through just as many stations up to the beginning of the promised inheritance. But if you have understood how great a mystery this number of the descent and the ascent contains, come now, and let us begin to ascend through those things by which Christ descended, and to make that first station which he made last, namely that by which he was born of a virgin; and let this be the first station for us who wish to go out of Egypt, in which, having left behind the worship of idols and of demons — not the veneration of gods — we believe that Christ was born of a virgin and of the Holy Spirit, and that the Word made flesh came into this world. After this, let us now strive to advance and to ascend to each and every degree of faith and of the virtues; and if we linger over each of these long enough until we come to perfection, we shall be said to have made a station in each of the degrees of the virtues, until, as we reach the very summit of instruction and of progress, the promised inheritance may be fulfilled for us.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the soul too, when it sets out from the Egypt of this life, that it may make its way to the land of promise, necessarily journeys along certain particular roads and, as we have said, completes certain fixed encampments. Mindful of these, I believe, the prophet said: "These things I have remembered, and I have poured out my soul upon myself, for I shall pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God." These are the encampments, and these the tabernacles, of which in another place also he says: "How lovely are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord." Therefore in yet another place the same prophet says: "My soul has been a great wanderer." Understand then, if you can, what these wanderings of the soul are, in which with a certain groaning and grief it laments that it wanders too long. But the understanding of these things grows dull and is darkened while as yet the soul wanders; but then it will be more truly instructed and will more truly understand what was the reason of its pilgrimage, when it has returned to its rest, that is, to its homeland, paradise; and gazing on this under a mystery the prophet said: "Return, O my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you." But in the meantime it wanders and pursues its journey and completes its encampments, dispensed through these things, without doubt for the sake of some benefit, by the providences of God, as also in a certain place he says: "I afflicted you, and fed you with manna in the desert, which your fathers did not know, that it might be discerned what is in your heart." These, then, are the encampments by which the journey is made from the lands to heaven. And who will be found so fit and so privy to the divine secrets that he can describe the encampments of this journey and ascent of the soul, and set forth either the labors or the rests of each place? For how should he relate that after the first and the second and the third encampment Pharaoh still pursues, the Egyptians pursue, and, though they do not overtake, yet they give chase, and, though they are drowned, yet they have given chase? How should he declare that the people of God, once made safe, after several encampments first sang a song, saying: "Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored; horse and rider he has cast into the sea"? But these things, as I have said, whoever should dare to open up through the individual encampments and, from the contemplation of the names, to conjecture also the qualities of the encampments — I do not know whether either the understanding of the one who speaks would suffice for the weight of the mysteries, or the hearing of the listeners would grasp it. For how should either the onset of the war of the Amalekites be explained, or the various temptations, and how should those be narrated whose limbs fell in the desert, and that it was not at all the sons of Israel, but the sons of the sons of Israel, who were able to reach the holy land, and that all that old people fell, who had had their converse and habitation with the Egyptians, while only the new people, who knew not the Egyptians, reached the kingdom, apart from the priests and the Levites? For if anyone has been able to place himself in the order of the priests and the Levites, if anyone has been able to have no portion in any lands, but the Lord alone, that man does not fall in the desert, but reaches the land of promise. Hence you too, if you wish not to fall in the desert, but to reach the promises of the fathers, have no lot in the land, and let there be nothing common to you with the earth. Let your portion be the Lord alone, and you will never fall. The ascent, then, is made from Egypt to the land of promise, through which, by mystical descriptions, as I have said, we are taught the ascent of the soul to heaven and the sacrament of the resurrection from the dead.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now names are also assigned to the resting-places. For it did not seem fitting that every place under heaven should be called by the names of mountains or valleys or plains, while that ascent, by which the soul ascends to the kingdom of God, should not have the names of its own resting-places. It has names of resting-places fitted with mystical designations; it has too as its guide not Moses — for he himself did not know where he was going — but the pillar of fire and the cloud, that is, the Son of God and the Holy Spirit, just as in another place the prophet says: "the Lord himself was leading them." Such, then, will be the ascent of the blessed soul, when all the Egyptians and Amalekites and all who had assailed it have been drowned; so that, passing on through each and every resting-place — those many, namely, which are said to be with the Father — it may be enlightened yet more, and, coming from one to another, may ever gain greater increases of illumination, until it grow accustomed to endure the gaze of that true light itself, which enlightens every man, and to bear the radiance of the true majesty. But if we return to that second exposition which we mentioned above, and understand the advances of the soul set in this life to be taught through these things — the soul which, converted from a gentile manner of life, follows not so much Moses as the law of God, and not Aaron, but that priest who abides forever — before it comes to perfection, it dwells in the desert, where, namely, it may be trained in the precepts of the Lord and where its faith may be proved through temptations. And there, when it has overcome one temptation and its faith has been proved in it, from thence it comes to another, and passes as it were from one resting-place to another; and there, when it has held fast to the things that have befallen it and has borne them faithfully, it proceeds to another; and thus, through each and every trial of life and faith, the soul's advances are said to have resting-places, in which through each single thing increases of the virtues are sought. And there is fulfilled in these that which is written: "they shall go from strength to strength," until one arrives at the last — nay rather, at the highest — degree of the virtues, and the river of God is crossed and the promised inheritance is received.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Using this twofold exposition, therefore, we ought to consider this whole order of the encampments that has been recited, so that from both there may come a progress for our soul, as we learn from these things either how this life, which follows the law of God through conversion from error, ought to be conducted, or how great is the expectation of the future hope that is promised through the resurrection. For thus I think that in these things which are read there is taught an understanding worthy of the laws of the Holy Spirit. For to know in that desert what that place is called where, for example, the sons of Israel, then passing through, encamped — what usefulness does this bring to me, or what progress will be conferred by this upon those who read and meditate on the law of God day and night? — especially since we see that there was such great care on the Lord's part concerning the recording of these encampments that a description of them was inserted a second time into the divine laws. For these names were commemorated, though in some cases altered, already then, when the sons of Israel are said, through each place, to have set out from that place and to have encamped in that place; but now again they are ordered to be described by Moses through the word of the Lord. Hence this very fact, that this description is repeated a second time, seems to me quite fittingly suited to the mystery of the exposition which we have proposed; for they are repeated twice in order to show the two ways of the soul: one, by which, placed in the flesh, it is exercised in the virtues through the law of God, and ascending through certain steps of progress it advances, as we have said, from virtue to virtue and uses these very advances as encampments; but the other, by which, after the resurrection, being about to ascend to the heavens, it does not suddenly or importunately climb to the summit, but is led through many encampments, in which, illuminated through each one and always receiving an increase of splendor, made bright in each encampment by the light of wisdom, it may come at last to the very Father of lights. "The sons of Israel therefore went out," he says, "with their power." There was with them that power which had said: "I will go down with you into Egypt"; and because this power was with them, therefore the prophet says: "and there was none feeble in their tribes." "And they went out by the hand of Moses and Aaron." For going out of Egypt the one hand of Moses is not enough; the hand of Aaron also is required. Moses indicates the knowledge of the law, Aaron the skill of sacrificing and offering to God. It is needful, therefore, that we who go out of Egypt should have as fruit not only the knowledge of the law and of faith, but also of works, by which God is pleased. For this reason both the hand of Moses and of Aaron is mentioned, that by the hands you may understand works. For indeed, if going out of Egypt and being converted to God I cast away pride, I have sacrificed a bull to the Lord through the hands of Aaron. If I destroy wantonness and lasciviousness, I shall believe that I have slaughtered a he-goat to the Lord by the hands of Aaron. If I conquer lust, a calf; if folly, I shall be seen to have offered a sheep. Thus therefore, when the vices of the soul are purged, the hand of Aaron works in us; and the hand of Moses is with us, when we are illuminated from the law to understand these very things. And therefore both hands are necessary for those going out of Egypt, so that there may be found in them the perfection not only of faith and knowledge, but also of acts and works; and yet these two are not two hands, but one. For the Lord led them out "by the hand of Moses and Aaron," and not "by the hands of Moses and Aaron"; for the work of both hands is one, and one the fulfillment of perfection.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But lest this kind of exposition, which runs through the meanings of the Hebrew names, should seem to those unacquainted with the properties of that language to be forced and violently wrested out, we will give a comparison also in our own tongue, by which the reasoning of this sequence may become clear. In the schoolroom, where boys take up their first rudiments, some are called "alphabet-learners," others "syllable-learners," others "word-learners," and others are now called "reckoners"; and when we have heard these names, from them we recognize what progress there is in the boys. Likewise also in the liberal studies, when we have heard someone recite a passage, or an address, or a panegyric, or the other exercises in their order, from the name of the exercise we perceive the young man's progress. How then, even through these things which are recorded as the names of places, as it were of exercises, should we not believe that the progress of learners in divine instruction can be indicated? And just as those who linger over each several subject of learning seem, as it were, to make certain resting-places in them, and to advance from one to another and from that one again to yet another, so also here why should not the name of the "stations," and the advance from one to another and from one again to another, be believed to indicate the progress of the mind and to signify the increase of the virtues?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now let us come to the beginning of the very reading that was recited, so that with the Lord's help we may be able, even if not with perfect clarity, yet at least in summary, to gather and explain their meaning. He says, then: "And these are the stages of the children of Israel, from the time they went out of the land of Egypt with their power by the hand of Moses and Aaron. And Moses wrote down their settings-out and their stages by the word of the Lord," and so forth. You have heard that Moses wrote these things by the word of the Lord. And why did the Lord will these things to be written? That this writing of the stages which the children of Israel made might be of some profit to us, or that it might be of no profit? And who would dare to say that the things which are written by the word of the Lord have no usefulness and confer nothing of salvation, but merely narrate an event that happened — one that indeed passed by at that time, and from the report of which nothing now reaches us? This opinion is impious and foreign to the catholic faith, and belongs only to those who deny that the one sole wise God, of the law and of the gospels, is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. What, therefore, the faithful understanding ought to perceive from these stages, let us attempt to treat in summary, as far as the time allows. In the earlier discussion, when the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt had furnished us with occasion to speak of it, we said that each person can be seen to go out spiritually from Egypt in two ways: either when, forsaking the life of the Gentiles, we come to the knowledge of the divine law, or when the soul departs from the dwelling of this body. To both, then, do these stages look which Moses now describes by the word of the Lord. For concerning those stages which the soul, stripped of the body — nay rather, clothed again with its own body — is to inhabit, the Lord declared in the gospel, saying: "There are many mansions with the Father; otherwise I would have told you: I go and prepare a mansion for you." There are, then, those many mansions which lead to the Father, in each of which what cause, what usefulness the soul's lingering receives, or what instruction or illumination, He alone knows, the Father of the age to come, who says of Himself: "I am the door; no one comes to the Father except through me." He, perhaps, in each of these mansions will become a door for each soul, so that through Him it may enter and through Him go out and find pastures, and again enter into another, and thence into yet another mansion, until it comes to the Father Himself. But we, almost forgetful of our preface, have suddenly lifted your hearing to lofty and exalted things. Rather, let us return to those things that are done among us and within us. In Egypt were the children of Israel; they were afflicted in the works of Pharaoh the king with clay and brick, until, groaning, they cried out to the Lord, and He, hearing their groaning, sent to them His word through Moses and led them out of Egypt. And we too, therefore, when we were in Egypt — I mean in the errors of this world and in the darkness of ignorance, working the works of the devil in the desires and pleasures of the flesh — the Lord had mercy on our affliction and sent His Word, His only-begotten Son, to rescue us from the ignorance of error and lead us to the light of the divine law.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And Moses wrote down, it says, their completions and their stations by the word of the Lord. He wrote these things, therefore, by the word of the Lord, so that we, reading and seeing how many departures and how many stations lie ahead of us for the journey that leads to the kingdom, might prepare ourselves for this way; and, considering the road that lies before us, might not allow the time of our life to be consumed sluggishly or slackly, lest perchance, while we linger among the vanities of this world and take delight in each and every thing that comes to sight or hearing, or even to touch and smell and taste, the days slip away, the time passes by, and we fail to accomplish the traversing of the whole span of the journey before us, and we give out midway, and there befall us that which is reported of certain ones who could not arrive, but whose limbs fell in the desert. We are on a journey, therefore, and we have come into this world for this purpose: that we might pass from virtue to virtue, not that we might remain on the earth for the sake of earthly things, like that man too who said, "I will pull down my barns and build others larger, and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many good things laid up for many years; eat, drink, be merry" — lest perchance the Lord say to us also, as to him: "You fool, this night your soul shall be taken from you." He did not say "in this day," but "in this night." For here too a man is destroyed in the night, like the firstborn of the Egyptians, as one who has loved the world and its darkness and has been a partaker of the rulers of this world of this darkness. And this world is called darkness and night on account of those who live in ignorance and do not receive the light of truth. But such as these do not set out from Rameses nor cross over to Succoth.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Yet let us first see when the children of Israel set out from Rameses. "In the first month," it says, "on the fifteenth day of the month." By the Lord's command they had kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month in Egypt, slaughtering the lamb on the day before they set out, and in a certain sense they kept the beginning of the festival while still situated in Egypt. On the following day, then, which is the first day of unleavened bread, on the fifteenth day of the first month, they set out from Rameses and come to Succoth, that they might there keep the day of the festival of unleavened bread. "Who is wise, and shall understand these things? Prudent, and shall know them?" — nay rather, who is there who knows even these things in part, as the Apostle says: "We know in part, and we prophesy in part"? Who understands how we too keep festal days in part, so that "no one may judge us in respect of a portion of a feast day, or of a new moon, or of a sabbath"? For every feast day that is kept on earth by men is kept in part, not in whole nor with the full and perfect title of festivity; but when you have gone out of that Egypt, then there will be for you a perfect festivity, then you will attend to the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth unto perfection, then you will keep the day of Pentecost in the wilderness, and then perhaps for the first time you will receive the heavenly food of manna, and you will keep each of the several festivities of which we have already spoken above, as far as we were able. Yet know that after that Passover which was made in Egypt, we find the Passover observed once in the desert, when the law was given, and another, as we have noted, in Numbers, and after these it is nowhere kept, save in the land of promise. Therefore, on the fifteenth day of the first month, on the day following the Passover, which is the first day of unleavened bread, the children of Israel set out from Rameses "with a lofty hand," it says, "in the sight of all the Egyptians." What is the lofty hand? For elsewhere too it says: "Let your hand be exalted." Where there is no human work nor earthly, but it is divine, there it is called a lofty hand. For it has already often been said that by "hand" a work is understood. "With a lofty hand," therefore, "in the sight of all the Egyptians" they set out.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And the Egyptians," it says, "were burying their dead"; the dead were burying their dead, but the living were following the Lord their God. After this it is said that: "and upon their gods the Lord took vengeance." But in Exodus too it says thus: "and upon all the gods of the Egyptians the Lord shall take vengeance." Here, however, it says that the Lord took vengeance upon them. There are certain beings which are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, the Apostle says. But in the Psalms too it is said: "all the gods of the nations are demons." Therefore it is not the images, but the demons who preside over the images, that he calls gods, upon whom the Lord took vengeance. But I should like to inquire how God takes vengeance upon the demons, since assuredly the day of vengeance and of judgment has not yet come. But I think that this vengeance is wrought upon the demons when he who had been deceived by them into worshipping idols, being converted through the word of the Lord, worships the Lord; and from the very work of conversion vengeance is dealt upon him who had deceived. Likewise also, if he who had been deceived by the demons into fornicating is converted to chastity, loves purity, and weeps that he had gone astray, the demon is burned and set aflame by the tears of his repentance, and thus vengeance is dealt upon the author of the deception. Likewise too, if anyone returns from pride to humility, from luxury to frugality, through each of these things he scourges and torments the demons who had deceived him into them. With how great torments do you suppose they are driven, if they see someone, according to the word of the Lord, sell all his goods that he possesses and give to the poor, and take up his cross and follow Christ?
